## Bereshit — בְּרֵאשִׁית (Genesis 1:1–6:8)

### Reading text

<sup>1:1</sup> When God began to create the heavens and the earth — <sup>1:2</sup> the earth was desolate and empty, with darkness over the face of the deep and the wind of God hovering over the face of the waters — <sup>1:3</sup> God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. <sup>1:4</sup> God saw that the light was good, and God separated the light from the darkness. <sup>1:5</sup> God called the light day, and the darkness he called night. There was evening and there was morning, one day.

<sup>1:6</sup> God said, "Let there be an expanse in the middle of the waters, and let it divide water from water." <sup>1:7</sup> God made the expanse and divided the water below the expanse from the water above the expanse. And it was so. <sup>1:8</sup> God called the expanse Sky. There was evening and there was morning, a second day.

<sup>1:9</sup> God said, "Let the waters under the sky be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear." And it was so. <sup>1:10</sup> God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters he called Seas. God saw that it was good. <sup>1:11</sup> God said, "Let the earth sprout green growth, plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit, each of its own kind, with its seed in it, on the earth." And it was so. <sup>1:12</sup> The earth brought forth green growth, plants yielding seed, each of its own kind, and trees bearing fruit with its seed in it, each of its own kind. God saw that it was good. <sup>1:13</sup> There was evening and there was morning, a third day.

<sup>1:14</sup> God said, "Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to separate the day from the night, and let them be for signs and for appointed times, and for days and years, <sup>1:15</sup> and let them be lights in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth." And it was so. <sup>1:16</sup> God made the two great lights, the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars. <sup>1:17</sup> God set them in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth. <sup>1:18</sup> and to rule over the day and the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. God saw that it was good. <sup>1:19</sup> There was evening and there was morning, a fourth day.

<sup>1:20</sup> And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the sky." <sup>1:21</sup> And God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarmed, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. <sup>1:22</sup> And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let the birds multiply on the land." <sup>1:23</sup> And there was evening and there was morning, a fifth day.

<sup>1:24</sup> God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures, each according to its kind: livestock and crawling things and the wild animals of the earth, each according to its kind." And so it was. <sup>1:25</sup> God made the wild animals of the earth, each according to its kind, and the livestock according to its kind, and every crawling thing of the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good. <sup>1:26</sup> God said, "Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness, and let them rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and the livestock and all the earth and every crawling thing that crawls on the earth." <sup>1:27</sup> God created the human in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. <sup>1:28</sup> God blessed them, and God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and every living thing that crawls on the earth." <sup>1:29</sup> God said, "See, I have given you every plant bearing seed that is on the surface of the whole earth, and every tree that has in it fruit of a tree bearing seed. It shall be yours for food." <sup>1:30</sup> And to every wild animal of the earth and to every bird of the sky and to everything that crawls on the earth, in which there is a living soul, I have given every green plant for food. And so it was. <sup>1:31</sup> God saw everything that he had made, and indeed it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.

<sup>2:1</sup> So the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their host. <sup>2:2</sup> On the seventh day God finished his work that he had made, and on the seventh day he rested from all his work that he had made. <sup>2:3</sup> God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he rested from all his work that God created in order to make.

<sup>2:4</sup> These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, on the day the LORD God made earth and heavens. <sup>2:5</sup> No tree of the field was yet on the earth, and no plant of the field had yet sprung up, for the LORD God had not sent rain on the earth, and there was no human to work the ground. <sup>2:6</sup> But a mist rose from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground. <sup>2:7</sup> Then the LORD God formed the human out of dust from the ground, and blew into his nostrils the breath of life, and the human became a living being. <sup>2:8</sup> The LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and put there the human whom he had formed. <sup>2:9</sup> The LORD God made grow from the ground every tree desirable to look at and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. <sup>2:10</sup> A river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides and becomes four headwaters. <sup>2:11</sup> The name of the first is Pishon; it is the one that encircles the whole land of Havilah, where the gold is. <sup>2:12</sup> The gold of that land is good; bdellium is there, and onyx stone. <sup>2:13</sup> The name of the second river is Gihon; it is the one that encircles the whole land of Cush. <sup>2:14</sup> The name of the third river is the Tigris; it is the one that flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates. <sup>2:15</sup> The LORD God took the human and set him in the garden of Eden to work it and guard it. <sup>2:16</sup> The LORD God commanded the human, saying: "You may eat freely from every tree of the garden. <sup>2:17</sup> But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you must not eat from it, for on the day you eat from it you will surely die. <sup>2:18</sup> The LORD God said, "It is not good for the human to be alone; I will make for him a helper corresponding to him." <sup>2:19</sup> The LORD God formed from the ground every animal of the field and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the human to see what he would call it. Whatever the human called each living creature, that was its name. <sup>2:20</sup> The human gave names to all the livestock and the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for himself the human did not find a helper corresponding to him. <sup>2:21</sup> Then the LORD God cast a deep sleep upon the human, and he slept; and he took one of his sides and closed up flesh in its place. <sup>2:22</sup> The LORD God built the side that he had taken from the human into a woman, and brought her to the human. <sup>2:23</sup> Then the human said, "This one, this time, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. This one shall be called woman, for from man this one was taken." <sup>2:24</sup> Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh. <sup>2:25</sup> The two of them were naked, the human and his wife, and they were not ashamed. <sup>3:1</sup> Now the serpent was shrewder than every wild animal that the LORD God had made. It said to the woman, “Is it really so that God said, ‘You must not eat from any tree of the garden’?” <sup>3:2</sup> The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat from the fruit of the trees of the garden.” <sup>3:3</sup> As for the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God said, “You must not eat from it, and you must not touch it, or you might die.” <sup>3:4</sup> The serpent said to the woman, “You will certainly not die.” <sup>3:5</sup> For God knows that on the day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like divine beings, knowing good and evil. <sup>3:6</sup> The woman saw that the tree was good for eating, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was desirable for gaining insight. She took some of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband with her, and he ate. <sup>3:7</sup> Then the eyes of the two of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths. <sup>3:8</sup> They heard the sound of the LORD God walking about in the garden at the breeze of the day, and the human and his wife hid from the LORD God among the trees of the garden. <sup>3:9</sup> The LORD God called to the human and said to him, "Where are you?" <sup>3:10</sup> He said, "I heard your sound in the garden, and I was afraid because I am naked, and I hid." <sup>3:11</sup> He said, "Who told you that you are naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?" <sup>3:12</sup> The human said, "The woman whom you put with me, she gave me from the tree, and I ate." <sup>3:13</sup> The LORD God said to the woman, "What is this you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate." <sup>3:14</sup> The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you more than all the livestock and more than all the wild animals of the field. On your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life." <sup>3:15</sup> I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will strike you on the head, and you will strike him on the heel.

<sup>3:16</sup> To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain and your pregnancy; in pain you will bear children. Your desire is for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

<sup>3:17</sup> And to Adam he said, “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You will not eat from it,’ cursed is the ground because of you; in toil you will eat of it all the days of your life. <sup>3:18</sup> It will sprout thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the plants of the field. <sup>3:19</sup> By the sweat of your face you will eat bread until you return to the ground, for from it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you will return. <sup>3:20</sup> The human called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all the living. <sup>3:21</sup> The LORD God made tunics of skin for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.

<sup>3:22</sup> The LORD God said, "Look, the human has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever." <sup>3:23</sup> So the LORD God expelled him from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken. <sup>3:24</sup> He drove out the human, and east of the garden of Eden he stationed the cherubim and the flame of the turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.

<sup>4:1</sup> Now the human had known Eve his wife, and she had conceived and borne Cain, and she said, "I have acquired a man with the LORD." <sup>4:2</sup> She went on to bear his brother, Abel. Abel was a herder of flocks, and Cain was a worker of the ground. <sup>4:3</sup> At the end of a year, Cain brought an offering of the fruit of the ground to the LORD. <sup>4:4</sup> And Abel brought, he too, some of the firstlings of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD turned to Abel and to his offering, <sup>4:5</sup> but to Cain and to his offering he did not turn. And Cain was very angry, and his face fell. <sup>4:6</sup> The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?" <sup>4:7</sup> Is it not so that if you do well, there is forgiveness, and if you do not do well, at the door sin crouches? Its desire is for you, but you can rule over it. <sup>4:8</sup> Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him. <sup>4:9</sup> The LORD said to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He said, "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?" <sup>4:10</sup> He said, "What have you done? Listen: the blood of your brother is crying out to me from the ground." <sup>4:11</sup> And now you are cursed from the ground, which opened its mouth to take your brother's blood from your hand. <sup>4:12</sup> When you work the ground, it will no longer give you its strength. You shall be a restless wanderer on the earth. <sup>4:13</sup> Cain said to the LORD, "My punishment is too great to bear." <sup>4:14</sup> Look, you have driven me out today from the face of the ground, and from your presence I will be hidden. I will be restless and wandering on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me. <sup>4:15</sup> Then the LORD said to him, "Therefore, whoever kills Cain—! After seven generations vengeance will be taken." And the LORD set a sign for Cain, so that no one who found him would strike him down. <sup>4:16</sup> Then Cain went out from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. <sup>4:17</sup> Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. He was building a city, and he named the city after his son Enoch. <sup>4:18</sup> To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech. <sup>4:19</sup> Lamech took for himself two wives: the name of the first was Adah, and the name of the second Zillah. <sup>4:20</sup> Adah bore Jabal; he was the first of those who live in tents and have livestock. <sup>4:21</sup> His brother's name was Jubal; he was the first of all who handle the lyre and the pipe. <sup>4:22</sup> Zillah too bore Tubal-cain, who sharpened every tool of the craft in bronze and iron; and Tubal-cain's sister was Naamah. <sup>4:23</sup> Lamech said to his wives, "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; wives of Lamech, listen to my speech: have I killed a man by my wounding, a boy by my bruising?" <sup>4:24</sup> For if vengeance is taken on Cain sevenfold, then on Lamech seventy-seven. <sup>4:25</sup> Adam was intimate once more with his wife, and she bore a son and named him Seth, "for God has appointed me another offspring in place of Abel, because Cain killed him." <sup>4:26</sup> To Seth, too, a son was born, and he named him Enosh. Then people began to call on the name of the LORD.

<sup>5:1</sup> This is the record of the descendants of Adam. When God created Adam, he made him in the likeness of God. <sup>5:2</sup> Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called their name Adam, on the day they were created.

<sup>5:3</sup> Adam lived one hundred thirty years, and he fathered a son in his likeness, according to his image, and named him Seth. <sup>5:4</sup> The days of Adam after he fathered Seth were eight hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:5</sup> So all the days of Adam that he lived were nine hundred thirty years, and he died.

<sup>5:6</sup> Seth lived one hundred and five years, and he fathered Enosh. <sup>5:7</sup> After he fathered Enosh, Seth lived eight hundred and seven years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:8</sup> All the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years, and he died.

<sup>5:9</sup> Enosh lived ninety years, and he fathered Kenan. <sup>5:10</sup> After he fathered Kenan, Enosh lived eight hundred and fifteen years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:11</sup> All the days of Enosh were nine hundred and five years, and he died.

<sup>5:12</sup> Kenan lived seventy years, and he fathered Mahalalel. <sup>5:13</sup> After he fathered Mahalalel, Kenan lived eight hundred and forty years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:14</sup> All the days of Kenan were nine hundred and ten years, and he died.

<sup>5:15</sup> Mahalalel lived sixty-five years, and he fathered Jared. <sup>5:16</sup> After he fathered Jared, Mahalalel lived eight hundred and thirty years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:17</sup> All the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred and ninety-five years, and he died.

<sup>5:18</sup> Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years, and fathered Enoch. <sup>5:19</sup> Jared lived, after he fathered Enoch, for eight hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:20</sup> All the days of Jared were nine hundred and sixty-two years, and he died.

<sup>5:21</sup> Enoch lived sixty-five years, and fathered Methuselah. <sup>5:22</sup> Enoch walked with God, after he fathered Methuselah, for three hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:23</sup> All the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. <sup>5:24</sup> Enoch walked with God, and he was no more, for God took him.

<sup>5:25</sup> Methuselah lived one hundred eighty-seven years, and he fathered Lamech. <sup>5:26</sup> Methuselah lived, after he fathered Lamech, seven hundred eighty-two years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:27</sup> All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty-nine years, and he died.

<sup>5:28</sup> Lamech lived one hundred eighty-two years, and he fathered a son. <sup>5:29</sup> He named him Noah, saying, "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the toil of our hands, from the ground that the LORD has cursed." <sup>5:30</sup> Lamech lived, after he fathered Noah, five hundred ninety-five years, and he fathered sons and daughters. <sup>5:31</sup> All the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy-seven years, and he died.

<sup>5:32</sup> When Noah was five hundred years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth. <sup>6:1</sup> When humankind began to multiply over the surface of the ground and daughters were born to them, <sup>6:2</sup> The sons of the rulers saw that the daughters of humankind were beautiful, and they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose. <sup>6:3</sup> Then the LORD said, "My spirit will not contend over humankind for long, since they are also flesh; their days will be one hundred and twenty years." <sup>6:4</sup> The giants were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, whenever the sons of the rulers came to the daughters of humankind and they bore children to them. They were the warriors of old, the men of renown.

<sup>6:5</sup> The LORD saw that the evil of the human was great on the earth, and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil all day long. <sup>6:6</sup> The LORD regretted that he had made the human on the earth, and was grieved in his heart. <sup>6:7</sup> The LORD said, "I will wipe out the human whom I created from the face of the ground, from human to beast, to creeping thing, and to the birds of the sky, for I regret that I made them." <sup>6:8</sup> But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.

### Bereshit by verse

#### Genesis 1:1

> בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים אֵ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם וְאֵ֥ת הָאָֽרֶץ׃

**When God began to create the heavens and the earth —**

Literal: in-beginning-of created God [object-marker] the-heavens and-[object-marker] the-earth

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית | in the beginning of — בְּרֵאשִׁית is pointed as a noun that can be read in the construct state, 'in the beginning of (God's) creating'. The pack parses it as absolute; the data is kept and the construct reading is argued from Rashi and Ibn Ezra. | ב: in, with, by + רֵאשִׁית | ראשׁ | preposition + noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 1.a |
| בָּרָ֣א | created — Qal perfect, 3rd masculine singular of בָּרָא; the verb has God alone as subject in the Qal. | בָּרָא | ברא | verb (qal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal |
| אֱלֹהִ֑ים | God — plural in form (אֱלֹהִים) but takes a singular verb (בָּרָא). | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| אֵ֥ת | (object marker) — אֵת marks the definite direct object. | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם | the heavens — שָׁמַיִם has a dual-looking plural ending and is always plural in Hebrew. | ה: the + שָׁמַיִם | שׁמה | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 1.a |
| וְאֵ֥ת | and (object marker) — וְאֵת: the conjunction repeats the object marker before the second object. | ו: and + אֵת | אות | conjunction + particle (direct object marker) |  |
| הָאָֽרֶץ׃ | the earth | ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.a |

Grammar:

- בְּרֵאשִׁית is read as a construct: 'in the beginning of God's creating'. Rashi cites בְּרֵאשִׁית מַמְלֶכֶת יְהוֹיָקִים (Jer 26:1) and תְּחִלַּת דִּבֶּר ה' בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ (Hos 1:2) for a noun of beginning bound to a finite verb. Ibn Ezra adds the same two parallels and קִרְיַת חָנָה דָוִד (Isa 29:1).
- On Rashi's reading the verse is a subordinate clause, verse 2 is a parenthesis that describes the earth at that time, and the main clause comes in verse 3 (וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים). Ibn Ezra also reads a construct, but takes the ו of וְהָאָרֶץ like the Arabic fa that opens a main clause, so for him the main clause is verse 2: 'the earth was ...'. The English follows Rashi.
- The etnaḥta on אֱלֹהִים divides the verse in two: subject and verb, then the two objects.
- אֵת ... וְאֵת: the object marker is repeated before each of the two objects; הַשָּׁמַיִם וְהָאָרֶץ is the standard pair for 'everything'.
- אֱלֹהִים is plural in form with a singular verb; Ibn Ezra takes the plural as a plural of honour, and notes that the verb is בָּרָא, not בָּרְאוּ.

Note: The English follows the construct reading of both normative commentators. They differ on the main clause: Rashi has it in verse 3 (וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים), Ibn Ezra in verse 2 (וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה, with the ו like Arabic fa); the English follows Rashi and records Ibn Ezra. The other reading, an independent sentence 'In the beginning God created', takes רֵאשִׁית as absolute (Radak); the accents do not settle the question. Ibn Ezra denies that בָּרָא by itself means creation out of nothing; 'create' is kept as the plain English verb without that claim.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi, citing Rabbi Isaac: the Torah ought to have begun at 'This month is for you' (Exod 12:2); it begins with creation so that Israel can answer the nations who call them robbers of Canaan. This is homily on why the Torah opens here, not on the words.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: if you would explain it by its plain sense, 'In the beginning of the creation of heaven and earth, the earth was formless and void ... and God said, Let there be light'. רֵאשִׁית is always bound to the word after it (as in Jer 26:1, Gen 10:10, Deut 18:4), so בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא is like בְּרֵאשִׁית בְּרֹא. The verse does not teach the order of creation.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the verse says אֱלֹהִים and not the LORD (יהוה) because God first intended to create by the attribute of justice, then joined mercy to it. This is a homily on the divine names, not on the sense of the words.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra rejects three views: that the ב is added as in בָּרִאשֹׁנָה (then it would have qamets); that רֵאשִׁית is always construct and a word like 'evening' or 'darkness' is understood (but וַיַּרְא רֵאשִׁית לוֹ, Deut 33:21, is absolute); and that the ב is added without meaning. His own view: it is construct, like בְּרֵאשִׁית מַמְלֶכֶת יְהוֹיָקִים, and a construct before a perfect verb is not strange, as in תְּחִלַּת דִּבֶּר ה' בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ and קִרְיַת חָנָה דָוִד. The sense is explained at verse 2.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: most commentators say בְּרִיאָה means producing something out of nothing, but he cites ויברא אלהים את התנינים, את האדם and ובורא חשך (darkness is the opposite of existing light) against that. He takes בָּרָא as 'to cut, decide, set a limit' (cf. ובראת לך, וברא אותהן), and tells the wise to understand. The English keeps 'create' without the claim of creation from nothing.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: since the singular אֱלוֹהַּ exists, אֱלֹהִים is a plural of honour, like אֲדֹנִים and בְּעָלִים, and therefore the verb is singular (בָּרָא, not בָּרְאוּ). God is also called by the plural because all his works are done through the angels who do his will. The name is a title, not a proper noun, like 'king', and human judges are called by it too. The English renders it 'God', singular.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אֵת means 'the very thing' and is the sign of the object, though it is sometimes omitted (Deut 4:32) and once or twice stands for 'with' or 'from'. Here it is the object marker, with no English word.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הַשָּׁמַיִם takes the article of knowledge to show that the visible heavens are meant, and the word is always plural. In his view 'the heavens and the earth' here are the firmament and the dry land, because only one thing was created on each day: light on the first, the firmament on the second, plants on the third, and so on. He rejects the proof from Isa 48:13 that heaven and earth were created at once. The English has 'the heavens'.

Apparatus:

- Radak (non-normative) reads בְּרֵאשִׁית as absolute, 'at first', as in מַגִּיד מֵרֵאשִׁית אַחֲרִית (Isa 46:10); this is the alternative reading 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth'.
- Radak and Sforno take הַשָּׁמַיִם as the spheres; Ibn Ezra as the firmament.

#### Genesis 1:2

> וְהָאָ֗רֶץ הָיְתָ֥ה תֹ֙הוּ֙ וָבֹ֔הוּ וְחֹ֖שֶׁךְ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י תְה֑וֹם וְר֣וּחַ אֱלֹהִ֔ים מְרַחֶ֖פֶת עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הַמָּֽיִם׃

**the earth was desolate and empty, with darkness over the face of the deep and the wind of God hovering over the face of the waters —**

Literal: and-the-earth was desolation and-emptiness and-darkness over face-of deep and-wind-of God hovering over face-of the-waters

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וְהָאָ֗רֶץ | and the earth — The ו opens a clause that describes the state of things; it is not a step in the narrative. On Rashi's reading the clause is a parenthesis before the main clause in verse 3. Ibn Ezra compares the ו to the Arabic fa (כְּפ"א רָפָה בִּלְשׁוֹן יִשְׁמָעֵאל), which opens the main clause after a time clause. | ו: and + ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | conjunction + particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1.a |
| הָיְתָ֥ה | was — Qal perfect, 3rd feminine singular, of הָיָה; the subject הָאָרֶץ is feminine. | הָיָה | היה | verb (qal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, feminine, singular) | Qal III |
| תֹ֙הוּ֙ | desolate — תֹהוּ: Rashi: a word of astonishment and desolation (תֵּמַהּ וְשִׁמָּמוֹן), Old French estordison; Ibn Ezra, with the Targum (צָדְיָא): desolate, that which has no substance. BDB also gives 'formlessness' (sense 1). | תֹּ֫הוּ | תהה | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 2 |
| וָבֹ֔הוּ | and empty — בֹּהוּ: emptiness; paired with תֹהוּ as an alliterating pair; the pack lists no senses for it. Ibn Ezra: it is the brother of תֹהוּ, the ו standing in place of a final ה. | ו: and + בֹּהוּ | בהה | conjunction + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| וְחֹ֖שֶׁךְ | and darkness | ו: and + חֹ֫שֶׁךְ | חשׁך | conjunction + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| עַל | over — עַל־ with the maqqef is bound to the next word. | עַל | עלה | preposition | II.1 |
| פְּנֵ֣י | the face of — פְּנֵי is plural construct; the idiom עַל־פְּנֵי means 'over the surface of'. | פָּנֶה | פנה | noun (common, both genders, plural, construct) | I.5 |
| תְה֑וֹם | the deep — תְהוֹם is a noun with no article; it is used for the primeval ocean and is a poetic word, mostly without the article. | תְּהוֹם | תהם | noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 3 |
| וְר֣וּחַ | and the wind of — רוּחַ is construct here. 'Wind' is chosen; the alternatives 'spirit' and 'breath' are recorded. | ו: and + רוּחַ | רוח | conjunction + noun (common, both genders, singular, construct) | 2 |
| אֱלֹהִ֔ים | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| מְרַחֶ֖פֶת | hovering — Piel feminine singular participle, agreeing with רוּחַ, which is feminine. The verb is used of an eagle over its young in Deut 32:11. | רָחַף | רחף | verb (piel, participle, feminine, singular, absolute) | Pi |
| עַל | over | עַל | עלה | preposition | II.1 |
| פְּנֵ֥י | the face of | פָּנֶה | פנה | noun (common, both genders, plural, construct) | I.5 |
| הַמָּֽיִם׃ | the waters — מַיִם is plural in form only and always takes plural agreement; the pack lists no senses. | ה: the + מַי |  | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) |  |

Grammar:

- The clause begins with ו + noun + verb (וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה), not with a wayyiqtol: it describes a state, not the next event. Rashi reads it as a parenthesis between the time clause of verse 1 and the main clause of verse 3. Ibn Ezra takes the ו like the Arabic fa (כְּפ"א רָפָה, the letter pe without dagesh, i.e. Arabic fa), the particle that opens the main clause after a time clause, so for him this verse is the main clause.
- תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ is an alliterating pair of nouns, with the ו before the second one pointed וָ because of the stress.
- רוּחַ is feminine, so the participle is feminine (מְרַחֶפֶת, Piel); the participle gives an ongoing scene, not a sequence.
- The zaqef qaton on וָבֹהוּ, the etnaḥta on תְהוֹם and the zaqef qaton on אֱלֹהִים divide the verse: the earth, then the darkness over the deep, then the wind of God over the waters.
- The repetition of עַל־פְּנֵי in the two halves (the deep, the waters) is a parallel; Rashi takes תְהוֹם as the water that was upon the earth, so תְהוֹם and מַיִם are the same body of water.

Note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra both read verse 1 as a time clause but differ on the main clause. For Rashi verse 2 describes the earth before God's first word, and the main clause is verse 3; for Ibn Ezra the ו of וְהָאָרֶץ is like the Arabic fa and verse 2 is the main clause. The English follows Rashi, with verse 2 set off by dashes. תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ is 'desolate and empty' with both commentators. For רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים Ibn Ezra takes the wind as God's agent that dries the water; Rashi has the throne of glory hovering by the breath of God's mouth. 'Wind of God' follows Ibn Ezra; 'hovering' follows Rashi's image of the dove. 'The spirit of God' and 'a mighty wind' (Radak, אלהים as intensifier) are recorded in the apparatus.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: תֹּהוּ is a word of astonishment and desolation: a person would be astonished and appalled at the emptiness (בֹּהוּ) in it. The English 'desolate and empty' follows him.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi glosses תֹהוּ with the Old French word 'estordison' (astonishment). It confirms the sense of desolation.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בֹּהוּ is a word of emptiness and desolation (רֵקוּת וְצָדוּ). The English has 'void'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'over the face of the deep' means over the face of the water that was upon the earth. The English 'the deep' is the covering water.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: the throne of glory stands in the air and hovers over the face of the waters, by the breath of God's mouth and by his word, like a dove that hovers over the nest. The English keeps 'hovering' (the dove image) but renders רוּחַ as 'wind', not as the throne of glory.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the word is strange, since the alef has a qamets after the he (and not a pataḥ) in every place, unlike הָאֶלֶף (Song 5:12). This is a note on the vowels of the article, not on the sense.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra rejects Saadia's derivation of תֹהוּ from תְהוֹם, since the מ of תְהוֹם is a root letter, and cites the Sefer Yetzirah reading (תֹהוּ a green line, בֹהוּ wet stones). The right sense is the Aramaic translator's (צָדְיָא, desolate), as in בְּתֹהוּ יְלֵל יְשִׁמֹן and אַחֲרֵי הַתֹּהוּ, 'that which has no substance'. The English 'desolate' follows him.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: בֹּהוּ is the brother of תֹהוּ, the ו standing for a ה. The sense is that at the beginning of the creation of the firmament and the dry land there was no habitation on the earth, since it was covered with water. The ו of וְהָאָרֶץ is like the Arabic fa (as in וְאֵד יַעֲלֶה, Gen 2:6), so verse 2 is the main clause of the sentence begun in verse 1. The English follows Rashi's structure, with the main clause in verse 3, and records this one.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the רוּחַ is attributed to God because it is a messenger sent to do God's will, to dry the water. The English takes it as 'wind' (God's wind, the agent).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: מַיִם is a plural word that is never singular, and it is in the form of a dual, because it includes male and female waters; it is found with a singular sense in לֹא זֹרַק עָלָיו. The English has 'waters'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: מְרַחֶפֶת means 'blowing' (נוֹשֶׁבֶת) above, over the water, as in עַל גּוֹזָלָיו יְרַחֵף (Deut 32:11). This fits his reading of רוּחַ as a wind. The English 'hovering' follows Rashi's image of the dove over the nest; Ibn Ezra's 'blowing' is recorded.

Apparatus:

- רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים: 'spirit of God' (sense 9 of the lexicon) is a real alternative; Radak (non-normative) offers 'the will of God', 'the elemental air', or a 'mighty wind' with אֱלֹהִים as an intensifier (cf. עִיר גְּדוֹלָה לֵאלֹהִים).
- Structure of verses 1-3: Ibn Ezra makes verse 2 the main clause ('When God began to create the heavens and the earth, the earth was desolate and empty ...'); the English follows Rashi, with the main clause in verse 3.
- מְרַחֶפֶת: Ibn Ezra 'blowing' (נוֹשֶׁבֶת), as Onkelos מְנַשְּׁבָא; the English 'hovering' follows Rashi.
- תְהוֹם is feminine according to Radak (Ezek 26:19) but is also found as masculine (Ps 42:8); the verse gives no agreement to show it.
- The pack parses 1:2.9 רוּחַ as feminine construct; the verb is feminine, so the data is consistent.

#### Genesis 1:3

> וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֖ים יְהִ֣י א֑וֹר וַֽיְהִי־אֽוֹר׃

**God said, "Let there be light," and there was light.**

Literal: and-said God let-be light and-was light

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיֹּ֥אמֶר | and said — wayyiqtol (וַיֹּאמֶר), the narrative verb form for a sequence of events in the past; the ו is rendered by the sequence of the sentence. | ו: and + אָמַר | אמר | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| אֱלֹהִ֖ים | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| יְהִ֣י | let there be — jussive of הָיָה (יְהִי), a short form that expresses a command or wish in the 3rd person. | הָיָה | היה | verb (qal, jussive, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal III.1 |
| א֑וֹר | light | אוֹר | אור | noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| וַֽיְהִי | and there was — wayyiqtol of הָיָה (וַיְהִי), the same root as the jussive; the narrator uses the same word to report the fulfilment. | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal III.1 |
| אֽוֹר׃ | light | אוֹר | אור | noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1 |

Grammar:

- וַיֹּאמֶר is a wayyiqtol; on the construct reading of 1:1 it is the main verb of the sentence that began in 1:1.
- יְהִי is a jussive, the short form of יִהְיֶה; וַיְהִי is the wayyiqtol of the same root. The command and its fulfilment use the same verb with the same word order.
- The etnaḥta on אוֹר divides the verse into the command and its execution.
- Ramban notes that the verse does not have וַיְהִי־כֵן, 'and it was so', as the later days do.

Note: The English follows Ibn Ezra in taking the saying literally, as a way to say that the act cost God no effort. אוֹר is rendered 'light' throughout.

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: Saadia said that וַיֹּאמֶר means 'he willed', but if so the text should have said 'light' alone; it is as it sounds, as in בִּדְבַר ה' שָׁמַיִם נַעֲשׂוּ and כִּי הוּא צִוָּה וְנִבְרָאוּ. The sense is a figure that the work was not done with effort, a parable of a king and his servants. The English keeps 'said'.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: this light was above the wind (רוּחַ). This is a statement about the position of the light in the cosmos and does not bear on the English.

Apparatus:

- Ramban (non-normative) reads אֲמִירָה as will or thought, 'God willed that there be light'; Ibn Ezra rejects the equation of 'said' with 'willed'.

#### Genesis 1:4

> וַיַּ֧רְא אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶת־הָא֖וֹר כִּי־ט֑וֹב וַיַּבְדֵּ֣ל אֱלֹהִ֔ים בֵּ֥ין הָא֖וֹר וּבֵ֥ין הַחֹֽשֶׁךְ׃

**God saw that the light was good, and God separated the light from the darkness.**

Literal: and-saw God [object-marker]-the-light that good and-separated God between the-light and-between the-darkness

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיַּ֧רְא | and saw — wayyiqtol of רָאָה; Ibn Ezra takes it as perception in thought, 'considered'. | ו: and + רָאָה | ראה | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1.a |
| אֱלֹהִ֛ים | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| אֶת | (object marker) — אֶת־ with maqqef; the marker is bound to the next word. | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| הָא֖וֹר | the light | ה: the + אוֹר | אור | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| כִּי | that — כִּי introduces the content of what was seen. | כִּי |  | conjunction | 1 |
| ט֑וֹב | good — the predicate adjective; there is no verb 'to be' in the Hebrew clause. | טוֹב | טוב | adjective (adjective, masculine, singular, absolute) | 3 |
| וַיַּבְדֵּ֣ל | and separated — Hiphil wayyiqtol of בָּדַל; the root has the sense 'to divide, to set apart'. | ו: and + בָּדַל | בדל | conjunction + verb (hifil, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph 1 |
| אֱלֹהִ֔ים | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| בֵּ֥ין | between — בֵּין is repeated before each of the two things divided: 'between ... and between ...'. | בֵּין | בין | preposition | 1 |
| הָא֖וֹר | the light | ה: the + אוֹר | אור | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| וּבֵ֥ין | and between | ו: and + בֵּין | בין | conjunction + preposition | 1 |
| הַחֹֽשֶׁךְ׃ | the darkness | ה: the + חֹ֫שֶׁךְ | חשׁך | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |

Grammar:

- וַיַּרְא ... כִּי־טוֹב: the object of 'saw' is the light (אֶת־הָאוֹר), and the content is the clause כִּי־טוֹב, a verbless clause 'that it was good'.
- וַיַּבְדֵּל is a Hiphil wayyiqtol (הִבְדִּיל, 'to cause to be apart'); the Hebrew idiom is 'separate between X and between Y'.
- The etnaḥta on טוֹב divides the verse into the seeing and the separating.
- הַחֹשֶׁךְ, with the article, is the darkness of verse 2 that has just been mentioned.

Note: Both normative commentators read the seeing as approval, and Rashi's plain sense is that light and darkness were given each its own limit, one for day and one for night. Ibn Ezra takes the separation to be done by naming (see verse 5); the English keeps 'separated', which does not decide the question.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: his midrashic reading is that God saw that the light was not fit for the wicked to use and set it apart for the righteous in the future. By its plain sense: he saw that it was good, and it was not fitting that it and the darkness should be used mixed together, so he fixed a limit for the one by day and the other by night. The English follows the plain sense.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיַּרְא is like וְרָאִיתִי אֲנִי (Eccl 2:13, Dan 10:7), and it is in thought. The English 'saw' is kept, with the meaning of considering, and it says nothing of physical sight.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the sense of וַיַּבְדֵּל is 'in the calling of the names', that is, the separation is made by naming day and night (verse 5). The English keeps the plain 'separated' and records his reading.

Apparatus:

- Ramban (non-normative) rejects Ibn Ezra: seeing is the continuing existence of what was spoken into being, and the darkness here is the absence of light, not the elemental fire of verse 2.
- Radak (non-normative) says וַיַּבְדֵּל is by naming, because darkness is not a thing that can be separated from light.

#### Genesis 1:5

> וַיִּקְרָ֨א אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ לָאוֹר֙ י֔וֹם וְלַחֹ֖שֶׁךְ קָ֣רָא לָ֑יְלָה וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם אֶחָֽד׃

**God called the light day, and the darkness he called night. There was evening and there was morning, one day.**

| אֱלֹהִ֤ים | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 3 |
| לָאוֹר֙ | to the light — the ל marks the thing named; in English 'the light' is the object. | ל: to, for + אוֹר | אור | preposition (with definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| י֔וֹם | day — יוֹם here is the daylight period, the name given to the light. | יוֹם |  | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| וְלַחֹ֖שֶׁךְ | and to the darkness — the object is put first for contrast with the first half of the verse. | ו: and + ל: to, for + חֹ֫שֶׁךְ | חשׁך | conjunction + preposition (with definite article) + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| קָ֣רָא | he called — a perfect (qatal) after the fronted object, not a wayyiqtol: the second naming is contrasted with the first. Ibn Ezra's point about the next word is that לַיְלָה is always masculine. | קָרָא | קרא | verb (qal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 6 |
| לָ֑יְלָה | night — לַיְלָה has the final ָה ending, which is not a feminine sign (Ibn Ezra: the ה is added; the word is always masculine). The pack lists no senses. | לַ֫יְלָה |  | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| וַֽיְהִי | and there was | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal III.1 |
| עֶ֥רֶב | evening | עֶ֫רֶב | ערב | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1.a |
| וַֽיְהִי | and there was | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal III.1 |
| בֹ֖קֶר | morning | בֹּ֫קֶר | בקר | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| י֥וֹם | day — here יוֹם covers the whole cycle of evening and morning, not only the daylight. | יוֹם |  | noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |
| אֶחָֽד׃ | one — a cardinal number, not the ordinal 'first' used in later days (שֵׁנִי, שְׁלִישִׁי); the adjective follows its noun. | אֶחָד | אחד | adjective (cardinal number, masculine, singular, absolute) | 1 |

Grammar:

- וַיִּקְרָא ... לָאוֹר יוֹם: 'call X Y' is expressed with ל before the thing named and the name after it.
- וְלַחֹשֶׁךְ קָרָא לָיְלָה puts the object first and uses a qatal, which gives a contrast with the first half of the verse.
- Ibn Ezra: the final ה of לַיְלָה is an addition, because the word is stressed on the first syllable (מִלְעֵיל); it is not a feminine ending, and the word is always masculine.
- The etnaḥta on לָיְלָה divides the verse between the naming and the formula of the day; the formula וַיְהִי־עֶרֶב וַיְהִי־בֹקֶר ends each day of the account.
- יוֹם אֶחָד has the cardinal 'one' where later days have ordinals (שֵׁנִי, שְׁלִישִׁי); the paragraph mark פ closes the first section.

Note: The English 'one day' follows Rashi, Ibn Ezra, and the Hebrew, which says אֶחָד and not רִאשׁוֹן. Ibn Ezra insists the evening cannot be a 'day' since the light has been called 'day'; the clause is 'there was evening and there was morning, of one day', and the English line keeps the Hebrew order without extra words.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: by the order of the language of the passage, the Torah should have written 'first day', as the others have 'second, third, fourth'. It wrote אֶחָד ('one') because God was alone in his world, since the angels were created only on the second day (so it says in Genesis Rabbah). The English gives 'one day'; the reason is a midrash and is not in the English.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the ה of לַיְלָה is an addition because the word has penultimate stress, and it is always masculine. This is a grammar note on the form of the word.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: עֶרֶב is close in sense to חֹשֶׁךְ and is so called because the forms are mixed together (נִתְעָרְבוּ) in it; בֹּקֶר is the opposite, because one can look carefully (לְבַקֵּר) among the forms. This is an etymology; it does not alter the English words 'evening' and 'morning'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'one day' refers to the motion of the sphere, and there is a secret in the midrash (שית אלפי). Since the light was called 'day', the evening cannot also be called 'day'; the meaning is that there was an evening and also a morning belonging to one day. If evening and morning together were one day, what would 'second day' mean? The English gives 'There was evening and there was morning, one day'.

Apparatus:

- Radak (non-normative): 'one' and not 'first' because there is no first without a second, and the second had not yet been made; or, with Moses ibn Ezra, because 'one' is the sign of a beginning that nothing precedes.
- Ramban (non-normative): evening is the beginning of the night, so called because the forms are mixed; morning is the beginning of the day.

#### Genesis 1:6

> וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֔ים יְהִ֥י רָקִ֖יעַ בְּת֣וֹךְ הַמָּ֑יִם וִיהִ֣י מַבְדִּ֔יל בֵּ֥ין מַ֖יִם לָמָֽיִם׃

**God said, "Let there be an expanse in the middle of the waters, and let it divide water from water."**

Literal: and-said God let-be expanse in-midst-of the-waters and-let-be dividing between water to-water

| אֱלֹהִ֔ים | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 4 |

| מַבְדִּ֔יל | dividing — participle: a continuing function | בָּדַל | בדל | verb (hifil, participle, masculine, singular, absolute) | Hiph 1 |
| בֵּ֥ין | between | בֵּין | בין | preposition | 1 |
| מַ֖יִם | water | מַי |  | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) |  |
| לָמָֽיִם׃ | to water — בֵּין ... לְ idiom: 'between X and Y' | ל: to, for + מַי |  | preposition + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) |  |

Grammar:

- יְהִי is a jussive: a command addressed to the world, not a statement.
- וִיהִי מַבְדִּיל joins a verb 'to be' to a Hifil participle, so the sense is a lasting function: let it be a divider.
- בֵּין מַיִם לָמָיִם uses לְ for the second term; the same idiom as Ibn Ezra cites from Ezekiel.
- The zaqef on אֱלֹהִים and the etnaḥta on הַמָּיִם divide the speech into the creation of the expanse and its function.

Note: בְּתוֹךְ is 'in the midst of', as Rashi takes it. The English 'divide' renders the participle of the Hifil of בדל; 'expanse' for רָקִיעַ follows the root רקע, to beat out, spread (Ibn Ezra, Radak).

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: יְהִי רָקִיעַ means 'let the expanse become firm' (יֶחֱזַק הָרָקִיעַ): the heavens made on day one were still moist (לַחִים) and set hard on the second day at God's rebuke, as Job 26:11 says the pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at His rebuke. On this reading the verb strengthens an existing heaven; the English 'let there be' follows the plain sense of a new making (cf. Ibn Ezra), and Rashi's reading is kept here.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בְּתוֹךְ הַמַּיִם is 'in the middle of the water'; the upper waters are as far from the expanse as the expanse from the waters on earth, so they hang by the King's word. The English keeps 'in the middle of the waters'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: רָקִיעַ is something stretched out (cf. וַיְרַקְּעוּ, אֲרִקֵּעֵם), and he identifies it with the air, not a solid vault. The English 'expanse' leaves this open.

Apparatus:

- Ramban cites Rav: the heavens were wet on day one and congealed on day two; Rabbi Judah: 'let the expanse be made a sheet'.

- בֵּין ... וּבֵין is the second way the idiom is built; Ibn Ezra lists the three forms.
- מֵעַל לָרָקִיעַ means 'above' with space between, not 'on' the expanse.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Scripture says מֵעַל, not עַל, because the upper waters hang in the air. He also says כִּי טוֹב is absent on day two because the work of the waters was not finished until day three.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: notes the three constructions of הבדלה with בין (בין X ל Y; בין X וּבין Y; and both). A matter of idiom, not of sense.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: וַיְהִי־כֵן belongs with what follows: when it was so, he called it heavens. The English keeps it with this verse, as the accents do.

Apparatus:

- Ramban 1:7 on וַיְהִי־כֵן and Bereshit Rabbah on Ben Zoma: why 'and it was so' follows the making here.

Apparatus:

- Ibn Ezra on 1:9: 'seen' is a hidden thing coming to view, not a creation.

- יַמִּים is the plural: the one gathering is named by several seas.
- כִּי־טוֹב: a clause of seeing, 'that it was good'.
- The paseq after אֱלֹהִים and the pashta on לַיַּבָּשָׁה lead to the zaqef on אֶרֶץ, which divides the two namings; the etnaḥta on יַמִּים sets the namings apart from God's seeing.

Note: 'Seas' is plural, as the Hebrew has it. Rashi and Ibn Ezra both give a reason for the plural (see commentary).

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: it is one sea, so why 'seas'? The taste of a fish from the sea at Acre is not that of a fish from the sea in Spain. The English keeps the plural 'Seas'.

- תַּדְשֵׁא is a Hifil jussive 'let (the earth) sprout' with a cognate object דֶּשֶׁא.
- עֵץ פְּרִי עֹשֶׂה פְּרִי is a chain of construct and participle: a fruit tree that produces fruit.
- לְמִינוֹ, 'to its kind', is a single phrase: each kind produces its own.
- The revia on אֱלֹהִים and the many disjunctives (pashta, revia, yetiv) divide the list of growth into three.

Note: 'Green growth' for דֶּשֶׁא follows Rashi: דשא is the earth's green covering, עשב the individual plants (Ramban disputes this and takes דשא as the young growth). Ibn Ezra glosses only the verb: תַּדְשֵׁא is תַּצְמִיחַ. 'Fruit trees' keeps עֵץ פְּרִי; Rashi's reading of a tree that tastes of fruit is kept in the commentary.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: דֶּשֶׁא is not the same as עֵשֶׂב: דשא is the earth's covering when full of grasses; each kind of plant is called עשב. The English divides them as 'green growth' and 'plants'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: תַּדְשֵׁא הָאָרֶץ means the earth should fill and cover itself with a garment of plants. In Old French דֶּשֶׁא is ארבריץ ('herbage'), all kinds mixed together, while each root by itself is called עֵשֶׂב. The English 'sprout green growth'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: מַזְרִיעַ זֶרַע means the plant grows its seed so that it can be sown elsewhere. The English 'yielding seed'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: עֵץ פְּרִי means a tree whose taste equals its fruit's; the earth did not do so but produced a tree making fruit, so it was cursed when Adam was. The English reads the plain 'fruit tree'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: אֲשֶׁר זַרְעוֹ בוֹ means the stones of every fruit from which the tree grows when planted.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the text says 'let the earth sprout', 'let the waters swarm', 'let the earth bring forth': power was placed in earth and water to act at God's command.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: תַּדְשֵׁא means the same as תַּצְמִיחַ, 'let it cause to grow'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the seed is in the fruit, and each keeps its own kind.

- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): The pack's text of Ibn Ezra here is only the letter 'n'; it has no content bearing on the English.

Apparatus:

- Ibn Ezra's text on 1:12 in the pack is a single letter (a damaged fetch).

> וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֗ים יְהִ֤י מְאֹרֹת֙ בִּרְקִ֣יעַ הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם לְהַבְדִּ֕יל בֵּ֥ין הַיּ֖וֹם וּבֵ֣ין הַלָּ֑יְלָה וְהָי֤וּ לְאֹתֹת֙ וּלְמ֣וֹעֲדִ֔ים וּלְיָמִ֖ים וְשָׁנִֽים׃

- יְהִי is singular before the plural מְאֹרֹת; Ibn Ezra notes that the verb 'to be' often does not agree in number or gender (cf. Deut 22:23 כִּי יִהְיֶה נַעֲרָה).
- לְהַבְדִּיל is an infinitive of purpose; the pashta on מְאֹרֹת and the zaqef on הַשָּׁמַיִם set off 'lights in the expanse' from the purpose clause.
- The etnaḥta on הַלָּיְלָה divides the verse: purpose of separation, then the further functions after it.
- וְהָיוּ is a weqatal continuing the jussive, so it is also a wish-command: 'and let them be'.
- Three of the four nouns carry ל of purpose (לְאֹתֹת, וּלְמוֹעֲדִים, וּלְיָמִים); וְשָׁנִים has none and shares the ל of וּלְיָמִים. Ibn Ezra rejects the view that the ל of לְאֹתֹת is superfluous.

Note: מְאֹרֹת is written without vav; Rashi hears מְאֵרָה 'curse' in it, which is homiletic and not adopted. 'Appointed times' follows Rashi's reading of the festivals. Ibn Ezra glosses לְאֹתֹת as moments (רגעים) and מוֹעֲדִים as hours (שעות), or else takes the signs as portents (eclipses of moon and sun); kept in the notes.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the lights were created on the first day and on the fourth day God commanded them to be hung in the expanse; everything was created on day one and fixed on its own day. This is about order of creation, not the sense of the words.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: מְאֹרֹת is written defectively (מארת), because the fourth day is a day of curse (מְאֵרָה), when diphtheria strikes children. A homiletic reading, not adopted in the English.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'to separate between day and night' is after the first light was stored away; during the seven days of creation the first light and darkness served day and night together. Bears on the cosmic history, not the English.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: when the luminaries are eclipsed it is a bad omen for the world (Jer 10:2). 'Signs' is the English rendering.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'appointed times' is said for the future, when Israel will be commanded concerning the festivals, which are counted by the birth of the moon. The English keeps 'appointed times' for מוֹעֲדִים.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the work of the sun is half a day and that of the moon is half, together a whole day. 'Days' is kept.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: at the end of 365 days the lights complete their course through the twelve constellations, which is a year, and begin again. 'Years' is kept.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the word יְהִי means 'will be'; because it is used so often it serves singular and plural and also feminine, as in 'if there be a virgin girl' (Deut 22:23). The English 'let there be lights' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: לְאֹתֹת are moments (רגעים) and מוֹעֲדִים are hours (שעות); or the signs may be portents: eclipses of moon and sun and the changing appearance of the stars, as in 'be not dismayed at the signs of the heavens' (Jer 10:2). Whoever says the ל of לְאֹתֹת is superfluous 'has said nothing'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: a great Spanish sage held that the expanse is divided into eight parts; Ibn Ezra rejects this, and holds that the sun, moon and stars are lights in the expanse because they are seen there. The English 'in the expanse of the sky' follows.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders 'lights' by נְהוֹרִין and 'appointed times' by זִמְנִין, 'and to count by them days and years'.
- Radak: בְּרָקִיעַ הַשָּׁמַיִם is the air; Ramban reads the lights as formed from the heavens' substance.

Grammar:

- אֵת marks each definite direct object; here it is repeated for the two lights and for the stars.
- הַגָּדוֹל and הַקָּטֹן are positive adjectives used where English says 'greater' and 'lesser'.
- לְמֶמְשֶׁלֶת is the construct of מֶמְשָׁלָה: 'for the dominion of the day'.
- The etnaḥta on הַגְּדֹלִים divides the verse; the stars are added in a short last clause under the silluq.
- וְאֵת הַכּוֹכָבִים has no verb of its own: it depends on וַיַּעַשׂ and is added almost as an afterthought.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: they were created equal, and the moon was made smaller because she accused, saying two kings cannot use one crown. A homily; the English says 'two great lights' and 'greater' and 'lesser' without it.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: because He made the moon smaller He multiplied her hosts, to appease her. A homiletic comment on the stars.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the two are called great against the stars, as the three eldest sons of Jesse are called the great ones against the others. The English 'great' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'the rule of the day' is the sun's rule by day and not by night, and the light of the moon and stars is not seen by day. If one objects that the astronomers hold Jupiter and every star except Mercury and Venus to be larger than the moon, the answer is that 'great' refers to their light, not their bodies; the moon's light is many times that of the stars because she is near the earth, and so the text says מָאוֹר.
- Ramban (not-applicable): Ramban: the lights were not made of the body of the expanse but are bodies set in it.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'great' here is of their light, not body, since the stars are greater than the moon in body.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: וְיָת נְהוֹרָא רַבָּא לְמִשְׁלַט בִּימָמָא; it renders the noun לְמֶמְשֶׁלֶת 'for the rule of' by the infinitive לְמִשְׁלַט 'to rule', as the English does.

- The two infinitives, 'to rule' and 'to separate', continue the purpose of verse 17.
- בַּיּוֹם has the article fused into the preposition בַּ.
- MAM writes וּֽלְהַבְדִּיל with shewa under the ל and a meteg (ga'ya) on the וּ; WLC, and Ramban's lemma, have ḥataf pataḥ: וּלֲהַבְדִּיל. The sense is the same.
- הָאוֹר and הַחֹשֶׁךְ are the 'light' and 'darkness' of day one: whether these refer to day and night, or to light and dark as such, is discussed by the commentators.

The English keeps the plain 'the light from the darkness'.

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the day of the Torah runs from sunrise to sunset, and the night from the appearance of the stars; with the light of the sun by day and the moon by night, the lights separate the light from the darkness. The English keeps 'to rule over the day and the night' and 'to separate the light from the darkness'.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: 'rule' covers the sign-giving of verse 14, since the lights rule over changes on earth; sun by day causes growth, moon by night fertility. A further reading is that rule is the power of emanation. These readings of 'rule' are recorded here, not put in the English.
- Ramban (records): Ramban disagrees with Ibn Ezra: 'light' and 'darkness' here are the names of day and night (v. 5); the great light rules in the day and the small in the night.
- Radak (records): Radak: from sunrise it is light, which is the day, and from the appearance of the stars it is darkness, called thus because it is dark relative to the light of day.

Apparatus:

- Variant: WLC reads וּלֲהַבְדִּיל for MAM וּלְהַבְדִּיל in 1:18.4 (vowel only).

- וּֽלְהַבְדִּ֔יל: WLC reads וּֽלֲהַבְדִּ֔יל (vowels)

Grammar:

- יִשְׁרְצוּ is a yiqtol with jussive force: 'let the waters swarm'. It is transitive, with שֶׁרֶץ as its object.
- שֶׁרֶץ is in the construct state before נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה: 'swarmers of living creatures'.
- וְעוֹף is a collective singular, and יְעוֹפֵף is a polel (intensive, repeated motion): 'fly about'.
- The etnaḥta on חַיָּה divides the verse: the waters' part, then the birds' part.
- עַל־הָאָרֶץ and עַל־פְּנֵי רְקִיעַ הַשָּׁמָיִם are two parallel locations of the birds; the expanse of 1:6-8 is the setting.

Note: Ibn Ezra reads יִשְׁרְצוּ as transitive (as in Exodus 7:28) and says the sense is 'bring forth offspring', so the English gives the waters a cognate object. 'living creatures' renders נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה following Rashi (a being with life in it). For על פני רקיע the Gaon, cited by Ibn Ezra, takes the birds to fly in the air below the expanse; the English 'across the expanse of the sky' keeps the Hebrew's preposition without deciding this.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה means 'that there be life in it' (שֶׁיְּהֵא בָהּ חַיּוּת).
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: anything alive that is not tall off the ground is called שֶׁרֶץ: flies among birds, ants and worms among the vermin, mole and mouse among beasts, and all fish.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: יִשְׁרְצוּ is a transitive verb (פועל יוצא), like 'and the Nile shall swarm frogs' (Exodus 7:28); its sense is 'תולדות עם הגבהה', offspring with raising up. The words 'the birds shall fly on the face of the expanse' are evidence for what רָקִיעַ means. The Gaon said that עַל פְּנֵי means עִם פְּנֵי, 'in front of', so the 'face' of the heavens is their lower side; the doubled pe of יְעוֹפֵף is like the nun of יְכוֹנֵן (Isaiah 62:7).

Apparatus:

- The Gaon (cited by Ibn Ezra): עַל פְּנֵי means עִם פְּנֵי, 'in front of', so the 'face' of the heavens is their underside and the birds fly beneath it; the English 'across' keeps the plain preposition without deciding this.

Grammar:

- The verse opens with בָּרָא, used only of God. The great sea creatures are named first, then all living things, then birds.
- הָרֹמֶשֶׂת is a feminine singular participle agreeing with נֶפֶשׁ; Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'the going'.
- אֲשֶׁר שָׁרְצוּ הַמַּיִם is a relative clause with no resumptive word: 'which the waters swarmed (with)'.
- לְמִינֵהֶם (plural suffix) and לְמִינֵהוּ (singular suffix) divide creatures by kind; the birds are a single collective.
- The etnaḥta on הַגְּדֹלִים divides the verse: the great sea creatures, then everything else. In the second half a paseq (׀) follows הַחַיָּה, the disjunctive pazer on הָרֹמֶשֶׂת sets 'every living creature that moves' off from the relative clause, and the geresh on הַמַּיִם closes that clause before לְמִינֵהֶם.

Note: תַּנִּינִם is rendered 'sea creatures' following Rashi (great fish of the sea); 'sea monsters' would also fit the lexicon, and Rashi's aggadic Leviathan is recorded in the commentary. The suffix on לְמִינֵהֶם is plural, matching the many swimming creatures, and on לְמִינֵהוּ singular, matching the collective bird.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: הַתַּנִּינִם are the great fish of the sea; in aggadah they are Leviathan and his mate, created male and female, after which the female was killed and salted for the righteous in the future, since if they bred the world could not stand before them.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: נֶפֶשׁ הַחַיָּה means 'that has life in it'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הָרֹמֶשֶׂת has the sense of הוֹלֶכֶת, 'going'; some say the shin stands in place of a samekh.

Apparatus:

- Some (cited by Ibn Ezra) take the shin of הָרֹמֶשֶׂת to stand for a samekh, which would give רָמַס, 'tread, trample'; the English 'moves' follows Ibn Ezra's own gloss הוֹלֶכֶת, 'going'.

Grammar:

- Three plural imperatives, פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ וּמִלְאוּ, address the sea creatures; the birds are addressed in the third person with the jussive יִרֶב.
- פְּרוּ is from פָּרָה and רְבוּ from רָבָה; the pair is a standard blessing formula.
- The first blessing in Genesis is given to living creatures; the same words are spoken to humans in 1:28.
- The etnaḥta on לֵאמֹר sets off the speech; the zaqef on בַּיַּמִּים divides the sea's part from the birds' part.

Note: Rashi reads the blessing as a response to the creatures' vulnerability (they are hunted and eaten), which the English does not need. Ibn Ezra takes the imperatives as promises ('you will be fruitful'), not commands, since this is not in their power; the English keeps the imperative and records his reading. The lexicon lists פָּרָה only in the Hiphil; the pack's parse is Qal, and the data are kept.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: because creatures of the sea are diminished, caught and eaten, they needed a blessing; the land animals needed one too, but the serpent, destined for a curse, was left out so that it would not be included.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: פְּרוּ means 'make fruit', from פְּרִי.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: if the text said only 'be fruitful' one would beget one and no more; 'multiply' means one begets many.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the sense of פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ is 'you will be fruitful, you will multiply', as in 'and die on the mountain' (Deuteronomy 32:50), because this is not in their power.

Apparatus:

- Ibn Ezra: the imperatives are promises, not commands.

- תּוֹצֵא is a Hifil jussive: the earth is addressed in the third person, 'let the earth cause to come out'.
- The list has three kinds, בְּהֵמָה, רֶמֶשׂ and חַיְתוֹ־אֶרֶץ, joined by ו except for the first.
- חַיְתוֹ is the construct of חַיָּה with an extra final ו; Ibn Ezra and Radak compare בְּנוֹ בְעֹר (Num 24:3).
- The etnaḥta on the second לְמִינָהּ divides the command from וַיְהִי־כֵן.
- The suffix of לְמִינָהּ is feminine singular, agreeing with נֶפֶשׁ: one 'living being' brought out kind by kind.

Note: Rashi says the earth needed only to bring out what was created on the first day, so the English says 'bring forth', not 'create'. The three kinds follow Ibn Ezra and Rashi: livestock live with people; crawling things are small and low; wild animals live where no one settles. 'Each according to its kind' is repeated because the Hebrew repeats it.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: as I explained, everything was created on the first day, and the earth only needed to bring them out. The English 'bring forth' renders the Hifil without 'create'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה means that it has life. The English 'living creatures' keeps this.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: רֶמֶשׂ are swarmers, low creatures that creep on the earth and seem dragged along, since their going is not noticeable. The English 'crawling things' adopts this.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the clause is a general term for what fire, water and earth bring forth, the human included. It bears on the structure of the chapter, not on the English wording.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בְּהֵמָה are those that are with people, for riding and eating. The English 'livestock' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: רֶמֶשׂ are the small ones that go on the earth.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: wild animals are those in the open country where no one settles, and the last ו of וחיתו is an added letter, as in בנו בעור. The English 'wild animals of the earth' follows.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: בְּהֵמָה are the grazing kinds, tame or wild. The English keeps Ibn Ezra's 'livestock'; Ramban's wider sense is recorded.

Apparatus:

- Ramban reads בְּהֵמָה as all grazers and חַיָּה as meat-eaters, tame or wild; the English takes Ibn Ezra's sense.

- Verse 24 asked the earth to 'bring forth'; this verse says וַיַּעַשׂ, 'and God made'. Radak explains why the making follows וַיְהִי־כֵן.
- רֶמֶשׂ הָאֲדָמָה uses 'ground' where verse 24 used 'earth'.
- כִּי־טוֹב has no verb; the English adds 'it was'.
- The etnaḥta on לְמִינֵהוּ divides the making from the verdict.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַיַּעַשׂ means he fixed them in their beauty and in their stature. The English keeps 'made' and takes it as God fitting each kind, not only producing it.

Grammar:

- נַעֲשֶׂה is 1st person plural: Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take it as God speaking with the angels (Rashi: his court); the royal plural, which Ibn Ezra reports from the Gaon, he rejects. The English keeps 'us'.
- אָדָם has no article, so 'a human' or 'humankind', not yet a name; the article comes in 1:27.
- בְּצַלְמֵנוּ and כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ stand side by side with no ו: 'in our image, like our likeness'.
- וְיִרְדּוּ is a plural jussive, so the one אָדָם is collective. The root רדה sounds like ירד, 'go down' (Rashi).
- Five domains of rule are listed: fish, birds, livestock, all the earth, and crawling things.

Note: The plural 'Let us make': Rashi takes it as God taking counsel with his heavenly court, to teach humility; Ibn Ezra rejects the Niphal reading and the Gaon's royal plural, and reads God speaking to the angels. The English keeps 'us'. 'Humankind' is used because אָדָם has no article and the following verb is plural; 1:27 then has הָאָדָם. 'All the earth' follows the Hebrew word for word; Radak reads it as the wild animals of the earth.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: we learn God's humility here. Since the human is in the likeness of the angels and they would be jealous, God consulted them; a king deciding a case consults his court, as in Micaiah's vision before Ahab. The English keeps 'us' as a true plural.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: although they did not help in forming the human, Scripture teaches courtesy and humility, that the great consults and takes leave of the small. Had it said 'I will make', we would not learn this; the answer to the heretics is written beside it: 'and God created' (singular).
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בְּצַלְמֵנוּ means in our mold (בדפוס שלנו). The English 'image' renders צֶלֶם and this sense goes in the notes.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ means to understand and to discern. The English 'likeness' keeps דְּמוּת.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the word carries both rule and descent: if he is worthy, he rules over the animals; if not, he goes down before them and the animal rules over him. The English takes 'rule', as the context requires, and the second sense is kept here.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: some take נעשה as a Niphal participle (Neh 5:18) and 'in our image' as Moses' words; he calls this lacking sense. He reports the Gaon (image = rule; the plural is how kings speak, citing Gen 29:27, Dan 2:36, Num 22:6) and rejects those proof texts as 'false witnesses'. His own reading: God said to the angels, 'Let us make a human; we will busy ourselves with him, not the water and the earth'; the image is the human's upper soul, which does not die, and בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים means the image of an angel.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: because the human is male and female, he says 'let them rule'.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'all the earth' means the animals of the earth, the wild animals not in settled land, as it is called חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ.

Apparatus:

- Plural 'us': Rashi (God and his court) and Ibn Ezra (God and the angels) agree; the royal plural of the Gaon, reported and rejected by Ibn Ezra, is not adopted.
- Radak reads 'all the earth' as 'the wild animals of the earth'; this is not adopted in the English.

- The verse has three lines: God created the human in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
- הָאָדָם now has the article: it points back to the indefinite אָדָם of 1:26. It is not yet a proper name.
- The object suffix changes from singular (אֹתוֹ) to plural (אֹתָם): one human, then male and female.
- The first בָּרָא is a wayyiqtol; the next two are qatal and restate the act.
- בְּצַלְמוֹ and בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים use the same noun: 'his image' and 'the image of God'.

Note: The suffix of 'in his image' could refer to God or to the human; Rashi takes the image as a mold made for the human, and says that mold is the likeness of his maker. Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'in a mold made for him'; everything was created by word, but the human by hands (Ps 139:5); he was made with a seal, like a coin struck with a die. The English keeps 'in his image'; the mold sense goes in the notes.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Scripture explains that the image prepared for him is the image of the likeness of his maker. The English 'in the image of God' follows.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the plain meaning is that here we are told both were created on the sixth day, with how explained elsewhere; the midrash says he was made with two faces and then divided. The English 'male and female' follows the plain meaning.

Apparatus:

- The suffix of בְּצַלְמוֹ ('in his image') is not fixed by the Hebrew: God or the human. The next clause names God.

- וְכִבְשֻׁהָ is written without the second ו of the verb form; Rashi draws a lesson from the spelling.
- After the etnaḥta on וְכִבְשֻׁהָ, the second half opens with וּרְדוּ: rule over three domains, fish, birds and every living thing that crawls, where 1:26 listed five.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: וכבשה lacks a ו to teach that the male subdues the female so that she will not be a gadabout, and that the man, who is used to subduing, is commanded to be fruitful and multiply, not the woman. This is drawn from the spelling and does not change the English 'subdue it'.

- עֵשֶׂב זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע and פְּרִי־עֵץ זֹרֵעַ זָרַע are parallel, each a participle with its cognate noun: 'seed-sowing seed'.
- The zaqef qaton on הָאָרֶץ divides the plants from the trees; the revia on זֶרַע sets off the relative clause אֲשֶׁר עַל־פְּנֵי כָל־הָאָרֶץ; the etnaḥta on זָרַע ends the gift.
- יִהְיֶה is singular: 'it shall be', with the whole gift as one subject, not each plant.
- לְאָכְלָה is 'for food'; the commentators note that this verse does not yet allow meat.

Note: The verb זֹרֵעַ is 'sowing' and the English 'bears seed' renders the sense; the cognate noun is in English 'seed'. The commentators agree that the gift is plants only; the English says nothing about meat, which is not in the Hebrew.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: he put cattle and wild animals on a par with them in food, and did not allow the human and his wife to kill a creature and eat flesh; all of them together were to eat only green herbs. When the sons of Noah came, he permitted flesh to them (Gen 9:3). The English 'for food', with plants alone, follows this.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: he permitted people, and everything with a living soul, to eat every herb; every tree fruit is permitted to people; the green herb is for the animals and for everything that crawls; meat was not permitted until after the flood. The English follows: the human has the plants and the fruit.

- The telisha gedola on הָאָרֶץ is a rare doubled accent mark.
- The English adds 'I have given' where the Hebrew has an object marker and no verb.

Note: The Hebrew leaves out the verb 'I have given', so the English supplies it from 1:29 in the phrase that holds the object marker. The relative clause 'in which there is a living soul' stands after 'everything that crawls on the earth' and the English keeps it there; it can be read of all three groups.

Apparatus:

- The relative clause 'in which is a living soul' could limit only the crawling things or the three groups together; the English keeps the Hebrew order.

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: some say יוֹם in יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי is in the construct state (סמוך) and the sense is 'the day of the sixth sphere'; this is not true. It means the day that is sixth from the first day, so also יוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי: a noun followed by an adjective with the article, as אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי (Lev 24:10), and רְקִיעַ הַשָּׁמַיִם (1:20), 'the firmament that is heaven'. The English 'the sixth day' follows this.

Apparatus:

- The paragraph mark פ follows this verse.

Grammar:

- וַיְכֻלּוּ is Pual (passive): the heavens and earth 'were completed', with no agent named.
- The wayyiqtol וַ + יְכֻלּוּ continues the narrative of chapter 1 and closes it.
- The tevir on וַיְכֻלּוּ and the tipḥa on וְהָאָרֶץ divide the verse; the silluq ends it.
- צְבָאָם ('their host') is normally an army or the stars; here it covers everything that fills heaven and earth.

Note: 'So' renders the narrative waw. 'Host' is kept literal, because the commentators differ on what it contains (living things, luminaries, angels).

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the form is passive, the agent not named; the sense is 'were finished'. The sea is included in 'earth', since sea and land are as one bundle.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the host of earth is the creatures and plants and humans; the host of heaven is the luminaries and stars, and may also include the separate intellects (angels). The English keeps 'host' and does not decide this.
- Radak (records): Radak: the host are the offspring of heaven and earth, all finished on the sixth day; after that nothing new is made except by miracle.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos renders the passive 'were completed' (אשתכללו) and 'their hosts'.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: the verb means that the purpose of existence was attained, in its entirety.

#### Genesis 2:2

**On the seventh day God finished his work that he had made, and on the seventh day he rested from all his work that he had made.**

Grammar:

- The verse repeats 'on the seventh day' and 'his work that he made' in two clauses: he finished, and he rested.
- The etnaḥta after עָשָׂה divides the verse into the finishing and the resting.
- וַיִּשְׁבֹּת is the verb from which 'Sabbath' comes; its sense is 'cease, desist', not 'be weary'.
- אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה is a qatal inside a relative clause; the English pluperfect 'had made' shows that the work was done before.
- The ב of בַּיּוֹם means 'on'. Some read it as 'before' (the work done before the seventh day); Ibn Ezra cites this view and rejects it: finishing a work is not doing work.

Note: The English keeps 'On the seventh day' (Rashi's reading and the plain Hebrew). The view that the ב means 'before' (the work was finished before the seventh day) is cited by Ibn Ezra and rejected, and is recorded in the apparatus. The verbs finished and rested are not the same: 'finished' is Piel of כלה, 'rested' is Qal of שבת.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: God knows his times and moments exactly, so he entered the seventh day by a hair's breadth and it looked as though he finished in it; another reading: what was the world lacking? Rest; when Sabbath came, rest came, and the work was finished.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra cites two views and rejects both: that the days were themselves created and the work was completed by the creation of the seventh day ("וזה הפירוש תפל"), and that the ב here means 'before', as in 'on the first day you shall remove leaven' (Ex 12:15). "ולמה זאת הצרה": the finishing of work is not work, as if it said he did no work on it; so too וַיְכַל and וַיִּשְׁבֹּת. The English keeps the plain 'on the seventh day'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'his work that he made' means the work he made on the sixth day, before the Sabbath. The English 'had made' fits.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'rested on the seventh day from all his work' means from all the creations that he created.
- Radak (records): Radak: when the seventh day came the work was complete and nothing was left to make on it; so on the seventh day he finished, in the sense that it was a finished work.
- Radak (records): Radak: nothing was created after the sixth day; the Torah speaks in human language, since he does not tire; or 'rested' means 'ceased'.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'and the LORD finished on the seventh day his work' and 'rested' (נח).
- Sforno (records): Sforno: at the beginning of the seventh day, the indivisible instant that begins the future time, as Genesis Rabbah has it, 'like a hair's breadth'.

Apparatus:

- Rashi (R. Shimon): flesh and blood adds from the weekday to the holy day because he does not know his times; God does, so he finished exactly at the day's edge. Others, cited and rejected by Ibn Ezra: ב has the sense of 'before', as in Ex 12:15.
