Grammar:

- Terah is the subject of וַיִּקַּח, the three objects are Abram, Lot, and Sarai, each with the object marker; Radak explains that Terah leads the group because he is the father.
- וַיֵּצְאוּ is plural and has no stated subject; אִתָּם 'with them' shows the group went together, led by Abram according to Ramban and Radak.
- לָלֶכֶת אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן: infinitive construct of הלך (the Hebrew of this verb uses the form of ילך) with directional ה: 'to go to the land of Canaan'.
- The accents: geresh on אִתָּם, revia on כַּשְׂדִּים; the departure is set off from its goal and from the stay in Haran.
- וַיָּבֹאוּ עַד־חָרָן: 'came as far as Haran'; the verb of settling, וַיֵּשְׁבוּ, shows that the journey stopped there.

Note: Rashi reads וַיֵּצְאוּ אִתָּם as 'Terah and Abram went out with Lot and Sarai'; the English follows, with 'they' for the group and 'with them' kept in the line. 'Settled' follows Qal 3 of יָשַׁב. The pack's entry for הָלַךְ lists no Qal sense 'go', and the entry for עַד lists only its temporal senses, so no sense is given for לָלֶכֶת or for the spatial עַד.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'Terah and Abram went out with Lot and Sarai.' The English adopts this: the subject of 'went out' is Terah and Abram, and the object is Lot and Sarai.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: because Abram was greater than his father, those who followed his counsel went with him, so the text says 'with them'; Lot and Sarai went on Abram's account, even after he parted from his father.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: after God said 'Go' to Abram, Abram told his father in God's name and Terah agreed; Nahor refused; Lot was taken because his father was dead.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: here the going is credited to Abram, since the command was his.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: God had not told Abram to go to Canaan but to the land that I will show you; Canaan is the first land on the way out of Aram.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: Terah stopped at Haran, near the border and near Canaan, to be near Abram.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the text repeats 'wife of Abram his son' for emphasis.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: Sarai left willingly, following her husband in faith.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Targum Onkelos follows the Hebrew.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: Canaan was suited to intellectual perfection, desirable among all lands, and its air was not spoiled by the flood.

#### Genesis 11:32

> וַיִּהְי֣וּ יְמֵי־תֶ֔רַח חָמֵ֥שׁ שָׁנִ֖ים וּמָאתַ֣יִם שָׁנָ֑ה וַיָּ֥מׇת תֶּ֖רַח בְּחָרָֽן׃

**The days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and Terah died in Haran.**

Literal: and-were days-of Terah five years and-two-hundred year and-died Terah in-Haran

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיִּהְי֣וּ | and were — wayyiqtol plural of היה | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, plural) | Qal III |
| יְמֵי | the days of — construct plural; 'the days of his life' | יוֹם |  | noun (common, masculine, plural, construct) | 4 |
| תֶ֔רַח | Terah | תֶּ֫רַח |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| חָמֵ֥שׁ | five | חָמֵשׁ | חמשׁ | adjective (cardinal number, feminine, singular, absolute) |  |
| שָׁנִ֖ים | years | שָׁנָה | שׁנה | noun (common, feminine, plural, absolute) |  |
| וּמָאתַ֣יִם | and two hundred — dual of מֵאָה, 'two hundred'. The pack's entry lists only the sense 'hundredth', which does not fit, so no sense is given. | ו: and + מֵאָה | מאה | conjunction + adjective (cardinal number, both genders, dual, absolute) |  |
| שָׁנָ֑ה | years | שָׁנָה | שׁנה | noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) |  |
| וַיָּ֥מׇת | and died — wayyiqtol | ו: and + מוּת | מות | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| תֶּ֖רַח | Terah | תֶּ֫רַח |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| בְּחָרָֽן׃ | in Haran | ב: in, with, by + חָרָן |  | preposition + noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים וּמָאתַיִם שָׁנָה: the smaller number comes first; 'five years and two hundred years'. The dual מָאתַיִם is 'two hundred'.
- The verse closes the genealogy with Terah's whole life, as the genealogies of Genesis 5 do.
- The inverted nun in בְּחָרָן, which Rashi and Radak comment on, belongs to the text's note, not to the English line.
- Terah's death at Haran stands before Abram's departure in 12:4, a question which Rashi and Ramban discuss.

Note: Terah lived 205 years: at Abram's birth he was seventy, so Abram was 135 at his death; yet Abram left Haran at seventy-five (12:4). Rashi and Ramban face this: the text names Terah 'dead' early. The English follows the plain reading and records the chronology problem in the commentary. The paragraph mark פ follows this verse.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: Terah died after Abram left Haran for Canaan, since Abram was seventy-five at his departure and Terah was seventy at Abram's birth, making Terah 145; the text places the death first so that people would not say Abram failed to honor his father, and calls the wicked 'dead' even while alive. The English states the death in the verse's order and records Rashi's reading.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the text of this comment is an incomplete fragment, a parenthesis opening the next remark on the inverted nun.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the nun of בחרן is inverted to say: until Abram, the anger of the Place (God's wrath, חרון אף) was in the world. The English does not reflect the letter's shape.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: he questions Rashi's reasoning; he says it is the text's custom to give the father's life and death, then turn to the son; and Terah's case differs because the earlier genealogies omit death.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: Terah's days were 205; Abram was 135 at his death; by Seder Olam Abraham buried Terah two years before Sarah died.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the verse says Terah died in Haran to show he did not abandon his idols and left for love of his son, not for love of God.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak (continuing his previous comment, which ends 'and the nun of'): the nun of חָרָן is written 'wrapped' (מְלֻפֶּפֶת), that is, inverted. The sages drew from it that God killed Terah in wrath (חֲרוֹן אַף) because he did not repent; another midrash says he did repent, from 15:15 'you shall come to your fathers in peace'.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Targum Onkelos: 'And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years; and Terah died in Haran.'
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: Terah did not pursue what they had set out to reach and never came to Abram in Canaan.

Apparatus:

- Paragraph break (פ) after the verse. Chronology: 70 + 75 = 145, whereas Terah lived to 205 (Rashi; Ramban; Radak).

## Lekh Lekha — לֶךְ־לְךָ (Genesis 12:1–17:27)

### Reading text

<sup>12:1</sup> The LORD said to Abram, "Go forth from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you." <sup>12:2</sup> I will make you into a great nation, I will bless you, and make your name great, and you shall be a blessing. <sup>12:3</sup> I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse, and all the families of the earth will bless themselves by you. <sup>12:4</sup> So Abram went, as the LORD had spoken to him, and Lot went with him. Now Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran. <sup>12:5</sup> Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all the property that they had amassed, and the people they had acquired in Haran, and they set out for the land of Canaan, and they came to the land of Canaan. <sup>12:6</sup> Abram passed through the land as far as the site of Shechem, as far as the terebinth of Moreh. The Canaanite was then in the land. <sup>12:7</sup> The LORD appeared to Abram and said, "To your offspring I will give this land." So he built an altar there to the LORD who had appeared to him. <sup>12:8</sup> He moved his tent from there to the mountain east of Bethel and pitched it, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to the LORD and called on the name of the LORD. <sup>12:9</sup> Abram set out, going on from stage to stage toward the Negeb.

<sup>12:10</sup> Now there was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine in the land was severe. <sup>12:11</sup> As he drew near to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, "Look now, I know that you are a woman beautiful in appearance. <sup>12:12</sup> When the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife,’ and they will kill me, but you they will let live. <sup>12:13</sup> Say, please, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me on your account, and I may live because of you. <sup>12:14</sup> When Abram came to Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful. <sup>12:15</sup> Pharaoh's officials saw her and praised her for Pharaoh, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house. <sup>12:16</sup> And Pharaoh treated Abram well because of her, and he came to have flocks and herds, donkeys, male and female slaves, she-donkeys, and camels. <sup>12:17</sup> Then the LORD struck Pharaoh with great plagues, and his household too, on account of Sarai, Abram's wife. <sup>12:18</sup> Pharaoh summoned Abram and said, "What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she is your wife?" <sup>12:19</sup> Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her as my wife? Now, here is your wife: take her and go. <sup>12:20</sup> Pharaoh gave men orders concerning him, and they escorted him on his way, together with his wife and all that was his. <sup>13:1</sup> So Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that was his, and Lot with him, to the Negeb. <sup>13:2</sup> Now Abram was very heavily laden with livestock, with silver and with gold. <sup>13:3</sup> He went on his journeys from the Negeb as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai, <sup>13:4</sup> to the place of the altar that he had made there at first; and there Abram called on the name of the LORD. <sup>13:5</sup> Also, Lot, who went with Abram, had flocks and herds and tents. <sup>13:6</sup> But the land could not support them to live together, for their property was great, and they could not live together. <sup>13:7</sup> So there was a quarrel between the herders of Abram's livestock and the herders of Lot's livestock. The Canaanites and the Perizzites were then living in the land. <sup>13:8</sup> Abram said to Lot, "Please, let there be no quarrel between me and you, or between my herders and your herders, for we are kinsmen." <sup>13:9</sup> Is not the whole land before you? Please separate from me. If you go left, I will go right; and if you go right, I will go left. <sup>13:10</sup> Lot lifted up his eyes and saw the whole plain of the Jordan, that all of it was well watered, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as you come to Zoar. <sup>13:11</sup> Lot chose for himself the whole plain of the Jordan, and Lot set out from the east, and they separated, one from the other. <sup>13:12</sup> Abram lived in the land of Canaan, while Lot lived in the cities of the plain and pitched his tent as far as Sodom. <sup>13:13</sup> Now the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners against the LORD, exceedingly. <sup>13:14</sup> The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward." <sup>13:15</sup> for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever. <sup>13:16</sup> I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if anyone can count the dust of the earth, then your offspring too can be counted. <sup>13:17</sup> Get up, walk about the land through its length and its breadth, for I will give it to you. <sup>13:18</sup> Abram moved his tent, came and settled at the terebinths of Mamre, which are in Hebron, and built there an altar to the LORD.

<sup>14:1</sup> It happened in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim, <sup>14:2</sup> they made war on Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar. <sup>14:3</sup> All these joined forces in the Valley of Siddim, which is the Salt Sea. <sup>14:4</sup> For twelve years they served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled. <sup>14:5</sup> In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, and the kings who were with him, and they struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim at Ham, and the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim, <sup>14:6</sup> and the Horites in their mountain, Seir, as far as El-paran, which is by the wilderness. <sup>14:7</sup> Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat, which is Kadesh, and struck all the territory of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar. <sup>14:8</sup> Then the king of Sodom went out, and the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar, and they drew up battle lines against them in the Valley of Siddim. <sup>14:9</sup> with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar: four kings against the five. <sup>14:10</sup> The Valley of Siddim was pit upon pit of bitumen, and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell there, and the survivors fled into the hills. <sup>14:11</sup> They took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and went away. <sup>14:12</sup> They took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, and his goods, and went away; he was living in Sodom. <sup>14:13</sup> The fugitive came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the terebinths of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner; they were allies of Abram. <sup>14:14</sup> When Abram heard that his brother had been taken captive, he armed his trained men, those born in his household, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued as far as Dan. <sup>14:15</sup> He and his servants divided themselves against them by night and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is north of Damascus. <sup>14:16</sup> He brought back all the goods, and also brought back Lot his brother and his goods, and also the women and the people. <sup>14:17</sup> The king of Sodom went out to meet him, after his return from striking down Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, to the Valley of Shaveh, that is, the King's Valley. <sup>14:18</sup> Now Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine. He was a priest of God Most High. <sup>14:19</sup> He blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth." <sup>14:20</sup> And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand. And Abram gave him a tenth of everything. <sup>14:21</sup> The king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the people, and take the goods for yourself." <sup>14:22</sup> Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I raise my hand in oath to the LORD, God Most High, maker of heaven and earth: <sup>14:23</sup> I will not take so much as a thread or a sandal strap, nor anything that is yours, so that you cannot say, 'I made Abram rich.' <sup>14:24</sup> Not for me, only what my servants have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol and Mamre. They may take their share."

<sup>15:1</sup> After these events the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, saying: Do not be afraid, Abram. I am a shield for you; your reward is very great. <sup>15:2</sup> Abram said, My Lord, the LORD, what will you give me, when I go on childless, and the steward of my house is Eliezer of Damascus? <sup>15:3</sup> Abram said, Look, you have given me no offspring, and so a member of my household is my heir. <sup>15:4</sup> Then the word of the LORD came to him, saying: This man will not be your heir; but rather one who comes from your own body will be your heir. <sup>15:5</sup> He brought him outside and said, Look toward the sky, please, and count the stars, if you are able to count them. Then he said to him, So will your offspring be. <sup>15:6</sup> He trusted in the LORD, and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness. <sup>15:7</sup> He said to him, I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to take possession of it. <sup>15:8</sup> He said, My Lord, the LORD, by what will I know that I shall take possession of it? <sup>15:9</sup> He said to him, "Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon." <sup>15:10</sup> He took all these for him, cut them in the middle, and set each half opposite the other; but the birds he did not cut in two. <sup>15:11</sup> The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them off. <sup>15:12</sup> As the sun was about to go down, a deep sleep fell on Abram, and suddenly dread, a great darkness, was falling on him. <sup>15:13</sup> He said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land not theirs, and they will serve them, and they will oppress them, for four hundred years. <sup>15:14</sup> And also the nation that they will serve, I will judge; and afterward they will come out with great wealth. <sup>15:15</sup> As for you, you will go to your fathers in peace; you will be buried at a good old age. <sup>15:16</sup> And in the fourth generation they will return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete. <sup>15:17</sup> When the sun had set and it was thick darkness, there was a smoking furnace and a flaming torch that passed between these pieces. <sup>15:18</sup> On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying: To your offspring I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates: <sup>15:19</sup> the Kenites, the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites; <sup>15:20</sup> the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Rephaim; <sup>15:21</sup> the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.

<sup>16:1</sup> Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had not borne him a child. She had an Egyptian maidservant, and her name was Hagar. <sup>16:2</sup> Sarai said to Abram, "Look, the LORD has kept me from bearing children. Please go in to my maidservant; perhaps I shall be built up through her." And Abram listened to Sarai's voice. <sup>16:3</sup> Then Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her maidservant, at the end of ten years of Abram's dwelling in the land of Canaan, and gave her to Abram her husband to be his wife. <sup>16:4</sup> He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. She saw that she had conceived, and her mistress became of little account in her eyes. <sup>16:5</sup> Sarai said to Abram, "The wrong done to me is on you! I myself gave my maidservant into your arms, and when she saw that she had conceived, I became of little account in her eyes. May the LORD judge between me and you." <sup>16:6</sup> Abram said to Sarai, "Here, your maidservant is in your hand. Do to her what is good in your eyes." Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her presence. <sup>16:7</sup> Then the angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, by the spring on the way to Shur. <sup>16:8</sup> He said, "Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?" She said, "I am fleeing from Sarai my mistress." <sup>16:9</sup> The messenger of the LORD said to her, "Go back to your mistress, and submit to her authority." <sup>16:10</sup> The messenger of the LORD said to her, "I will greatly multiply your offspring, so that they cannot be counted for their multitude." <sup>16:11</sup> The messenger of the LORD said to her, "Here you are, pregnant: you will bear a son, and you are to name him Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your affliction." <sup>16:12</sup> He will be a wild ass of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he will dwell over against all his kin. <sup>16:13</sup> She called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are El Roi," for she said, "Have I even here seen, after the one who sees me?" <sup>16:14</sup> Therefore the well is called Beer Lahai Roi; there it is, between Kadesh and Bered. <sup>16:15</sup> Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram named his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael. <sup>16:16</sup> Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.

<sup>17:1</sup> When Abram was ninety-nine years old, the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, "I am El Shaddai. Walk before me and be whole." <sup>17:2</sup> I will set my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly. <sup>17:3</sup> Abram fell on his face, and God spoke with him, saying: <sup>17:4</sup> As for me, here is my covenant with you: you shall become the father of a multitude of nations. <sup>17:5</sup> No longer shall your name be called Abram; your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. <sup>17:6</sup> I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come forth from you. <sup>17:7</sup> I will establish my covenant between me and you and between your offspring after you, throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you. <sup>17:8</sup> I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession, and I will be their God. <sup>17:9</sup> God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you, throughout their generations." <sup>17:10</sup> This is my covenant, which you shall keep between me and you and between your offspring after you: every male among you is to be circumcised. <sup>17:11</sup> You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of covenant between me and you. <sup>17:12</sup> At eight days old every male among you is to be circumcised, throughout your generations: the one born in the house, or bought with money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring. <sup>17:13</sup> The one born in your house and the one bought with your money must be circumcised, and my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. <sup>17:14</sup> Any uncircumcised male who does not circumcise the flesh of his foreskin, that person shall be cut off from his kin; he has broken my covenant.

<sup>17:15</sup> God said to Abraham, "Sarai your wife: do not call her name Sarai, for Sarah is her name." <sup>17:16</sup> I will bless her, and I will also give you a son from her. I will bless her, and she shall become nations; kings of peoples shall come from her. <sup>17:17</sup> Abraham fell on his face and laughed, and said in his heart, "Will a child be born to a man a hundred years old? And will Sarah, a woman of ninety years, bear a child?" <sup>17:18</sup> Abraham said to God, "If only Ishmael might live before you!" <sup>17:19</sup> God said, "Truly, Sarah your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his descendants after him." <sup>17:20</sup> As for Ishmael, I have heard you. Look, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and will increase him exceedingly. He will father twelve chieftains, and I will make him a great nation. <sup>17:21</sup> But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear for you at this appointed time next year. <sup>17:22</sup> When he had finished speaking with him, God went up from Abraham. <sup>17:23</sup> Then Abraham took his son Ishmael and all those born in his house and all those bought with his money, every male among the men of Abraham's household, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskin on that very day, as God had spoken with him. <sup>17:24</sup> Now Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised, in the flesh of his foreskin. <sup>17:25</sup> And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. <sup>17:26</sup> On that very day Abraham was circumcised, and Ishmael his son. <sup>17:27</sup> And all the men of his household, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.

### Lekh Lekha by verse

#### Genesis 12:1

> וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהֹוָה֙ אֶל־אַבְרָ֔ם לֶךְ־לְךָ֛ מֵאַרְצְךָ֥ וּמִמּֽוֹלַדְתְּךָ֖ וּמִבֵּ֣ית אָבִ֑יךָ אֶל־הָאָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַרְאֶֽךָּ׃

**The LORD said to Abram, "Go forth from your land, from your birthplace, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you."**

Literal: and-said the-LORD to-Abram go-(you) to-you from-land-of-you and-from-birthplace-of-you and-from-house-of father-of-you to the-land that I-will-show-you

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיֹּ֤אמֶר | and said — wayyiqtol of אמר: narrative sequence, 'and he said' | ו: and + אָמַר | אמר | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| יְהֹוָה֙ | the LORD — the divine name, rendered 'the LORD' by the edition's decision | יהוה | הוה | noun (proper name) |  |
| אֶל | to | אֶל |  | preposition | 1 |
| אַבְרָ֔ם | Abram | אַבְרָם | אבה | noun (proper name) |  |
| לֶךְ | go — imperative of הלך (the first root letter falls away in the imperative: לֶךְ). The plain sense 'go' is not among the senses the pack lists for this entry (Qal II.1 'die' and II.2 'live, walk' are figurative), so no sense is given. | יָלַךְ | הלך | verb (qal, imperative, 2nd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| לְךָ֛ | for yourself — ל + 2nd person suffix, the so-called ethical dative: לֶךְ־לְךָ is an idiom of going, 'be off'. Rashi reads it as 'for your benefit'; Ramban and Radak say it is only idiom. | ל: to, for |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| מֵאַרְצְךָ֥ | from your land — מִ 'from' + construct אַרְצְ + suffix ךָ | מ: from, than + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | preposition + noun (common, both genders, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | 2 |
| וּמִמּֽוֹלַדְתְּךָ֖ | and from your birthplace — מוֹלֶדֶת, from ילד 'to bear': the place or kin of one's birth | ו: and + מ: from, than + מוֹלֶ֫דֶת | ילד | conjunction + preposition + noun (common, feminine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| וּמִבֵּ֣ית | and from the house of — construct state: 'the house of'; בַּיִת here means household, family | ו: and + מ: from, than + בַּ֫יִת |  | conjunction + preposition + noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 5 |
| אָבִ֑יךָ | your father | אָב | אבה | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | 1 |
| אֶל | to | אֶל |  | preposition | 1 |
| הָאָ֖רֶץ | the land | ה: the + אֶ֫רֶץ | ארץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) | 2 |
| אֲשֶׁ֥ר | that | אֲשֶׁר | אשׁר | particle (relative) |  |
| אַרְאֶֽךָּ׃ | I will show you — Hifil imperfect 1st person singular of ראה with the 2nd person suffix: 'I will show you'. The segol and the dagesh in the kaf (־ֶךָּ) come from an assimilated (energic) nun, a suffix form that III-ה verbs often take in pause, here under silluq. The land is not named. | רָאָה | ראה | verb (hifil, imperfect (yiqtol), 1st person, common, singular) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph 1.a |

Grammar:

- לֶךְ־לְךָ is the imperative of הלך with a reflexive-looking dative. The first-letter loss in the imperative (הלך gives לֶךְ) is regular for this root. Ramban and Radak list parallel idioms: אֵלְכָה לִּי, קְחוּ לָכֶם.
- The three prepositional phrases מֵאַרְצְךָ, וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ, וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ run from the widest circle to the narrowest: land, kin, household. The accents mark the list; the etnaḥta falls on אָבִיךָ and splits the verse between what he leaves and where he goes.
- The destination is deliberately not named: אֶל־הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ. The hifil of ראה governs two accusatives (here the suffix and the land, which is the object of the relative clause).
- In pause, under the silluq, the suffix of אַרְאֶךָּ is ־ֶךָּ: the dagesh in the kaf is an assimilated (energic) nun.

Note: The narrative order is kept: the command follows 11:31–32, where Terah and Abram have already reached Haran. Rashi's reading (the command means 'move further away') fits that order; Ibn Ezra takes the command as given earlier, in Ur of the Chaldeans. The English says only 'said' and does not choose a pluperfect. 'Birthplace' is chosen for מוֹלֶדֶת because the pack's lexicon gives 'birth, kindred'; Ramban shows that the word covers the family's home. The ethical dative is dropped from the English as idiom; Rashi's reading is recorded.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: לֶךְ־לְךָ means 'for your own benefit and good': there He will make you a great nation, here you do not merit children; and also so that your nature (reputation) becomes known. Ramban and Radak say instead that this is simply the idiom of the language; the English does not translate the dative.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: but he had already left Ur with his father and come to Haran; so the command means 'distance yourself even further from there and leave your father's house'. The English leaves 'your land' as it stands and the verse order (Haran, then this command) is kept in the English.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: He did not reveal the land at once, in order to make it dear in Abram's eyes and to give him reward for every single utterance (compare Isaac in 22:2). The English keeps the destination unnamed: 'the land that I will show you'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: God commanded Abram while he was still in Ur of the Chaldeans to leave his land, his birthplace and his father's house. The reason: God knew that Terah, once he had set out for Canaan, would settle in Haran, and Terah did not die until sixty years after Abram left his father's house in Haran; Scripture simply does not give Abram's age when he left Ur. After 'that I will show you' God revealed the secret to him (12:5, 'they set out for the land of Canaan'), or 'I will show you' refers to 13:15, 'all the land that you see I will give to you'. The English does not take the verb as pluperfect, and this reading is recorded as the alternative.
- Ramban (not-applicable): Ramban quotes Rashi ('distance yourself further'), then rejects Ibn Ezra's view that the command came in Ur. Genesis 11:31 says Terah took Abram, so Abram left Ur on his father's initiative. Joshua 24:3 says 'from beyond the River', not 'from Ur'. And in Genesis 24:4, 10 'my land and my birthplace' is Aram Naharaim, the city of Nahor. His own view: Haran is Abram's land and birthplace, the land of his fathers, and the command to leave them came there. The three terms are named because each is harder to leave than the last. The comment concerns the history of the narrative and does not change the English.
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos translates the verse closely: אִיזֵל לָךְ מֵאַרְעָךְ; it keeps the idiom לָךְ as the Hebrew has it.

Apparatus:

- 12:1.2, the divine name: MAM writes יְהֹוָה, the pack's analysis reads יְהוָה; the English is 'the LORD' in both.
- The tense of וַיֹּאמֶר: simple past (Rashi's sequence) against pluperfect 'had said' (Ibn Ezra, Radak: he spoke to him before leaving Ur, as in 15:7).

#### Genesis 12:2

> וְאֶֽעֶשְׂךָ֙ לְג֣וֹי גָּד֔וֹל וַאֲבָ֣רֶכְךָ֔ וַאֲגַדְּלָ֖ה שְׁמֶ֑ךָ וֶהְיֵ֖ה בְּרָכָֽה׃

**I will make you into a great nation, I will bless you, and make your name great, and you shall be a blessing.**

Literal: and-I-will-make-you to-nation great and-I-will-bless-you and-I-will-make-great name-of-you and-be (you) blessing

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וְאֶֽעֶשְׂךָ֙ | and I will make you — וְ + yiqtol, 1st person singular, of עשׂה with a 2nd person suffix: not a wayyiqtol (the vav has shewa, and there is no doubling). After the imperative לֶךְ of 12:1 it states what will follow from the going. The ayin has a full segol where the plain form has ḥaṭef segol (אֶעֱשֶׂה), because a shewa follows it. | ו: and + עָשָׂה | עשׂה | conjunction + verb (qal, imperfect (yiqtol), 1st person, common, singular) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Qal II.1 |
| לְג֣וֹי | into a nation — ל + גּוֹי: 'to (become) a nation' | ל: to, for + גּוֹי | גוה | preposition + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| גָּד֔וֹל | great — the adjective agrees with גּוֹי: 'a great nation', great in number. The pack's entry lists only senses 4 'loud', 9 'do great things' and 10 'greatness', none of which fits, so no sense is given. | גָּדוֹל | גדל | adjective (adjective, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| וַאֲבָ֣רֶכְךָ֔ | and I will bless you — Piel: God blesses a person; the pack lists this as Pi 2. Rashi (from Bereshit Rabbah) takes it as 'with wealth'. | ו: and + בָּרַךְ | ברך | conjunction + verb (piel, imperfect (yiqtol), 1st person, common, singular) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Pi 2 |
| וַאֲגַדְּלָ֖ה | and I will make great — Piel of גדל 'make great'; the final ָה is the cohortative-like ending of the 1st person | ו: and + גָּדַל | גדל | conjunction + verb (piel, imperfect (yiqtol), 1st person, common, singular) | Pi 2 |
| שְׁמֶ֑ךָ | your name — שֵׁם here as reputation, renown | שֵׁם |  | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | 2.b |
| וֶהְיֵ֖ה | and be — imperative of היה: 'be!'. Radak says it stands in the place of 'and you will be'; Rashi takes it as a real command with a gift of power. | ו: and + הָיָה | היה | conjunction + verb (qal, imperative, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Qal II.2 |
| בְּרָכָֽה׃ | a blessing — בְּרָכָה, here a source of blessing, a byword in which others bless | בְּרָכָה | ברך | noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 2 |

Grammar:

- Three first-person imperfects (וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ, וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ, וַאֲגַדְּלָה) carry the promise. None is a wayyiqtol: the vav has shewa, or pataḥ before the ḥaṭef pataḥ of the guttural א (a first-person wayyiqtol would have וָאֲ with qamets).
- The fourth verb, וֶהְיֵה, is an imperative addressed to Abram, 'and be'. Radak takes it as an imperative standing for the future 'and you will be' (compare Deut. 32:50); Rashi reads it as a gift: the power of blessing is put into Abram's hand.
- וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ is Piel with a suffix; וַאֲגַדְּלָה is Piel of גדל, causative 'make great', with the cohortative ending ־ָה. The root גדל recurs: גּוֹי גָּדוֹל, וַאֲגַדְּלָה.
- In וֶהְיֵה the vav has segol because the imperative הֱיֵה begins with ה under ḥaṭef segol. Before a ḥaṭef the vav takes the matching short vowel, and the ḥaṭef becomes a silent shewa (וֶהְ־).
- The accents: the etnaḥta on שְׁמֶךָ divides the verse. The first half holds the three promises, and the second half holds וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה alone.

Note: Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah) reads the three promises as answering the three losses of travel, which diminishes children, wealth and name: 'nation' is children, 'bless' is wealth, 'make great your name' is fame. The English keeps 'bless' unspecified and records this. Radak agrees on wealth for 'bless' and on renown for the name. For וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה the English has 'you shall be', so that the imperative is plainly addressed to Abram. Rashi says the blessings are put in Abram's hand, Radak says the imperative stands for a future 'you will be', and Ramban says that people will invoke him in blessing.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the journey diminishes procreation, property and renown, so three blessings were needed; He promised him children, wealth and a name. 'Make you into a great nation' is the promise of children.
- Rashi (records): Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: 'I will bless you' means with wealth. The English keeps the verb general ('bless') and records the narrower reading, which Radak also gives (13:2, 'rich in cattle, silver and gold').
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the blessings are placed in your hand; until now they were in Mine (I blessed Adam and Noah), from now on you will bless whomever you wish. The English 'you shall be a blessing' addresses the imperative to Abram.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'I will make you into a great nation' is the origin of the phrase 'God of Abraham' in the Amidah blessing. A liturgical homily; it does not bear on the plain sense.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'I will bless you' is the origin of 'God of Isaac' in the Amidah. A liturgical homily.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'and make your name great' is the origin of 'God of Jacob'; one might have thought the blessing is concluded with all three, so the text says 'be a blessing': it is concluded with you (Abraham) alone. A liturgical homily.
- Radak (follows): Radak: וֶהְיֵה is an imperative in the place of a full-vowelled future, 'and you will be', as in 'go up and die on the mountain' (Deut. 32:50); your blessing will be so great that you will be a blessing to others, as a man blesses his son 'may God bless you like Abraham'.

Apparatus:

- וֶהְיֵה: an imperative (the parse; Rashi: the power of blessing is given into Abram's hand), which Radak reads in the sense of a future, 'you will be'. The English 'you shall be' carries both.

#### Genesis 12:3

> וַאֲבָֽרְכָה֙ מְבָ֣רְכֶ֔יךָ וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ֖ אָאֹ֑ר וְנִבְרְכ֣וּ בְךָ֔ כֹּ֖ל מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת הָאֲדָמָֽה׃

**I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse, and all the families of the earth will bless themselves by you.**

Literal: and-I-will-bless those-who-bless-you and-the-one-who-curses-you I-will-curse and-will-bless-themselves in-you all-of families-of the-ground

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַאֲבָֽרְכָה֙ | and I will bless — Piel imperfect, 1st person, with the vav of continuation; the pack's base vocalisation וַאֲבָֽרְכָה is noted in the variants (WLC: וַאֲבָֽרֲכָה) | ו: and + בָּרַךְ | ברך | conjunction + verb (piel, imperfect (yiqtol), 1st person, common, singular) | Pi 2 |
| מְבָ֣רְכֶ֔יךָ | those who bless you — Piel active participle, masculine PLURAL, construct with a suffix: 'blessers of you'. Ibn Ezra notes that it is plural. | בָּרַךְ | ברך | verb (piel, participle, masculine, plural, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Pi 3 |
| וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ֖ | and the one who curses you — Piel participle, masculine SINGULAR, construct with a suffix; Ibn Ezra and Radak note that it is singular, because those who curse him will be few | ו: and + קָלַל | קלל | conjunction + verb (piel, participle, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Pi |
| אָאֹ֑ר | I will curse — Qal imperfect 1st person singular of the geminate (doubled-letter) root ארר. The preformative א has qamets, as in geminate verbs (compare יָסֹב), and is followed by the root's first letter א with ḥolem; the doubled ר is written once. אָרַר is a different and stronger verb than קלל; the English has 'curse' for both. | אָרַר | ארר | verb (qal, imperfect (yiqtol), 1st person, common, singular) | Qal |
| וְנִבְרְכ֣וּ | and will bless themselves — Niphal perfect with vav (a weqatal continuing the promise): reflexive 'bless oneself', in the pack's Niph sense; some read it as passive, 'be blessed' | ו: and + בָּרַךְ | ברך | conjunction + verb (nifal, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, common, plural) | Niph |
| בְךָ֔ | by you — בְּ + suffix: 'by you', 'in you'; the preposition marks the person whose name will be used as the blessing | ב: in, with, by |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| כֹּ֖ל | all of — construct state: 'all of' | כֹּל | כלל | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | 1 |
| מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת | the families of — construct plural | מִשְׁפָּחָה | שׁפח | noun (common, feminine, plural, construct) | 1 |
| הָאֲדָמָֽה׃ | the earth — הָאֲדָמָה 'the ground', here the whole inhabited earth | ה: the + אֲדָמָה | אדם | particle (definite article) + noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 3 |

Grammar:

- The plural participle מְבָרְכֶיךָ and the singular מְקַלֶּלְךָ are kept apart in the English ('those who' / 'the one who'): many will bless, few will curse (Ibn Ezra, Radak).
- The object מְקַלֶּלְךָ is placed first in its clause and the verb אָאֹר follows: this fronting is the Hebrew's way of setting the two outcomes against each other.
- וְנִבְרְכוּ is Niphal. The Niphal of ברך can be reflexive ('bless oneself') or passive ('be blessed'); Rashi reads it as 'bless themselves': people will say 'may you be like Abraham' (compare 48:20, 'by you Israel will bless: may God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh').
- The two cursing verbs differ: קלל (Piel) is 'treat lightly, curse' and ארר (Qal) is the stronger 'lay under a curse'; the English uses 'curse' for both.
- The accents: the pashta on וַאֲבָרְכָה, the zaqef on מְבָרְכֶיךָ, the etnaḥta on אָאֹר mark the two halves of the first part, and the verse ends with the great blessing as a separate clause.

Note: The Niphal is read as reflexive following Rashi (who says 'this is its plain sense'); the passive 'will be blessed through you' is the alternative and is recorded here. Ramban holds that both are possible and adds that all will be blessed on account of him. The English preserves the number of the participles.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: there are many aggadot, but this is the plain sense: a man says to his son 'may you be like Abraham'; so every 'and they shall be blessed through you' in Scripture; and this proves it: 'by you shall Israel bless, saying: may God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh' (48:20). The English reads the Niphal as reflexive.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on מְבָרְכֶיךָ: plural ('רבים'). The English renders 'those who bless you'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ: singular ('יחיד'). The English renders 'the one who curses you'. Radak gives the reason: few will curse him.

Apparatus:

- 12:3.1 vowels: the base text has וַאֲבָֽרְכָה, WLC has וַאֲבָֽרֲכָה (a different ḥaṭef pattern); no difference in sense.
- וְנִבְרְכוּ: reflexive 'bless themselves' (Rashi) against passive 'be blessed through you' (a common alternative; Ramban allows both, 'be blessed on his account').
- וַאֲבָֽרְכָה֙: WLC reads וַאֲבָֽרֲכָה֙ (vowels)

#### Genesis 12:4

> וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ אַבְרָ֗ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבֶּ֤ר אֵלָיו֙ יְהֹוָ֔ה וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ אִתּ֖וֹ ל֑וֹט וְאַבְרָ֗ם בֶּן־חָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנִים֙ וְשִׁבְעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה בְּצֵאת֖וֹ מֵחָרָֽן׃

- וַיֵּלֶךְ is a wayyiqtol with the weak root's first letter dropped; it is repeated at the start of the second clause with a new subject (Lot).
- כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר ... יְהֹוָה: the perfect after כַּאֲשֶׁר refers back to the command of verse 1, hence 'had spoken'.
- The clause וְאַבְרָם בֶּן־חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים וְשִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה is verbless: 'and Abram (was) son of five years and seventy years'. The subject comes first; the vav marks a circumstance.
- בְּצֵאתוֹ is the preposition ב with an infinitive construct and a suffix: the Hebrew way to write a temporal clause 'when he went out'.

Note: The pluperfect in 'as the LORD had spoken' is needed in English; the Hebrew perfect is unmarked for time. The age is given as 'seventy-five' because the Hebrew counts units before tens.

Commentary:

- Radak (follows): Radak on כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר: he did not ask or test, but believed that God would fulfil what He had said to him.
- Radak (follows): Radak: he left his father there; perhaps he stayed some days to persuade him to come; he was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos renders the verse closely: וַאֲזַל אַבְרָם כְּמָא דִמַלֵּיל עִמֵּיהּ יְיָ.

Apparatus:

- No variant readings are listed for this verse in the pack.
- Terah was seventy at Abram's birth (11:26) and died at two hundred and five (11:32), so he died sixty years after Abram left Haran at seventy-five, though 11:32 tells of it first. Ibn Ezra on 12:1 says this: Terah did not die until sixty years after Abram left. The English translates the text as it stands.

Grammar:

- The verse is a string of wayyiqtols (וַיִּקַּח, וַיֵּצְאוּ, וַיָּבֹאוּ), each marking the next step; the objects of וַיִּקַּח are joined by repeated וְאֶת־.
- The two relative clauses אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁוּ and אֲשֶׁר־עָשׂוּ use perfects that describe what had been done before Abram took them, hence the English pluperfect. The root רכשׁ is in both the noun רְכוּשׁ and the verb רָכָשׁוּ.
- הַנֶּפֶשׁ is singular in form but collective in sense ('the persons'); the verb עָשׂוּ that follows is plural.
- אַרְצָה כְּנַעַן uses the directional he, ־ָה, on a noun in the construct state; the same expression appears twice, in the goal (to go) and in the arrival. The repetition is deliberate: they set out for Canaan and they arrived there, unlike Terah (11:31).
- The verb עָשָׂה, 'make', has the sense 'acquire' here; the pack's lexicon lists it as Qal II.7.

Note: עָשׂוּ is the difficulty. Rashi gives two readings: the aggadic one (Abram converted the men, Sarai the women, and Scripture counts it as if they had made them), and what he calls the plain sense, 'servants and maidservants that they acquired'. Ibn Ezra gives 'slaves born in the house, or 'made' is 'acquired'' and, as another view, 'souls whom they taught the truth'. Radak also gives the aggadic reading and Onkelos's, 'those whom they subjected to the Torah'. The English follows the plain sense and records the other readings.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'the people they had made in Haran': Abram converted the men and Sarai the women, and Scripture credits them as if they had made them; but the plain sense is servants and maidservants that they acquired, as in 'he made all this wealth for himself' (31:1) and 'Israel is making power' (Num. 24:18), a language of acquiring and gathering. The English takes the plain sense and records the homily here.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on רכושם: מִקְנֶה, 'what is acquired, possessions' (the word is used above all of livestock), as in 'for their property was great' (13:6). The English 'property' gives the general sense.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on הנפש: slaves born in the house, or 'made' means 'acquired' (compare Deut. 8:17); and some say they were the souls whom they taught the truth, to serve God. The English takes 'acquired'; the last reading is recorded.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the meaning of 'they set out to go' is toward the place that God had said. The English says 'set out for the land of Canaan' and does not add a purpose clause.
- Radak (follows): Radak on רָכָשׁוּ: Abram and Lot; the property includes silver and the other movable goods.
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos: וְיָת נַפְשָׁתָא דְּשַׁעְבִּידוּ לְאוֹרַיְתָא בְחָרָן: 'the souls whom they subjected to the Torah in Haran'. This is the aggadic reading.

Apparatus:

- 12:5.21: the pack gives the accents of לָלֶכֶת as pashta, pashta (a repeated accent); the word is a single infinitive.
- 12:5.18 עָשׂוּ: 'acquired' (plain sense, Rashi and Ibn Ezra) against 'converted' or 'taught' (aggadah, Onkelos, Radak, Ibn Ezra's alternative).
- The Hebrew is 'to the land of Canaan' in both the departure and the arrival clauses; the English repeats the phrase.

**Abram passed through the land as far as the site of Shechem, as far as the terebinth of Moreh. The Canaanite was then in the land.**

Literal: and-passed Abram in-the-land as-far-as place-of Shechem as-far-as terebinth-of Moreh and-the-Canaanite then in-the-land

| אַבְרָם֙ | Abram | אַבְרָם | אבה | noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- The verb עָבַר takes the preposition בְּ here: 'pass through (the land)'. The verse gives two stopping places in a chain of constructs: מְקוֹם שְׁכֶם and אֵלוֹן מוֹרֶה, each introduced by עַד.
- The first עַד carries yetiv (עַ֚ד), a disjunctive accent written before the first letter of the word. It stands in place of pashta on a word stressed on its first syllable with no conjunctive before it. The zaqef on שְׁכֶם marks a pause between the two places.
- וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי אָז בָּאָרֶץ is a verbless clause with the vav of circumstance; the singular gentilic with the article is collective.
- אָז 'then' is the point of the commentators' difficulty (see the note): it can mark the Canaanite's presence at that time, as distinct from later, or his recent seizure of the land (Rashi, Ibn Ezra).

Note: Three difficulties are kept open. (1) 'The site of Shechem': Ibn Ezra says that Moses called the place by this name, since there was no Shechem in Abraham's time; Ramban holds that Shechem is the name of the city and that Shechem son of Hamor was named after it. (2) 'The terebinth of Moreh': Ibn Ezra offers 'trees' or 'a field', and says Moreh may be Mamre, the ally of Abraham, or another, the name of a place; Rashi says that Elon Moreh is Shechem. (3) 'The Canaanite was then in the land': Rashi says Canaan was then conquering it from the descendants of Shem; Ibn Ezra says Canaan may have seized it from another's hand, and if not, 'it has a secret, and the wise will keep silent'. The English leaves the clause unexplained.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi on וַיַּעֲבֹר אַבְרָם בָּאָרֶץ: 'he entered into it'. The English takes עבר as passing through the land, which is what going into it and as far as Shechem comes to.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi on עַד מְקוֹם שְׁכֶם: he went there to pray for Jacob's sons, when they come to fight at Shechem. A homily on later events; it does not bear on the plain sense.
- Rashi (records): Rashi on אֵלוֹן מוֹרֶה: it is Shechem; He showed him Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where Israel took the oath of the Torah. The English keeps 'the site of Shechem' and 'the terebinth of Moreh' as two phrases and records the identification.
- Rashi (records): Rashi on וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי אָז בָּאָרֶץ: the Canaanite was going along conquering the land from the descendants of Shem, in whose share it fell when Noah divided the earth; therefore God said 'to your offspring I will give this land': I will return it to your sons, who are descended from Shem. The English leaves the clause as it stands.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra on the whole verse: this too is the place Shechem; Moses called it so, since there was no Shechem in the days of Abraham. The English uses the name 'Shechem' as the verse gives it; the remark is recorded.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on אלון: like אלה, and they are trees; others say a field, like 'the terebinth of Paran' in 14:6. The English takes 'terebinth'; the alternative is recorded.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on מורה: some say it is Mamre, the ally of Abraham; but it may be another, and 'Elon Moreh' is the name of a place. The English reads Moreh as a name of a place.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it may be that Canaan seized the land of Canaan from the hand of another (so that 'then' marks a new possession); if not, there is a secret in it, and the wise man will keep silent. The English says only that the Canaanite was then in the land.
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos renders אֵלוֹן by מֵישַׁר, 'plain', as does Radak; this is the alternative to 'terebinth' recorded in the note.

Apparatus:

- 12:6.8 אֵלוֹן: 'terebinth' (the pack's lexicon, Ibn Ezra's first view) against 'plain' (Onkelos, Radak, Ibn Ezra's second view).
- 12:6.9 מוֹרֶה: place name (Rashi, Ibn Ezra) against the name of a man who owned the place (Radak, Ramban).
- 12:6.11 אָז: 'then' (at that time) against 'already' (Canaan had taken the land before); the English keeps 'then'.

Grammar:

- וַיֵּרָא is the Niphal wayyiqtol of ראה, 'appeared'. The Niphal's nun is assimilated and should double the resh; resh cannot be doubled, so the yod takes tsere instead (Ibn Ezra). The final ה of the root falls away in the short form.
- In לְזַרְעֲךָ אֶתֵּן the recipient stands before the verb. Radak's point is the contrast: the land goes to your offspring, not yet to you.
- הַנִּרְאֶה is a Niphal participle with the article, used as a relative clause: 'who appeared'.
- The accents: the zaqef gadol on וַיֹּאמֶר, the etnaḥta on הַזֹּאת. The words of the promise stand between them.

Note: 'Appeared' is Ibn Ezra's reading of the Niphal, 'by way of prophecy'. Ramban holds that this is the first appearance: before it Abram had been told 'go' in a dream or by the holy spirit. The 'offspring' is given as a collective singular.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi on וַיִּבֶן שָׁם מִזְבֵּחַ: for the good news of the offspring and for the good news of the land of Israel. The English joins the building to the promise with 'So'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on וַיֵּרָא: by way of prophecy. The word is of the Niphal pattern, and the hidden quiescent between the yod and the resh (the long vowel of the yod) stands in place of the dagesh that should be in the resh, where the Niphal's nun is swallowed. The English has 'appeared'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on הַנִּרְאֶה אֵלָיו: it is an adjectival participle of the same pattern, like 'what was done' in Neh. 5:18. The English renders it as a relative clause.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: he gave thanks to the Name and sacrificed a thank offering because He had appeared to him, since until now He had not appeared to him in a vision; 'go' had come in a dream or by the holy spirit. A comment on what the phrase implies, recorded here.
- Radak (follows): Radak: although I took you out of your birthplace to settle you in this land, I did not say that I would give it to you now; to your offspring, who will be many, I will give it.
- Targum Onkelos (not-applicable): Onkelos translates the Niphal by the passive 'was revealed' (וְאִתְגְּלִי) and renders 'offspring' by 'son' (לִבְנָךְ).

Apparatus:

- 12:7.14 vowels: WLC reads לַיהוָה, the base text לַיהֹוָה; the English is 'the LORD' in both.
- לַיהֹוָ֖ה: WLC reads לַיהוָ֖ה (vowels)

Grammar:

- וַיַּעְתֵּק is Hifil, which makes the verb transitive: 'he caused (his tent) to move'. Ibn Ezra contrasts it with the intransitive Qal in Job 18:4.
- אָהֳלֹה is written with a final he where the usual form has vav (אָהֳלוֹ); the form is the same in meaning; Rashi reads 'her tent', as a hint in the spelling.
- מִקֶּדֶם and מִיָּם are directions given from the point of view of the land: 'east' (front) and 'sea' (the Mediterranean, to the west).
- וַיִּקְרָא בְּשֵׁם יְהֹוָה is a fixed idiom: 'he called on the name of the LORD'. It can be a prayer (Onkelos), a proclamation to people (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Ramban), or both.
- The accents: the etnaḥta on אָהֳלֹה closes the moving and the pitching of the tent. The second half gives the position of the camp (Bethel on the west, Ai on the east, up to the zaqef on מִקֶּדֶם) and then the altar and the calling.

Note: The English supplies 'his tent' as the object of the Hifil (Rashi and Ibn Ezra), and repeats it as 'it' at the next verb. Ibn Ezra gives 'called on the name' two readings, prayer or calling people to the service of God; the English keeps the idiom without choosing. The detail 'with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east' is read as the positions of the camp, with the sea as the west.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi on וַיַּעְתֵּק מִשָּׁם: 'his tent' (אָהֳלוֹ). The English supplies the object.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi on מִקֶּדֶם לְבֵית אֵל: east of Bethel; so Bethel is to the west, as the text says 'Bethel from the sea'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: אָהֳלֹה is written (with a he): at first he pitched the tent of his wife, then his own (Bereshit Rabbah). The English reads the ordinary 'his tent' and records the spelling's reading.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi on 'and built there an altar': he prophesied that his sons would stumble there over the sin of Achan, and he prayed for them. A homily; it does not bear on the plain sense.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on וַיַּעְתֵּק: it is from the Hifil and transitive, for 'the rock moved from its place' (Job 18:4) is intransitive. Its object is אָהֳלֹה, which is also the object of וַיֵּט, and 'moved' means 'set out, travelled'. In וַיֵּט the hidden quiescent after the yod stands in place of the nun, the first root letter, as in וְיֵז נִצְחָם (Isa. 63:3); both verbs are transitive.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra on מִיָּם: 'from the west', because the Mediterranean ('the Spanish sea', not the ocean) lies to the west of the land; he travelled from the east of Bethel westward until Ai was east of his camp. The English says 'on the west'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'called on the name of the LORD' means prayer, or calling people to serve God. The English keeps the idiom, which allows both.
- Ramban (follows): Ramban: Onkelos says he prayed there, but the right reading is that he called in a loud voice before the altar the name of the LORD, making Him known to people.
- Radak (follows): Radak: Bethel was west of the mountain and Ai east of it; on the mountain he pitched his tent, built the altar and called on the name; 'called' means that he called the dwellers of that mountain to the altar and taught them to serve the one God.
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos: וְצַלִּי בִּשְׁמָא דַיְיָ, 'and he prayed in the name of the LORD': the prayer reading of the idiom.

Apparatus:

- 12:8.8 אָהֳלֹה: the WLC note records that the base text differs from BHS in its ketib/qere; the English takes the ordinary 'his tent'.
- 12:8.17 vowels: WLC reads לַֽיהוָה, the base text לַֽיהֹוָה; the English is 'the LORD' in both.
- 12:8.18 וַיִּקְרָא בְּשֵׁם: prayer (Onkelos) against proclamation to people (Ramban, Radak, Ibn Ezra).
- לַֽיהֹוָ֔ה: WLC reads לַֽיהוָ֔ה (vowels)

- וַיִּסַּע is a wayyiqtol; the munaḥ joins it to אַבְרָם before the zaqef.
- הָלוֹךְ וְנָסוֹעַ: two infinitives absolute in a row, here describing continued action (going and setting out), not commands.
- The ending ־ָה on הַנֶּגְבָּה is the directional he, 'toward'; the word means both the region Negeb and 'south'.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: he stayed in each place a month or more, then pulled up and pitched his tent elsewhere, and all his journeys were toward the south (the Negeb) of the Land of Israel. The English follows the staged journey southward; the midrash on Judah's portion is not used.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הנגבה is the southern side, and the name is explained from Aramaic 'dry', since the south is hot and dry (cf. Josh 15:19). The English renders it as the Negeb, the southern region.

Apparatus:

- Radak and Sforno read the pair as travelling from place to place like shepherds; Onkelos has 'went and set out to the south'.

- מִצְרַיְמָה carries the directional he, 'to Egypt'. Pashta is written on the last letter; it is repeated on רַ because the word is stressed on the penult.
- לָגוּר is the infinitive construct with לְ, giving the purpose; גּוּר is to live as a resident alien, not to settle (Radak, Sforno).
- כִּי gives the reason, and the adjective כָּבֵד 'heavy' precedes its subject in the predicate.
- The etnaḥta on the first בָּאָרֶץ divides the verse: the famine, then Abram's going down and its reason.

Note: 'Severe' renders 'heavy', which is the idiom for a famine. Rashi's reading that the famine was a test for Abram is recorded but does not change the English.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the famine was in that land alone (בְּאוֹתָהּ הָאָרֶץ לְבַדָּהּ), to test Abram whether he would question God's word, who had told him to go to Canaan and now drives him out of it. His plain point, that 'the land' is Canaan, agrees with Ibn Ezra and with the English; the motive of testing is homiletic and does not change the English.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'in the land of Canaan'. The English 'the land' is read as Canaan and is so noted.

Apparatus:

- Radak: Egypt had plenty even in famine, being watered by the Nile rather than rain; Ramban: Abram went down to keep himself alive.

- The construction וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר + qatal + לְ + infinitive is a time clause that leads into וַיֹּאמֶר.
- הִנֵּה־נָא יָדַעְתִּי: the perfect of יָדַע is a present state, 'I know', and carries the sense of 'I have long known' (Rashi's plain sense: יָדַעְתִּי זֶה יָמִים רַבִּים).
- יְפַת־מַרְאֶה is a construct chain, 'beautiful of appearance'; in the nominal clause the predicate אִשָּׁה יְפַת־מַרְאֶה precedes the subject אָתְּ.
- The etnaḥta on מִצְרָיְמָה divides the verse: the time clause of arrival, then Abram's speech.
- הִקְרִיב is a Hifil used without an object: 'drew near' (or 'brought [his camp] near', Ibn Ezra, Radak).

Note: I follow Rashi's plain sense (the moment has come to worry about her beauty) and Ibn Ezra's gloss of נָא as 'now'. The verb הִקְרִיב is rendered intransitively.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi gives a midrash (until now he had not looked at her, out of modesty) and then the plain sense: 'now it is time to worry about your beauty' as they come among dark people who are not used to beautiful women. The English follows the plain sense and does not impose the midrash.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הקריב may mean 'his camp' understood, or is one of the verbs that are both transitive and intransitive. The English takes it as intransitive, 'drew near'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: נא means 'now', as in 'now I am old' (27:2) and 'woe now to us' (Lam 5:16). The English renders 'Look now'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'I know' means that in Sarai's own land there were women as beautiful as she, but in Egypt and the Negeb there was none like her, since people's looks change with the climate (האויר). The English keeps the plain 'I know', which is consistent with this.

Apparatus:

- The verse is spoken in two stages of narration: arrival time clause, then speech.

**Say, please, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me on your account, and I may live because of you.**

Grammar:

- אִמְרִי is a feminine singular imperative; נָא makes it a request.
- אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ: a nominal clause, predicate first. אֲחֹתִי is stressed on the penult (munaḥ on חֹ) because אָתְּ is stressed on its first syllable (Ibn Ezra; compare קָרָא לָיְלָה, 1:5).
- לְמַעַן + yiqtol is a purpose clause, 'so that it may go well'; בַּעֲבוּרֵךְ and בִּגְלָלֵךְ are a parallel pair, 'on your account' and 'because of you'.
- וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי is a weqatal continuing the purpose clause; נַפְשִׁי 'my soul' stands for 'I'.
- The etnaḥta on אָתְּ divides the request from its purpose.

Note: I keep 'it may go well with me' as the general phrase and record the commentators' sense of 'gifts' in the commentary. 'Live' is the Qal of חיה.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'they will give me gifts' as the content of 'it may go well'. The English keeps the plain 'go well' and treats the gift sense as the content, as the commentators agree.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: אֲחֹתִי is stressed on the penult (מלעיל) because the next word, אָת, is stressed on its first letter, as in קָרָא לָיְלָה (1:5); this is the rule of the language. The dagesh in the ת of אָת is there to absorb the nun, for אַתָּה is of the same formation as אני (with nun). A remark on accent and form that does not change the English.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: בַּעֲבוּר and בִּגְלַל occur only with the preposition ב, and the poet (השר) who drops the ב lacks sense (סר טעם). A remark on usage, not on the sense of the verse.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'it may go well with me' means a gift and an offering, as the sense of 'and he treated Abram well for her sake' (12:16). The English renders 'go well' and 12:16 'treated well' alike.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: וְתִתְקַיֵּם נַפְשִׁי בְּפִתְגָּמָיְכִי, 'and my soul will be preserved through your words', taking בִּגְלָלֵךְ as 'by what you say', as Radak also explains it (בַּעֲבוּר דְּבָרֵךְ שֶׁתֹּאמְרִי).
- Radak: the good Abram meant was only that they would not kill him, not gifts; Sforno: they would court him with bride-price and gifts.

- כְּבוֹא is a preposition with an infinitive construct and the subject אַבְרָם, 'at Abram's coming'.
- The etnaḥta on מִצְרָיְמָה closes the time clause; the wayyiqtol וַיִּרְאוּ then carries the main clause, with הַמִּצְרִים between the verb and its object.

Apparatus:

- Sforno: all of them set their eyes on her, as Abram had feared.

- וַיְהַלְלוּ is a Piel from הלל with the first lamed written without the expected doubling (Ibn Ezra).
- וַתֻּקַּח is passive, and the agent is left unnamed; the verse says only that she was taken.
- בֵּית פַּרְעֹה is a direction without a preposition: 'to the house of Pharaoh'.

Note: I take אֶל־פַּרְעֹה with Rashi as 'with regard to Pharaoh': the officials praised her among themselves as fit for the king. Ramban's other reading, that they praised her to Pharaoh himself, is recorded. The passive is kept without an agent.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they praised her among themselves, saying 'this one is fit for the king' (הֲגוּנָה זוֹ לַמֶּלֶךְ); אֶל־פַּרְעֹה is 'with regard to Pharaoh'. The English 'praised her for Pharaoh' follows him.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the first lamed lacks its dagesh to ease the pronunciation, though it ought to be doubled, like ואתפללה (Dan 9:4). A grammar note.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַתֻּקַּח is the passive of the heavy augmented stem (the Hifil), even though the active is not found; the full form would be like וַתֻּשְׁלְכִי (Ezek 16:5). The English renders it passively, 'was taken'.
- Ramban (records): Ramban quotes Rashi and Onkelos (וְשַׁבַּחוּ יָתַהּ לְוָת פַּרְעֹה) for 'among themselves', and then gives the other reading: they praised her to the king himself, and he sent and took her.

Apparatus:

- Radak: 'was taken' implies against her will; Sforno 12:16 on the same word: they did not first consult Abram to persuade him.

- לְאַבְרָם, the indirect object with לְ, is fronted before the Hifil הֵיטִיב, whose unstated subject is Pharaoh (Rashi).
- The etnaḥta on בַּעֲבוּרָהּ divides the verse: Pharaoh's favor, then what Abram came to have.
- וַיְהִי־לוֹ expresses possession, 'he came to have'; צֹאן and בָּקָר are collective singulars.
- Each item after the first is joined by waw. Male and female are paired: עֲבָדִים וּשְׁפָחֹת (slaves), and חֲמֹרִים and אֲתֹנֹת (donkeys), the latter pair separated in the list.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi's note on ולאברם היטיב is a single word, 'Pharaoh', supplying the subject. The English follows it.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi's note on בעבורה contains only punctuation in the pack, so it says nothing about the words.

Apparatus:

- Radak: the goods came from Pharaoh; Sforno: a bride-price and gift, as custom required, in the way of a king.

#### Genesis 12:17

**Then the LORD struck Pharaoh with great plagues, and his household too, on account of Sarai, Abram's wife.**

Literal: and-struck the-LORD [obj] Pharaoh plagues great and-[obj] house-his on-account-of Sarai wife-of Abram

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |

| וַיְנַגַּ֨ע | and struck — wayyiqtol, Piel of נגע: 'strike' (with a plague) | ו: and + נָגַע | נגע | conjunction + verb (piel, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Pi |
| יְהֹוָ֧ה | the LORD | יהוה | הוה | noun (proper name) |  |
| אֶת | (object marker) | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) |  |
| פַּרְעֹ֛ה | Pharaoh | פַּרְעֹה |  | noun (proper name) |  |

| גְּדֹלִ֖ים | great — attributive adjective, masculine plural, agreeing with נְגָעִים; the pack's entry lists no sense for plain 'great' in size or degree, so no sense is given | גָּדוֹל | גדל | adjective (adjective, masculine, plural, absolute) |  |
| וְאֶת | and (object marker) | ו: and + אֵת | אות | conjunction + particle (direct object marker) |  |
| בֵּית֑וֹ | his house, household — construct of בַּיִת with the suffix 'his' | בַּ֫יִת |  | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 5 |
| עַל | on account of | עַל | עלה | preposition | II |
| דְּבַ֥ר | matter of — construct; עַל־דְּבַר is an idiom, 'on account of' | דָּבָר | דבר | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) | IV |
| שָׂרַ֖י | Sarai | שָׂרַי |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| אֵ֥שֶׁת | wife of — construct state | אִשָּׁה | אנשׁ | noun (common, feminine, singular, construct) | 2 |
| אַבְרָֽם׃ | Abram | אַבְרָם | אבה | noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- וַיְנַגַּע is a Piel wayyiqtol with a cognate accusative, נְגָעִים גְּדֹלִים: the verb and its object come from one root.
- The darga on יְהוָה is a conjunctive accent; the vertical stroke after it is a paseq, a slight pause that keeps the divine name apart from the object marker. The tevir on פַּרְעֹה is a minor disjunctive, and the etnaḥta on בֵּיתוֹ closes the first half: both objects, Pharaoh and his household, stand in that half, and the reason clause follows.
- עַל־דְּבַר is a compound preposition, 'on account of', with the construct chain אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם closing the verse.

Note: Rashi's gloss (the plague of 'raathan', a disease that made intercourse painful) is a midrashic reading and does not change the plain wording, so the English says only 'plagues'. The Hebrew does not say whether 'great' applies to the household too; Sforno reads lesser plagues on the household, and the English 'and his household too' leaves the question open. On עַל־דְּבַר the English follows Ibn Ezra ('because of'); Rashi's 'at her word' is recorded.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi, from Genesis Rabbah: he was struck with the plague of ראתן, which made marital relations painful for him. The English keeps the general 'plagues'; the specific disease is kept here.
- Rashi (not-applicable): The anchor holds only an opening parenthesis; no comment on the words survives.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'and his household' is as the Targum has it, אֱנַשׁ בֵּיתֵהּ, the people of his house; the midrash adds his walls, pillars and vessels (from the old Rashi). The English takes the plain 'household' and keeps the midrash here.
- Rashi (records): Rashi reads עַל דְּבַר as עַל פִּי דִּבּוּרָהּ, 'by her word': she would say to the angel 'strike', and he struck. The English follows Ibn Ezra's 'on account of' (בעבור) and keeps Rashi's reading here.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: על דבר is like בעבור, 'on account of', and the sense is 'because of this matter'. The English follows this.

Apparatus:

- Ramban, Radak and Sforno also read the plagues as aimed at Pharaoh, with lesser plagues on the household (Sforno).
- Targum Onkelos: 'great afflictions' (מַכְתָּשִׁין רַבְרְבִין).

Grammar:

- הִגַּדְתָּ is a Hiphil qatal of נגד. The first nun of the root assimilates to the gimel, which therefore takes a dagesh (*hingadta > higgadta); Ibn Ezra lists the verb among those with a first-radical nun (בעלי הנוני"ן).
- מַה־זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ לִּי is a rhetorical reproach, 'what have you done to me?'.
- כִּי here introduces the content of what should have been told: 'that she is your wife'.
- The verse has two questions; the etnaḥta falls after לִּי, dividing them.

Note: The 'that' clause is read as the content that Abram should have told. Ramban notes that the question may be asked in doubt, to draw out the truth.

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הגדת belongs to the 'nun' verbs, i.e. a root whose first letter נ falls away in forms; the English takes it as a Hiphil of נגד, 'you told'.

Apparatus:

- Ramban: Pharaoh may have asked Sarai first, or spoken in doubt to draw out the truth (a point of reading, not of wording).

- וָאֶקַּח is a wayyiqtol in first person: the narrative sequence turns into result, 'so that I took'.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Pharaoh did not say, like Abimelech, 'my land is before you', but 'go and do not stay', for the Egyptians are given to lust (Ezekiel 23:20). The English renders the bare imperatives 'take her and go'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: ואקח אותה לי לאשה means he took her to be his wife and to lie with her, and the LORD brought plagues on him so that he could not touch her, to guard the wife of his friend; he compares Deuteronomy 21:10-13. The English says 'took her as my wife' and does not say more.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the qamets of the vav in ולך is because the accent called ענין is known; he compares לחם וָיין (Genesis 14:18). A point of vocalization only; the English is unaffected.

Apparatus:

- Ramban: Pharaoh wished her to be his reigning wife, not a concubine.
- Radak: 'here is your wife' means she is as she was, untouched.

- וַיְצַו is a Piel wayyiqtol; with עַל and a person it means to give orders about someone.
- The plural וַיְשַׁלְּחוּ has no stated subject beyond אֲנָשִׁים: 'the men escorted him'.
- The three objects, אֹתוֹ, אִשְׁתּוֹ and כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ, each take אֶת, listing Abram, his wife and his goods.
- Ibn Ezra reads וישלחו as an honourable escort, as in 18:16.

Note: The 'orders' are left as the Hebrew leaves them. Rashi and Radak read them as an order to guard Abram and send him off; Ibn Ezra, as a proclamation that no one touch him or his wife. The English says only 'orders concerning him'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: ויצו עליו means 'concerning him', to send him off and to guard him.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וישלחו is as the Targum has it, וְאַלְוִיאוּ, 'and they escorted'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the sense is escort with honour, as in 'and Abraham went with them to send them off' (18:16). The English 'sent him off' keeps that sense.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the right sense of ויצו עליו is that the command lay on others, to proclaim that no one touch him or his wife. The English stays with 'orders concerning him' and does not specify the content.

Apparatus:

- Radak: they were ordered to guard him and his wife and goods against the Egyptians, and escort him to the border.

- The independent הוּא followed by two more items lists those who went up with Abram.
- הַנֶּגְבָּה has the article and the directional ה: 'to the Negeb'.
- The telisha gedola on הוּא is a disjunctive accent that sets the pronoun off from the list after it. The darga on אִשְׁתּוֹ is conjunctive. The tevir on לוֹ and the tipḥa on עִמּוֹ divide the rest of the verse.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Abram went up to come to the south of the Land of Israel; the Negeb is the southern part of the land, and going from Egypt to Canaan he travels from south to north. The English takes הַנֶּגְבָּה as the region of the Negeb.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra refers the grammar of וַיַּעַל to his Sefer HaYesod; no comment on the sense of the words.

Apparatus:

- Ramban: 'he and his wife and all that was his' tells us that nothing was taken back from him, an element of miracle.
- Radak: Lot did not leave Abram even though he had plenty in Egypt.

He had much livestock, and much silver and gold besides.

Apparatus:

- Radak: heavy by reason of his livestock and wealth.
- Sforno: he had to travel slowly, though he wanted to return quickly to the altar.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the land of Egypt lies south of the land of Canaan. The English takes the Negeb as the southern region.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: he travelled many stages going from the south to Bethel, which is in the north, and came to the altar to thank the LORD for having come in peace. The English takes 'journeys' as stages.

- Radak: the 'beginning' refers to 'he pitched his tent' (12:8).
- Sforno: מסעים are the moves of shepherds from one place to another as the pasture runs out.
- אׇֽהֳלֹה֙: WLC reads אָֽהֳלוֹ֙ (spelling)
- אׇֽהֳלֹה֙: ketiv reads אהלה (ketiv-qere)

- Radak: 'again' is meant: he called a second time on the name of the LORD; he settled in the same place to teach that a person should fix a place for prayer.

Grammar:

- הָיָה with לְ expresses possession; the singular verb agrees with the first of the things possessed, צֹאן.
- הַהֹלֵךְ אֶת־אַבְרָם: participle with the article as a relative clause; אֶת here is the preposition 'with' (not the object marker).
- The etnaḥta on אַבְרָם divides the verse: the description of Lot, then what he had.
- אֹהָלִים has ḥolem on the aleph. Ibn Ezra: אֹהֶל is of the קֹדֶשׁ pattern, whose plural is בָּאֳהָלִים (Jer 35:7), with ḥaṭef qameṣ; the ḥolem of אֹהָלִים points to a singular of the גּוֹרָל pattern, which is not attested.

Note: The phrase 'who went with Abram' is kept as a relative clause because it is the cause of Lot's wealth in Rashi and Radak. The verse goes on to say that the land could not hold both. The English puts the possession as 'had'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi asks who caused him to have this, and answers: his going with Abram. The English keeps 'who went with Abram' so that the cause is visible.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the singular is of the קֹדֶשׁ pattern (אֹהֶל), whose plural would be בָּאֳהָלִים (Jer 35:7), like בַּקֳּדָשִׁים (Lev 22:4); אֹהָלִים, with ḥolem between aleph and he, is the plural of a singular of the גּוֹרָל pattern, even though that singular is not found. The point is the form only; the sense is 'tents'.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'also' adds to what was said in 13:2, that Abram was very rich.
- Radak (records): Radak: Lot's good fortune was in the merit of Abram, because he went with him and obeyed him.
- Radak (records): Radak: the tents show that Lot had many goods and a large household and needed many tents; the aleph of אֹהָלִים has ḥolem (as in 1 Sam 4:10, Deut 33:18), where the pattern of אֹהֶל would give ḥaṭef qameṣ, as in בָּאֳהָלִים (Jer 35:7); perhaps it is of the pattern of גּוֹזָל, תּוֹלָע.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'and also Lot who went with Abram had sheep and oxen and dwellings', agreeing with the plain sense.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders אֹהָלִים by מַשְׁכְּנִין, 'dwellings'.
