- נָשָׂא takes אֶרֶץ as a masculine subject (Radak compares נֶעְתַּם אָרֶץ in Isa 9:18); Rashi reads it as a short expression, 'the land did not bear them (its pasture)', so the verb is masculine to agree with the unexpressed מִרְעֶה.
- יַחְדָּו is repeated at both ends of the verse, framing the problem.
- The etnaḥta on יַחְדָּו ends the first clause; the pashta on רְכוּשָׁם and the zaqef on רָב set off the reason.
- The reason (כִּי) comes between the two statements, so the second 'could not' is the result of the great property.

Note: Rashi says the expression is short and needs 'with the pasture of the land'. The English keeps the short form 'support them' and does not supply the word. Ibn Ezra reads יַחְדָּו as related to יָחִיד, 'as one'; the English uses 'together'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the land could not provide enough pasture for their livestock; the expression is short and must be completed, 'did not bear them (the pasture of) the land', which is why the verb is masculine. The English 'support them' reflects this.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: יַחְדָּו is said of two and of many ('all the people answered יַחְדָּו', Exod 19:8); it is a rare form, and it does not mean the same as יַחַד but is like יָחִיד, 'as one'. The English 'together' is consistent with this.
- Radak (records): Radak: אֶרֶץ is construed here as masculine, as in נֶעְתַּם אָרֶץ (Isa 9:18).
- Radak (records): Radak: the pasture was too narrow for their livestock together with the livestock of the people of the land.
- Radak (records): Radak: therefore the herders quarrelled, each saying 'we will graze here'.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: the land could not hold them to dwell together, for their possessions were many.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: the pasture of the land was not enough for both of them, and therefore (the quarrel in verse 7).

- אָז is 'at that time'. Rashi reads the whole clause, 'the Canaanite and the Perizzite were then in the land', as the verse's answer to Lot's herders: Abram had not yet come into possession of the land.

Note: Rashi: the quarrel was because Lot's herders let the animals graze in others' fields and Abram's herders reproved them for theft; this is a midrash of the Rabbis (Gen. Rabbah). - Rashi (records): Rashi gives the cause of the quarrel as the wickedness of Lot's herders, who grazed in others' fields; Abram's herders reproved them, and they replied that the land was given to Abram, who has no heir, so Lot inherits; the verse says the Canaanite was still in the land. The English does not state this cause; it is kept as a midrashic reading.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the Perizzite may be one of the sons of Canaan, one of those named, with two names. The English lists the two peoples as in the text.
- Ramban (records): Ramban questions Rashi, since the gift was to Abram's seed, and gives a plain reading of a quarrel over pasture.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak refers to his earlier comment on the Canaanite.
- Radak (records): Radak: the Perizzite also lived in this land, where Bethel and Ai were.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'and there was strife between the herders of Abram's cattle and the herders of Lot's cattle; and the Canaanite and the Perizzite then dwelt in the land'.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: there was a quarrel about who would be pushed aside by whom from the pasture they would find.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: the quarrel between two foreign brothers harms their reputation with the inhabitants.

Apparatus:

- Ramban quotes Rashi in full.

Grammar:

- אֵימִנָה and אַשְׂמְאִילָה are denominative Hiphil verbs from יָמִין and שְׂמֹאל, 'to take the right / the left'; both cohortatives.
- The first form is pointed with ṣere under the aleph, אֵימִנָה, where one would expect אַיְמִינָה; Rashi compares לְהֵמִין (2 Sam 14:19), pointed thus and not לְהַיְמִין.

- Radak reads שְׂמֹאל as north and יָמִין as south, since a person faces east; the English keeps 'left' and 'right' as in the Hebrew.

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וְאֵימִנָה is from the root of יָמִין.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it appears that the aleph of שמאל is part of the root, but we do not know, since the word הימיני and השמילי lacks it. This is a point of grammar.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'before you' is like 'before me': wherever you are, its people will not kill you, since God's help will be with you.
- Radak (records): Radak: Abram is the main figure, and Lot dependent, so it is for Lot to part from him; yet he gives Lot the choice.
- Radak (records): Radak: if you go north, I will be in the south, where we are now (cf. 12:9, 13:3).
- Radak (records): Radak: if you wish to stay in the south, I will go north.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'Is not the whole land before you? Separate now from me; if you go north, I will go south, and if you go south, I north', rendering left and right as north and south.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: you will choose whichever place you wish.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno has only the word 'therefore'.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: separate to the side you choose, and I will travel to the opposite.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: if you choose to seek one pasture on the left side.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: I will seek mine on the right side.

- Onkelos translates 'left' and 'right' as north and south (לְצִפּוּנָא, לְדָרוֹמָא).

Grammar:

- כִּי introduces what Lot saw: that all of it was irrigated.
- לִפְנֵי שַׁחֵת יְהֹוָה: a time phrase with a Piel infinitive; the subject, the LORD, follows the verbal noun (Ibn Ezra: 'before he destroys', infinitive of the intensive stem).
- כְּגַן יְהֹוָה and כְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם are two similes; the first echoes Eden (2:10), the second Egypt's irrigated fields.
- בֹּאֲכָה צֹעַר: 'as you come to Zoar', with a 2ms suffix that the plain sense treats as a general address (Radak: the speaker addresses the reader who knows the place); Rashi: 'as far as Zoar'.

Note: Ibn Ezra explains כִּכָּר as a place of vegetation; Rashi (at 13:11) and the Targum as a plain. The English 'plain' follows Rashi and the Targum. Rashi takes 'garden of the LORD' as trees and 'land of Egypt' as crops; the English leaves both similes as written. The clause 'before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah' is the narrator's aside and is kept in place. Rashi and Radak take בֹּאֲכָה צֹעַר as 'as far as Zoar'; Rashi records an aggadic reading against Lot. The English 'as you come to Zoar' keeps the Hebrew's form and the sense 'up to'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: מַשְׁקֶה means a land of water-streams. The English 'well watered' follows.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah' — that plain was so (well watered, like the garden of the LORD); the description holds for the time before the destruction.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'like the garden of the LORD' refers to trees. The English keeps the simile and records this in the notes.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi (Gen. Rabbah): 'like the land of Egypt' refers to crops. The English keeps the simile and records this in the notes.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בֹּאֲכָה צֹעַר means 'as far as Zoar'; the aggadic midrash reads it against Lot, since he chose to live near the licentious. The English 'as you come to Zoar' gives the Hebrew idiom with the sense 'up to Zoar'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: כִּכָּר is a place of vegetation, from כַּר 'pasture' (כַּר נִרְחָב, Isa 30:23), the kaf being either doubled here or missing there; compare בַּת עַיִן from בְּבָבַת עֵינוֹ (Zech 2:12). The English 'plain' is consistent with this.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the masculine מַשְׁקֶה follows the feminine כֻּלָּהּ, as in 'fire not blown shall consume him' (Job 20:26). A grammatical point.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: לִפְנֵי שַׁחֵת means 'before he destroys', and שַׁחֵת is a verbal noun from the Piel stem. The English 'before the LORD destroyed' follows.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the whole plain was irrigated by foot from the Jordan, as the garden of the LORD (2:10) and Egypt (Deut 11:10); the Rabbis said garden for trees and Egypt for crops, meaning great rivers and streams in the plain, good for pasture.
- Radak (records): Radak: Lot looked from the hill where they were, a high place, and saw the plain, a land for livestock because it was all well watered.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak's comment on כֻּלָּהּ is cut off in the pack.
- Radak (records): Radak: כָּל here is for emphasis, as in 'all the kings of the nations, all of them' (Isa 14:18).
- Radak (records): Radak: כִּכָּר is, as the Targum, a plain; it was near the land of Sodom and Gomorrah and, before it changed, like the garden of the LORD, Eden, watered by four rivers.
- Radak (records): Radak: the Nile waters Egypt, all of it.
- Radak (records): Radak: the he of בֹּאֲכָה is like that of הַנִּצֶּבֶת עִמָּךְ (1 Sam 1:26); the kaf is not an addition but addresses the hearer who knows the place; the sense is that the place was watered as far as Zoar.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'Lot lifted his eyes and saw all the plain of the Jordan, for all of it was a place of water, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, reaching to Zoar'.

Apparatus:

- The Targum renders כִּכָּר by מֵישַׁר, 'plain'.
- BDB entry for עַיִן in the pack lists no plain sense 'eye'.

- לוֹ after the verb is a reflexive dative: 'for himself'.
- מִקֶּדֶם: 'from the east' or 'from of old'; Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it of direction (Sodom is west of Bethel); the aggada in Rashi reads it as 'from the Ancient One (קַדְמוֹנוֹ) of the world'.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: כִּכָּר means plain, as the Targum.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Lot left Abram's side and went to Abram's west, so he travelled from east to west; the aggadah: he removed himself from the Ancient One of the world, saying 'I want neither Abram nor his God'. The English follows the plain sense 'from the east'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: because Sodom is west of Bethel. The English 'from the east' is consistent with this.
- Radak (records): Radak: Lot chose one of the places in the whole plain, since all were good.
- Radak (records): Radak: Lot set out toward the east, since the Jordan is east of Canaan; the mem is explained by the earlier 'he went on his journeys from the Negev to Bethel' (13:3). The English does not adopt this.
- Radak (records): Radak: the two separated since Lot moved far away; Lot dwelt in the cities of the plain, finally in Sodom, unaffected by their wickedness.
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos: 'Lot chose for himself all the plain of the Jordan, and Lot journeyed מִלְּקַדְמִין, and they parted, a man from his brother'. מִלְּקַדְמִין is the word Onkelos uses for מִקֶּדֶם at 2:8, where it means 'from before, of old'; it need not mean 'from the east'.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: he chose all the place where he alone and his herders could seek pasture, so that Abraham and his herders could not be there.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: he travelled neither right nor left (north or south), but from east to west to be far from Abraham, who lived in the east of the land near Ai.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: they separated not in pasture only but in their dwelling.

Apparatus:

- מִקֶּדֶם can mean 'from the east' or 'from of old' (Rashi's midrash).

Grammar:

- The verse is a verbless clause: subject אַנְשֵׁי סְדֹם, predicates רָעִים and חַטָּאִים.
- The etnaḥta falls on וְחַטָּאִים, so the accents set לַיהוָה מְאֹד apart as a closing phrase. Radak takes it over both predicates ('all of it is sin to the LORD'). Ibn Ezra, who reads רָעִים as 'toward people', leaves it to חַטָּאִים, and the English follows him in joining 'against the LORD' to 'sinners'.
- Rashi divides the two words: רָעִים in their bodies, חַטָּאִים in their wealth. Onkelos has the reverse.
- מְאֹד is a noun used adverbially, 'exceedingly'.

Note: The adjectives are kept apart, 'wicked' and 'sinners', because the normative commentators distinguish them: Rashi, wicked 'in their bodies' (בְּגוּפָם) and sinners 'in their wealth' (בְּמָמוֹנָם); Ibn Ezra, wicked 'toward people' (לִבְנֵי אָדָם). 'Against' renders ל as the context requires.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: even so, Lot did not refrain from living among them; the rabbis learn from here 'the name of the wicked rots' (Prov 10:7). This is a comment on Lot, not on the words.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: רָעִים בְּגוּפָם, wicked in their bodies, that is in sins of the person, as against חַטָּאִים 'in their wealth'. The English keeps 'wicked'; the translator's note records the sense.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וְחַטָּאִים בְּמָמוֹנָם, sinners in their wealth (Sanhedrin 109a). This distinguishes the two terms; the English keeps them separate.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they knew their Master and intended to rebel against Him. This supports 'sinners against the LORD, exceedingly' as deliberate sin.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: רעים is said of people, and compares Ezekiel 16:49, 'they did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy'. So 'wicked' is toward other people, and 'sinners' toward the LORD.
- Ramban (not-applicable): Ramban: the verse faults Lot for not refraining from living among them, as Rashi says, and speaks in favour of the righteous Abram, whose lot did not fall where wickedness was. All the cities of the plain were exceedingly wicked, which is why they were overturned, though all the Canaanites practised abominations (Lev 18:27).
- Radak (records): Radak: wicked toward heaven and toward people, all of it sin against the LORD, since they broke the commandments given to Adam and Noah.

Apparatus:

- 13:13.5 vowels: WLC reads לַיהוָה; the base text has לַיהֹוָה. The English is the same.
- Onkelos: wicked 'in their wealth' and guilty 'in their bodies'; the reverse of Rashi's distribution.
- לַיהֹוָ֖ה: WLC reads לַיהוָ֖ה (vowels)

| וָנֶ֖גְבָּה | and southward — directional he; נֶגֶב is 'south' (the Negev) | ו: and + נֶ֫גֶב | נגב | conjunction + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) + suffix (directional he) |  |

Grammar:

- The clause opens with וַיהוָה אָמַר, a fronted subject and a qatal, so it reads as background: the LORD had spoken, or spoke, once Lot was gone.
- אַחֲרֵי הִפָּרֶד־לוֹט is a preposition with an infinitive construct and its subject.
- שָׂא נָא עֵינֶיךָ וּרְאֵה: two imperatives; נָא makes the command a request.
- Each of the four directions takes the directional ה, 'toward'; the sea is the west because the Mediterranean lies there.

Note: The perfect after a fronted subject is rendered as a simple past with 'after' carrying the order. The omitted נָא is recorded in the phrase note.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: as long as the wicked man was with him, the divine word held back from him. This fits the English, which puts the speech after the separation.
- Radak (records): Radak: Abram might have thought Lot also had a share in the land; now that Lot has left he is told that it is for Abram and his seed alone.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: this was not said while Lot was with him, lest Lot and his shepherds grow proud and seize it.

Apparatus:

- 13:14.1 vowels: WLC reads וַיהוָה; the base text has וַיהֹוָה.
- וַֽיהֹוָ֞ה: WLC reads וַֽיהוָ֞ה (vowels)

Grammar:

- The object, כָּל־הָאָרֶץ, comes first, then the relative clause, then the verb, so the whole land is stressed.
- אֶתְּנֶנָּה has a nun-energic suffix, a resumptive pronoun for the fronted object.
- רֹאֶה is a participle: the land is what Abram is looking at.
- The etnaḥta falls on אֶתְּנֶנָּה, so וּלְזַרְעֲךָ עַד־עוֹלָם stands apart: a second recipient and the term of the gift, added to the verb before the pause. It has no verb of its own.

Note: The resumptive suffix on אֶתְּנֶנָּה is not repeated in English because the fronted object already stands in the sentence.

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: לְךָ אֶתְּנֶנָּה is 'by speech': the giving is done by the spoken word, as in 'he shall put (וְנָתַן) them on the head of the goat' (Lev 16:21), where the sins are put on the goat by the spoken confession. So 'I will give' is a grant made in words, not yet a handing over.
- Radak (records): Radak: though Abram could not see it all, he saw its four sides, and as it is within its boundaries so it will be given.
- Radak (records): Radak: עַד עוֹלָם holds even though they may be exiled from the land, for in the end they will return to it. The promise is perpetual despite exile.

- אֲשֶׁר אִם introduces a conditional with a result sense: 'such that if ...'.
- The apodosis גַּם־זַרְעֲךָ יִמָּנֶה has no particle of its own; גַּם marks the parallel.
- The wordplay on the root מנה: יוּכַל ... לִמְנוֹת, then יִמָּנֶה.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: just as it is impossible for the dust to be counted, so your seed will not be counted. This is the English's reading of the conditional.
- Radak (records): Radak: a hyperbole, as in 'like the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven' (Gen 22:17); the midrash applies the dust to Israel when it does not do His will and the stars when it does.
- Radak (records): Radak: if this can be, so can that; that is, since the first is impossible so is the second. He compares Jer 13:23.

Apparatus:

- The sentence has a pause at ׀ after אֲשֶׁר (legarmeh in the base text); the reading follows the zaqef qaton after הָאָרֶץ.

- Sforno (records): Sforno: even in Abram's days he would be a prince of God in the eyes of the inhabitants (Gen 23:6).

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: מַמְרֵא is a man's name. So the English says 'the oaks of Mamre' as 'Mamre's oaks'.

- Radak (follows): Radak: he took up his tent from there and pitched it from place to place until he arrived.
- Radak (records): Radak: these are not the oak of Moreh (Gen 12:6); there were two or more plains belonging to a man called Mamre, brother of Eshkol and Aner.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: he set his livestock's tents in order here and there.

Apparatus:

- 13:18.12 vowels: WLC reads לַיהוָה; the base text has לַיהֹוָה.
- Onkelos renders אֵלֹנֵי as 'plains' (מֵישְׁרֵי) rather than 'oaks'.
- לַֽיהֹוָֽה׃: WLC reads לַֽיהוָֽה (vowels)

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi, after Genesis Rabbah, identifies Amraphel with Nimrod, who said to Abraham 'fall (פֹּל) into the fiery furnace'; a homiletic identification that does not bear on the plain translation.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: there is a place named Goiim because people gathered there from many nations and made a man named Tidal king over them. The English takes Goiim as a place name.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: Goiim is the name of a province like Elam, or else 'king of nations' whose names the text does not list, being others than the Shinarites and their allies. The first reading is followed; the second is kept as an alternative.

Apparatus:

- The word גּוֹיִם can also be read as the common noun 'nations' (Ibn Ezra's second reading).

- The five kings fall into groups: אֶת־בֶּרַע ... וְאֶת־בִּרְשַׁע, both with אֶת; then שִׁנְאָב ... וְשֶׁמְאֵבֶר, with no אֶת and with וְ only on the second; then וּמֶלֶךְ בֶּלַע, a king without a name. The etnaḥta on עֲמֹרָה divides the first pair from the rest.
- The pashta is written on the last letter of its word; on בֶּרַע and שֶׁמְאֵבֶר it is written twice because the stress is not on the last syllable (penultimate stress of the segolate forms).

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi on בֶּרַע: 'evil to Heaven and evil to people'; a homiletic play on רַע.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi on בִּרְשַׁע: 'one who rose in wickedness' (רֶשַׁע); homiletic.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi on שִׁנְאָב: 'hater of his Father in heaven'; homiletic.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi on שֶׁמְאֵבֶר: 'he put a wing to fly, to leap and rebel against the Holy One'; homiletic.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi on בֶּלַע: 'the name of the city'. The English takes Bela as the city's name, equated with Zoar.

Apparatus:

- 14:2.16 vowels: WLC reads צְבוֹיִים; the base text has צְבוֹיִם.
- 14:2.16 ketiv-qere: the ketiv reads צביים; the qere, which the base text prints, is צְבוֹיִם. The English is the same, Zeboiim.
- צְבוֹיִ֔ם: WLC reads צְבוֹיִ֔ים (vowels)
- צְבוֹיִ֔ם: ketiv reads צביים (ketiv-qere)

Grammar:

- כָּל־אֵלֶּה is the subject placed first; חָבְרוּ is 3rd plural perfect, with the zaqef after it dividing verb from place.
- אֶל־עֵמֶק with a verb of coming together: 'to' the valley, as a gathering point.
- הוּא יָם הַמֶּלַח is a pronoun-copula gloss: 'it (is) the Salt Sea', naming the place by its later name.
- עֵמֶק is in the construct state: 'the valley of (the Siddim)'.

Note: אֶל־ is rendered 'in' for English idiom (Radak: אֶל here as בְּ). The name of the valley is kept as 'Siddim': Rashi says the valley was named for its many fields; Ibn Ezra derives the name from שִׂיד 'plaster', recorded. 'Which is the Salt Sea' follows Rashi, that the sea later covered the valley; Ibn Ezra's 'the Valley of the Salt Sea' is recorded.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the valley is so named because it had many fields (שָׂדוֹת). The English transliterates the name but takes it as a proper name derived from this.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'afterward the sea drew into it and it became the Salt Sea'; the midrash says the rocks round it split and rivers flowed into it. The English gives 'which is the Salt Sea' as the later name.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: חָבְרוּ is 'from the light (qal) stem', that is, 'joined', not the intensive.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra takes הַשִּׂדִּים from שִׂיד 'lime, plaster', as in וְשַׂדְתָּ אֹתָם בַּשִּׂיד (Deut 27:2). For the form he compares סַד 'stocks' (Job 13:27) and פַּת, plural פִּתִּים, where the plural doubles the second letter.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: עֵמֶק 'draws itself and another with it' (מושך עצמו ואחר עמו), that is, it serves the next phrase too, as אַל does in 'Do not rebuke me in your anger [and do not] chasten me in your wrath' (Ps 6:2). So הוּא יָם הַמֶּלַח means 'it is the Valley of the Salt Sea'.

Apparatus:

- הוּא יָם הַמֶּלַח: Rashi, the valley later became the Salt Sea; Ibn Ezra, with עֵמֶק understood again, 'it is the Valley of the Salt Sea'; Radak gives both, the valley beside the Salt Sea or itself later the sea.

- בָּא is singular: a verb that stands before a compound subject often agrees with the first member, and Rashi says Chedorlaomer was the chief party. וְהַמְּלָכִים is added after him, then the plural wayyiqtol וַיַּכּוּ takes over.
- Three peoples are struck at three places, each with אֵת + people and בְּ + place.
- The zaqef on אִתּוֹ ends the account of who came, and the etnaḥta on בְּהָם ends the second people-and-place pair.
- רְפָאִים (here without the article), הַזּוּזִים and הָאֵימִים are gentilic names of ancient peoples; אֵימִים also means 'terrors'.

Note: The ancient peoples are named by transliteration: Rephaim, Zuzim, Emim. The English 'In the fourteenth year' follows the Hebrew order. 'Came' is singular because the verb stands before its compound subject, of which Chedorlaomer, the leader, is the first member.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi on 'in the fourteenth year': לְמִרְדָּן, 'of their rebellion'. He counts the year from the rebellion, so with Seder Olam he takes 14:4 as 'for thirteen years they rebelled'. The English follows Ibn Ezra, 'in the thirteenth year', and counts from the start of their service.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Chedorlaomer alone is named as coming because he was the chief party to the affair; 'he entered into the thickness of the beam', an idiom for being most deeply involved. The English, with the singular verb, names him first and then the kings with him.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi on וְהַמְּלָכִים: 'these three kings' who were with him; the English has 'the kings who were with him'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: הַזּוּזִים are the Zamzummim (זַמְזֻמִּים); an identification recorded, the English transliterates Zuzim.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: they are called Rephaim because whoever saw them, his heart would die and he would be counted among the Rephaim, which are the dead. He derives the name from רְפָאִים 'shades of the dead'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the Emim are so called because there is terror (אֵימָה) from them; an etymology, recorded.

- בְּהַרְרָם has a doubled resh; Rashi 'their mountain', Ibn Ezra a different reading (see commentary).
- The yetiv on עַד and the zaqef on פָּארָן bound the geographical phrase.
- עַל־הַמִּדְבָּר: 'on' the wilderness means 'beside' it.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi on בְּהַרְרָם: 'in their mountain'; the English reads 'in their mountain'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the Targum renders אֵיל as 'plain', but Rashi thinks אֵיל is not 'plain'; it is the name of the plain of Paran, as Elonei is that of Mamre and Kikkar of the Jordan. The English keeps El-paran as a name.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: עַל הַמִּדְבָּר means 'beside the wilderness', like 'and beside him the tribe of Manasseh' (Num 2); the English has 'by the wilderness'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: בְּהַרְרָם is from the intensive stem, like בְּדַבְּרָם (Exod 7:7), meaning 'when they went up to Mount Seir'; recorded as an alternative to 'their mountain'.

- הוּא/הִוא קָדֵשׁ is a gloss, with feminine הִוא (Pentateuch) agreeing with the place.

- Rashi (records): Rashi: En-mishpat is named for the future, since Moses and Aaron would be judged there in the matter of the spring, the waters of Meribah; Onkelos translates it simply, as the place where the people of the district gathered for every judgment. The English transliterates and follows the plain sense of the name.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Amalek was not yet born; the territory is called by the future name. The English keeps 'Amalekites' and notes this.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Hazazon-tamar is En-gedi; a verse says so explicitly (מִקְרָא מָלֵא) in Chronicles, in the story of Jehoshaphat (2 Chr 20:2).

- The verse is a long apposition continuing verse 8: the four kings are listed with their lands, each as 'king of X', and the list ends with the totals 'four kings against the five'.
- אֵת is the preposition 'with' (compare עִם): Ibn Ezra glosses אֵת כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר as 'with'. It is not the object marker here.
- The accents set each name-and-land pair apart: geresh/revia after Elam, pashta/zaqef qaton for the next two pairs, tipha and etnahta at Arioch and Ellasar; the merkha-tipha pair carries 'four kings' and silluq closes 'the five'.
- The numerals contrast four against five; the word order 'four kings against the five' sets the few against the many.

Note: Both אֵת in the verse (14:9.1, 14:9.16) are the preposition 'with', as the pack parses them and as Ibn Ezra glosses the first (כמו עם); in a battle 'with' the five means 'against' them. Goim (גּוֹיִם) is left as a name, as the lexicon gives it; the word is also 'nations', and Onkelos translates it 'of the peoples' (דְעַמְמִין). Onkelos reads 'Babel' for Shinar.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the few nevertheless won, to show they were mighty, and Abram was not deterred from pursuing them. This is a moral about the numbers, not a reading of the words.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra glosses אֵת in אֵת כְּדָרְלָעֹמֶר as 'like עִם', that is, 'with'. The English adopts this.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of the peoples, Amraphel king of Babel, Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five.'

- הֶרָה and שָׁמָּה take the directional ה, a locative ending without a preposition. Rashi says הֶרָה means 'to a mountain' (indefinite), unlike הָהָרָה with the article, 'to the mountain'.
- The word order changes at the end: 'and the remaining ones, to-the-hills they fled', with the subject and place fronted to contrast with the two kings who fell.
- Zaqef qaton on חֵמָר ends the first clause; etnahta on שָׁמָּה ends the second.

Note: I take חֵמָר as the lexicon gives it ('bitumen'); Rashi and Radak read 'clay, mud' for the building mortar, a reading the English does not adopt. וַיִּפְּלוּ־שָׁמָּה is kept open between 'fell into the pits' and 'threw themselves down there' (Ibn Ezra); the English line says only 'fell there'. הֶרָה is rendered 'into the hills', following Rashi's indefinite reading; Ibn Ezra's 'to the mountain' is recorded. Sforno takes the survivors to be the three remaining kings.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: there were many pits there, from which earth was taken for the mortar of buildings. The aggadic midrash: the mud was thick in them, and a miracle was done for the king of Sodom, who came out of it, because some among the nations did not believe that Abraham had been saved from the furnace at Ur Kasdim; once this king came out of the mud, they believed in Abram after the fact. The English takes his 'many pits' but keeps the lexicon's 'bitumen' for the material.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: הֶרָה is like לְהָר, 'to a mountain', with the ה replacing the לָמֶד at the front; it names no particular mountain, since each fled to whichever he found first, unlike הָהָרָה, which means a known mountain. The English adopts the indefinite reading.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: בְּאֵר everywhere in Scripture is a well with flowing water, and its form here (בֶּאֱרֹת) is changed because of the construct. The English accepts the construct, but where he and Rashi differ on the sense it takes Rashi's pits dug for earth rather than wells; his 'wells' is kept here.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: וַיִּפְּלוּ שָׁמָּה means they let themselves fall there of their own will, to escape (ברצונם להמלט), as in 'and he fell on his face' (Numbers 16:4). The English keeps the neutral 'fell there', which does not exclude this reading but does not adopt it.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: הֶרָה means 'to the mountain' and is a strange word. The English instead follows Rashi's indefinite 'into the hills'; Ibn Ezra's definite reading is kept here.

Apparatus:

- WLC reads הַשִׂדִּים with a different vowel pointing; MAM reads הַשִּׂדִּים (14:10.2).
- Onkelos: 'the plain of the field was pits, pits of clay; the king of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell there, and those who remained fled to the mountain.'
- הַשִּׂדִּ֗ים: WLC reads הַשִׂדִּ֗ים (vowels)

**They took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah and all their food, and went away.**

- The verse is a simple chain of wayyiqtol verbs with the plural subject of the four kings.
- רְכֻשׁ סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה is a construct chain with a double genitive: 'the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah'.
- The repetition of אֶת־כׇּל, 'all', stresses the completeness of the plunder: goods and food.
- The telisha gedola on the first word is a prepositive accent, written twice on וַיִּקְחוּ.

Note: וַיִּקְחוּ is rendered 'took' with the sense of plundering. Radak says 'their food' includes what was in the houses and the people in them; the English keeps 'food'. The entry for הלך lists no plain-'go' sense in the pack.

Commentary:

- Radak (follows): Radak: the Valley of Siddim lay within the border of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the battle was there; Admah, Zeboiim and Bela were not on that side. So the kings took the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah from those cities and their villages, and רְכֻשׁ includes movable property and livestock. The English 'goods' carries this.
- Radak (records): Radak: 'their food' means what they had in the houses, 'and the people in them'; the English keeps the plain 'food'.

- וְהוּא יֹשֵׁב is a circumstantial clause: a pronoun plus a participle that states a situation, not a sequence.

- The qadma on וַיִּקְחוּ and the darga on לוֹט are conjunctive and lead to the tevir on רְכֻשׁוֹ; the merkha on אֲחִי leads to the tipḥa on אַבְרָם, and the etnaḥta on וַיֵּלֵכוּ ends the first half.

Note: Ibn Ezra adds that Lot was living in Sodom 'on that day'; the English does not add a 'then'. Rashi's remark that his dwelling in Sodom was the cause is moral and is not a reading of the words.

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'Who caused him this? His living in Sodom.' This is a moral comment on the clause, not a reading of its words.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'he was on that day living in Sodom', which takes the participle as a state of affairs at the time of the capture. The English renders it as a circumstantial clause.

- 'Brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner' stands in apposition to מַמְרֵא; the accents (revia, then mahpakh and pashta) attach it to Mamre, not to Abram.
- בַּעֲלֵי בְרִית is an idiom: 'masters of a covenant', that is, allies. The same construction pairs a person with a thing owned.
- הַפָּלִיט has the article: 'the fugitive', one particular person known to the story; הָעִבְרִי is its only appearance as a title for Abram.
- Etnahta on הָעִבְרִי separates the report from the circumstantial clause that follows.

Note: Rashi's plain-sense identification of the fugitive as Og is recorded, not adopted in the English line. הָעִבְרִי is rendered 'the Hebrew'; Rashi's 'from across the river' is a gloss on the name, not an alternative translation. 'Eshcol' has a sense in its entry for a valley; here it is a personal name.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: on the plain sense this is Og, who escaped the war (Deuteronomy 3), since Amraphel and his allies did not kill him when they struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim. The English says only 'the fugitive'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi, after Genesis Rabbah: הָעִבְרִי means one who came from across the river. The English keeps 'the Hebrew', which can carry that sense.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: they had made a covenant with him. The English renders בַּעֲלֵי בְרִית as 'allies'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הַפָּלִיט is one who fled and escaped, one of the people of Sodom (מבני סדום), as in 'the fugitive from Jerusalem came to me' (Ezekiel 33:21); there is also a midrashic way. The English uses 'the fugitive'.

#### Genesis 14:14

> וַיִּשְׁמַ֣ע אַבְרָ֔ם כִּ֥י נִשְׁבָּ֖ה אָחִ֑יו וַיָּ֨רֶק אֶת־חֲנִיכָ֜יו יְלִידֵ֣י בֵית֗וֹ שְׁמֹנָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ וּשְׁלֹ֣שׁ מֵא֔וֹת וַיִּרְדֹּ֖ף עַד־דָּֽן׃

**When Abram heard that his brother had been taken captive, he armed his trained men, those born in his household, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued as far as Dan.**

Grammar:

- וַיִּשְׁמַע ... כִּי introduces the content of what Abram heard: 'that his brother was taken captive'. The Niphal נִשְׁבָּה is passive.
- וַיָּרֶק is Hiphil of רִיק, 'empty out'. The verb is used of drawing a sword (Leviticus 26:33) or a spear (Psalm 35:3), and so here 'armed'; its object is 'his trained men'.
- חֲנִיכָיו is the plural of חָנִיךְ with the suffix 'his', from the root חנך, 'train, initiate' (compare 'train up a child', Proverbs 22:6). Rashi cites a singular written form חנכו, which the MAM text does not have.
- The number is written 'eight ten and three hundreds': שְׁמֹנָה עָשָׂר 'eighteen' first, then שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת 'three hundred', with the short form of 'three' because מֵאָה is feminine. English reverses the order.
- Etnahta on אָחִיו divides the verse into the news and Abram's response.

Note: For וַיָּרֶק I choose 'armed' on the combined view of Rashi (armed, as Onkelos וְזָרִיז) and Ibn Ezra's first reading ('gave them weapons'); his second reading, 'drew out the swords from the sheath', is kept in the commentary entry. Rashi's singular spelling חנכו is recorded in the apparatus. Rashi's midrash that the three hundred and eighteen are Eliezer alone is not adopted, and Rashi's remark on Dan (the later calf-idol) is not a reading of the words.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַיָּרֶק means 'armed', as Onkelos renders it (וְזָרִיז); so 'I will unsheathe (וַהֲרִיקֹתִי) the sword after you' (Leviticus 26:33) means 'I will arm myself with my sword against you', and so 'I will draw my sword' (Exodus 15:9) and 'draw out the spear and close' (Psalm 35:3). The English takes 'armed'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the word is written חנכו, singular, 'his trained one': this is Eliezer, whom he had trained in the commandments. The word means a person's or a vessel's first entry into the craft it is to serve, as in 'train up a child' (Proverbs 22:6), 'the dedication of the altar' (Numbers 7) and 'the dedication of the house' (Psalm 30). The English renders the plural of the MAM text, 'trained men', in this sense.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: our rabbis said it was Eliezer alone, which is the numerical value of his name. The English takes the number at face value; the midrash is kept here.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: there his strength failed, since he saw that his descendants would set up a calf there. This is a homily on the place name, not a reading of the words.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: he gave them weapons of war, as in 'and draw out the spear' (Psalm 35:3); some say he drew the sword from its sheath, as in 'they empty their sacks'. The English adopts the first and records the second.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: חֲנִיכָיו are those he had trained many times in battle; the gematria of Eliezer is only a homiletic way and the text speaks in its plain sense. The English adopts 'trained men'.

Apparatus:

- Rashi reports the spelling חנכו, singular, 'his trained one', which he reads as Eliezer; the MAM text reads חֲנִיכָיו and the pack records no Ketiv/Qere at this word (14:14.8).

#### Genesis 14:15

> וַיֵּחָלֵ֨ק עֲלֵיהֶ֧ם ׀ לַ֛יְלָה ה֥וּא וַעֲבָדָ֖יו וַיַּכֵּ֑ם וַֽיִּרְדְּפֵם֙ עַד־חוֹבָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר מִשְּׂמֹ֖אל לְדַמָּֽשֶׂק׃

**He and his servants divided themselves against them by night and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is north of Damascus.**

Rashi's remark that no place is called Hobah and that Dan is meant is a midrash and is not adopted; the English keeps the name Hobah.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: on the plain sense the verse is transposed: 'he and his servants divided themselves against them at night', as pursuers split into parties after fugitives who flee in different directions. The English adopts this order.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'night' means that even after dark he did not hold back from pursuing them; the English 'by night' follows this plain sense. The aggadic midrash, that the night was divided, with a miracle done for him in its first half while the second half was kept for the midnight of Egypt, is not adopted.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: no place is named Hobah; Dan is called Hobah because of the idolatry that would be there. This is a homily and the English keeps the name.

Grammar:

- The proper name has two parts joined by maqqef, מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק. The pashta is written on the last letter of its word; because צֶדֶק is stressed on its first syllable, the accent is written a second time on the stressed syllable. The name can be read 'my king is Ṣedeq' or 'king of righteousness'.
- הוֹצִיא is a hifil perfect, 'brought out'; the verb comes after its subject, so the clause is a new scene, not the next step in a chain of wayyiqtols.
- וְהוּא כֹהֵן is a circumstantial clause giving his office: the pronoun opens the clause and the noun without article is the predicate.
- אֵל עֶלְיוֹן: 'God Most High', the first appearance of the title.

Note: I give שָׁלֵם as Salem and record Jerusalem (Ibn Ezra, Ramban, Radak, citing Psalm 76:3). Rashi's 'Shem son of Noah' (so Radak) is recorded, not adopted, since it identifies the man and does not change the English. Rashi holds that the bread and wine were what one gives those weary from war (so also Radak and Sforno); Ibn Ezra does not comment on them. The Targum's 'ministered' (מְשַׁמֵּשׁ) for כֹהֵן, which Ibn Ezra adopts, is rendered 'was a priest'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: according to the aggada, Melchizedek is the name of Shem son of Noah (Nedarim 32). The English keeps the name only.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: so one treats those weary from battle, and he showed Abram he bore no grudge for killing his sons; the aggada has it hint at the offerings and libations. The English takes the plain sense of a meal for the weary.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: he was so called because he was king over a place of righteousness, though some say it is a personal name. The English keeps the name.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: 'Salem is Jerusalem', proved by 'In Salem is his booth' (Psalm 76:3). The English prints 'Salem' and records the identification here.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: as the Aramaic translator has it, כֹהֵן means one who ministers, as in וְכִהֲנוּ לִי; Melchizedek spoke properly in blessing Abram first for his zeal to rescue captives. The English says he was priest of God Most High.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'Melchizedek king of Jerusalem brought out bread and wine, and he ministered before God Most High'.

- The accents divide the blessing: the zaqef on עֶלְיוֹן separates the blessing from the title 'maker of heaven and earth'.

Note: קֹנֵה is read 'maker' with Rashi (קֹנֶה like עֹשֶׂה, and by making them he acquired them as his own) and Radak (not one who buys from another, but one who makes or brings into being). Ramban holds the main sense is ownership, 'whose possession they are', and says Onkelos meant this by דִּקִנְיָנֵיהּ; that reading is recorded in the apparatus. בָּרוּךְ is a Qal passive participle.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: קֹנֵה is like עֹשֵׂה (Psalm 134), and by making heaven and earth he acquired them to be his. The English takes 'maker' and records 'acquirer' here.

- Onkelos has 'to God Most High whose possession is heaven and earth' (דִּקִנְיָנֵיהּ); Radak says 'make or provide'; Sforno 'heaven and earth are a possession for him'.

Grammar:

- מִגֵּן is a piel perfect, 'delivered up', as Rashi (הִסְגִּיר, Hosea 11:8) and Ibn Ezra (like נָתַן, Proverbs 4:9) say, not 'shielded'. The lexicon files it under the root גנן, which gives מָגֵן 'shield'; Ibn Ezra holds that the מ is a root letter.
- צָרֶיךָ is a plural construct (צָרֵי) with the suffix ךָ: 'your adversaries'.
- The pashta on בָּרוּךְ and the zaqef on עֶלְיוֹן divide the blessing from its relative clause.
- וַיִּתֶּן־לוֹ has no stated subject; the reader must decide who gives to whom, and Rashi says Abram gave.

Note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that מִגֵּן means 'handed over', like נָתַן, and the English follows them rather than 'shielded'. The subject of וַיִּתֶּן is Abram (Rashi, Ibn Ezra); the other reading, that Melchizedek gave Abram a tithe, is a real alternative that the Hebrew does not exclude, and I do not adopt it.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: אֲשֶׁר מִגֵּן means 'who handed over', like אֲמַגֶּנְךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל (Hosea 11).
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the giver is Abraham. The English names Abram.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the tithe was from all that Abram had, because Melchizedek was a priest. The English says 'of everything'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: מִגֵּן is like נָתַן, as in 'a crown of glory she shall deliver you' (Proverbs 4:9); the מ is a root letter; Abram took out the tithe in honor of God and found no one fitter than Melchizedek.

Grammar:

- נֶפֶשׁ with the article is a collective singular, 'the persons'; the word does not mean 'soul' here but the living captives.
- The two imperatives תֶּן and קַח are set against each other: the king asks for the people and offers the goods.
- הָרְכֻשׁ is placed before its verb for contrast with הַנֶּפֶשׁ.
- לָךְ is the pausal form of לְךָ 'to you' (masculine singular): at the silluq the suffix is written ךְ with qamets under the ל. The same form returns at the etnaḥta in 14:23.

Note: The pack parses the suffix of לָךְ as feminine; the form is the pausal ךְ spelling, and the sense is addressed to Abram. I keep the pack's data and note it here. 'The people' follows Rashi's 'the bodies alone'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'from my captives whom you rescued, return to me the bodies alone'. The English takes נֶפֶשׁ as the captured persons.

Apparatus:

- 14:22.6: MAM writes הֲרִמֹתִי (defective); WLC writes הֲרִימֹתִי (plene), the spelling of Ibn Ezra's and Ramban's lemmas. The sense is the same.
- הֲרִמֹ֨תִי: WLC reads הֲרִימֹ֨תִי (spelling)

**I will not take so much as a thread or a sandal strap, nor anything that is yours, so that you cannot say, 'I made Abram rich.'**

Grammar:

- The oath formula אִם ... אִם takes a negative sense: 'if I take ... may I be ...', that is 'I will not take'; the penalty is left unsaid.
- מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ־נַעַל is an idiom for 'the smallest thing', from a thread to a shoe strap.
- הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי is the hifil of עָשַׁר, the causative of the Qal 'be rich': 'I made rich'. The pronoun אֲנִי, not needed with a finite verb, stresses the claim: 'I, I made'.
- The etnaḥta on לָךְ ends the oath, and וְלֹא תֹאמַר starts the clause giving the purpose.

Note: אִם is the elliptical oath, 'not' (so Rashi's 'I will keep back for myself nothing from the captives'). Rashi reads the second clause as 'if you offer me a reward from your treasury, I will not take it' and the third as God's promise to enrich Abram (12:2), which is the reason; both bear on the sense but not on the wording of the English.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'I will keep for myself nothing of the captives', the sense of אִם as an oath.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: if you say to give me wages from your treasury, I will not take them. The English says 'nor anything that is yours'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Abram refuses because the Holy One had promised to make him rich, as it says 'and I will bless you' (12:2). The English is consistent; the reason is not stated in the text.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: חוּט is the thread from which every garment is sewn.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: שְׂרוֹךְ is the leather that binds the sandal.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: הַנְּעָרִים are my servants who went with me; though they fought and Aner, Eshcol and Mamre stayed with the baggage, they take their share, and David learned from it. The English says 'my servants'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'what the young men have eaten' means what his servants ate.

| לֵאמֹ֑ר | saying — לֵאמֹר, infinitive construct with ל: introduces direct speech | ל: to, for + אָמַר | אמר | preposition + verb (qal, infinitive construct) | Qal 1 |

| מָגֵ֣ן | a shield — no verb: a verbless clause, so present time by default | מָגֵן | גנן | noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) |  |

| שְׂכָרְךָ֖ | your reward — construct form שְׂכָר- with suffix | שָׂכָר | שׂכר | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | 2 |
| הַרְבֵּ֥ה | is great — hifil infinitive absolute, 'making much'; with מְאֹד it stands as the predicate, 'very much, very great' | רָבָה | רבה | verb (hifil, infinitive absolute) | Hiph 1 |
| מְאֹֽד׃ | very | מְאֹד | מאד | adverb | 2 |

Grammar:

- הָיָה דְבַר־יְהֹוָה אֶל־: the standard formula for the arrival of a prophetic word. Here it is joined to בַּמַּחֲזֶה, a rare word for the medium of the revelation.
- The two sentences אָנֹכִי מָגֵן לָךְ and שְׂכָרְךָ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד are verbless. The English present tense is a choice: Ibn Ezra takes the first as a past 'I was a shield' (see commentary), but the Hebrew has no tense.
- הַרְבֵּה is the hifil infinitive absolute of רבה, 'making much', used with מְאֹד as the predicate of the clause: 'very much, very great'.
- The etnaḥta on לֵאמֹר ends the narrative frame. In the speech the zaqef qaton on לָךְ closes the prohibition and its first ground; within that part the revia on אַבְרָם divides 'Do not be afraid, Abram' from 'I am a shield for you'. The pashta on אָנֹכִי is a lesser division inside 'I am a shield for you'.

Note: The speech is placed in a vision (בַּמַּחֲזֶה), which Ibn Ezra glosses as 'the visions of prophecy' and Radak says shows Abram an action, not only words. The present 'I am a shield' takes the verbless clause as Rashi does, of protection from punishment to come; Ibn Ezra's past reading, 'I was a shield to you (against the kings)', is recorded in the commentary.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: אחר means close in time (אחרי a remote interval). The reference is to the victory over the kings: Abram feared he had used up his reward or would be punished for the lives he took, so God says 'I am a shield' against punishment and 'your reward is great'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בַּמַּחֲזֶה means in the sights (visions) of prophecy, so the English 'in a vision'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra reads אָנֹכִי מָגֵן לָךְ as past, 'I was a shield to you and saved you from the kings, and I will also give you a reward because you went out to rescue your nephew with a few men and relied on me'. The English keeps the Hebrew's tenseless clause.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: Abram feared two things: that the kings, or those under them, would return with larger forces and he would fall in battle, or that his day would come to die without offspring. God promised to be his shield against them, and that the reward for his walking with the LORD would be very great; the fear of dying childless is not yet answered, as Abram's reply in 15:2 shows (Ramban there: 'from being cut off you have not promised me').
- Radak (records): Radak: שכרך הרבה מאד, 'great in this world and very great in the world to come'. The English does not split הרבה and מאד between two worlds.

Apparatus:

- The pack parses לָךְ as having a feminine suffix; the pausal ָךְ is the pausal form of the masculine suffix, since Abram is addressed. The data is kept.
- Onkelos has 'my Memra will be a strong shield for you' (מֵימְרִי תְּקוֹף לָךְ), a paraphrase of the shield image; it does not change the Hebrew sense.

#### Genesis 15:2

> וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אַבְרָ֗ם אֲדֹנָ֤י יֱהֹוִה֙ מַה־תִּתֶּן־לִ֔י וְאָנֹכִ֖י הוֹלֵ֣ךְ עֲרִירִ֑י וּבֶן־מֶ֣שֶׁק בֵּיתִ֔י ה֖וּא דַּמֶּ֥שֶׂק אֱלִיעֶֽזֶר׃

**Abram said, My Lord, the LORD, what will you give me, when I go on childless, and the steward of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?**

Grammar:

- וְאָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי: a circumstantial clause with a participle ('while I am going about without ...'). The sense of הוֹלֵךְ ('go on living' or 'go to my death') is open, see the note.
- בֶּן־מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי הוּא דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר: a difficult verse. מֶשֶׁק is a hapax, understood by Rashi and the Targum as 'one who manages (my house)', by Ibn Ezra as from שׁקק 'run about'. The English follows the sense 'steward' which both give.
- אֲדֹנָי יֱהֹוִה: the Masoretic pointing יֱהֹוִה tells the reader to say Elohim, not Adonai, after אֲדֹנָי. Radak says the title precedes the name because the name is the essence.
- The etnaḥta on עֲרִירִי divides the verse between Abram's complaint and its explanation.

Note: דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר is rendered 'Eliezer of Damascus' with the Targum and Radak (who supplies the missing relational yod). Another reading in Radak is that the man's own name was Damascus. For הוֹלֵךְ the English keeps the neutral 'go on'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi gives Menahem ben Saruq's view that עֲרִירִי means 'without an heir', lacking sons (he joins it to עֵר וְעֹנֶה, Malachi 2:12, with a privative sense like תְשָׁרֵשׁ 'uproot', Job 31:12); his own view joins עֵר to 'awake' (Song 5:2) and takes עֲרִירִי as 'desolation', as עָרוּ עָרוּ (Psalm 137:7). The English 'childless' gives Menahem's sense, which the plain context requires on either view.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi, after the Targum: בן משק ביתי is the one by whose word the whole house is fed (על פיך ישק), my steward; had Abram a son, he would be in charge of Abram's property. The English 'steward'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: according to the Targum he was from Damascus; according to the midrash he is called Damascus because he pursued the kings as far as Damascus. The Talmud reads דמשק as an acrostic: he 'draws and gives drink' (דולה ומשקה) of his master's teaching to others. The English takes the plain sense, 'of Damascus'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the yod of עֲרִירִי is like that in אכזרי and is dropped in ערירים יהיו; the sense is as the Targum says, 'without a child'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: מֶשֶׁק has the pattern of מֶכֶס and is from a doubled root, as in שׁוֹקֵק בּוֹ (Isaiah 33:4), with segol like דֶּבֶק: 'a son who draws himself and another with him', one who runs about the house. He concludes that בן משק ביתי is the man of Damascus, Eliezer. The English 'steward' agrees in sense; his derivation is kept here.
- Ramban (records): Ramban cites an interpretation (marked יב"ע) that הולך ערירי means 'I am dying childless', as in הולך האדם אל בית עולמו (Ecclesiastes 12:5). He prefers: Abram complains, what will my reward be when I have no sons, and I go wandering alone in a foreign land like a juniper in the desert, with none coming and going in my house but Eliezer, a stranger I took from Damascus. The English 'go on' does not narrow to either.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the yod of relation is missing, so דַּמֶּשֶׂק means 'the Damascene' like שבט הימני; or his name was Damascus and Abram named him Eliezer. The English takes the first.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'and the steward (בַּר פַּרְנָסָא) of my house, he is Eliezer the Damascene'.
- The pack gives the lemma אֲדֹנָי with parse 'plural, construct' and the name יהוה with the pointing יֱהֹוִה; both are kept.

**Abram said, Look, you have given me no offspring, and so a member of my household is my heir.**

- הֵן לִי לֹא נָתַתָּה זָרַע: 'to me you have not given seed'. The word order puts 'to me' first, against the promises Abram has heard.
- וְהִנֵּה בֶן־בֵּיתִי יוֹרֵשׁ אֹתִי: the participle יוֹרֵשׁ describes a state near at hand. Verbs of inheriting normally take the thing inherited as object, not the person, so 'inheriting me' means 'inheriting from me'.
- זֶרַע is singular but collective, 'offspring', and the English uses a singular noun for it.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'and what use is all that you might give me?' - the sentence is a complaint carrying on from מה תתן לי.
- Radak (follows): Radak: בֶּן בֵּיתִי is one Abram esteems as his own seed, as Eliezer who ruled all he had; hence 'you have given me no seed'.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: even if You give me a child later, he would be too young to manage the property, and the steward of the house would be the heir in practice.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'behold, to me you have given no child, and behold the son of my house is inheriting me (יָרִית יָתִי)'.

The qadma on וְהִנֵּה is conjunctive; the first divisions fall at the pashta on אֵלָיו and the zaqef qaton on לֵאמֹר.
- לֹא יִירָשְׁךָ זֶה: the verb has the 2nd person masculine suffix and the same verb occurs again at the end, so the verse is built around a contrast between two heirs. The etnaḥta on זֶה divides the rejected heir from the true one.

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: מִמֵּעֶיךָ is a 'kinuy', a euphemism for the limb, because it is near; hence 'from your own body'.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: because the son who would inherit him would come only after his old age, God promised him here only about the inheritance, that he should not worry: his own seed will inherit him. וְהִנֵּה means that while Abram was still saying 'my household member is my heir', the word of the LORD came to him suddenly.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the verse limits the earlier promise, 'to you and to your seed', to a true descendant who comes from your innards.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'This one will not inherit you, but one whom you will beget, he will inherit you.'

#### Genesis 15:5

> וַיּוֹצֵ֨א אֹת֜וֹ הַח֗וּצָה וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ הַבֶּט־נָ֣א הַשָּׁמַ֗יְמָה וּסְפֹר֙ הַכּ֣וֹכָבִ֔ים אִם־תּוּכַ֖ל לִסְפֹּ֣ר אֹתָ֑ם וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֔וֹ כֹּ֥ה יִהְיֶ֖ה זַרְעֶֽךָ׃

**He brought him outside and said, Look toward the sky, please, and count the stars, if you are able to count them. Then he said to him, So will your offspring be.**

Literal: and-brought-out him the-outside and-said look please the-heavenward and-count the-stars if you-are-able to-count them and-said to-him thus he-will-be your-seed

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיּוֹצֵ֨א | and he brought out — wayyiqtol of the hifil of יצא: 'caused to go out' | ו: and + יָצָא | יצא | conjunction + verb (hifil, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph 1 |
| אֹת֜וֹ | him | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| הַח֗וּצָה | outside — הַחוּצָה: with the directional ה, 'to the outside' | ה: the + חוּץ | חוץ | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) + suffix (directional he) |  |
| וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ | and said — doubled pashta on the verb | ו: and + אָמַר | אמר | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| הַבֶּט | look — imperative of the hifil of נבט; Rashi hears in it 'look down from above' | נָבַט | נבט | verb (hifil, imperative, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph |
| נָ֣א | please — נָא is a particle of entreaty or politeness | נָא |  | particle (exhortation) |  |
| הַשָּׁמַ֗יְמָה | toward the sky — directional ה on שָׁמַיִם: 'skyward' | ה: the + שָׁמַיִם | שׁמה | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) + suffix (directional he) | 1.a |
| וּסְפֹר֙ | and count | ו: and + סָפַר | ספר | conjunction + verb (qal, imperative, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| הַכּ֣וֹכָבִ֔ים | the stars | ה: the + כּוֹכָב | כבב | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) |  |
| אִם | if — אִם opens a conditional clause; it also introduces an indirect question, 'whether you can' | אִם |  | conjunction | 1 |
| תּוּכַ֖ל | you are able | יָכֹל | יכל | verb (qal, imperfect (yiqtol), 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| לִסְפֹּ֣ר | to count | ל: to, for + סָפַר | ספר | preposition + verb (qal, infinitive construct) | Qal 1 |
| אֹתָ֑ם | them | אֵת | אות | particle (direct object marker) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, plural) |  |
| וַיֹּ֣אמֶר | then he said — a second wayyiqtol of אמר, marking a new utterance after the etnaḥta | ו: and + אָמַר | אמר | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| ל֔וֹ | to him | ל: to, for |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| כֹּ֥ה | so — כֹּה: 'thus', pointing to the stars | כֹּה |  | adverb | 1 |
| יִהְיֶ֖ה | will be | הָיָה | היה | verb (qal, imperfect (yiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal III |
| זַרְעֶֽךָ׃ | your offspring | זֶ֫רַע | זרע | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | 4 |

Grammar:

- וַיּוֹצֵא אֹתוֹ הַחוּצָה: a hifil wayyiqtol. The subject is God, the object Abram. הַחוּצָה has the article and the directional ה together.
- הַבֶּט־נָא הַשָּׁמַיְמָה: שָׁמַיִם with the article and the directional ending ָה, 'skyward'. The imperative with נָא is courteous.
- אִם־תּוּכַל לִסְפֹּר: אִם introduces a conditional clause whose result is implied (the answer is no). The verb סָפַר is used twice (imperative and infinitive) in the one speech.
- כֹּה יִהְיֶה זַרְעֶךָ: the adverb כֹּה refers to the stars in sight; the verb is future and 'offspring' is collective.
- The pashta on וַיֹּאמֶר is written twice because the word is stressed on its first syllable: one mark shows the stress, the other is the accent's usual place on the last letter. It is one accent. The etnaḥta on אֹתָם ends the first speech, and the second begins with a new וַיֹּאמֶר.

Note: Rashi gives the plain sense (God took Abram out of his tent to see the stars) and the midrash (go out of your astrology; 'look down' from above the stars). The English follows the plain sense, with the midrashic alternatives recorded.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: by its plain sense He brought him out of his tent to see the stars. By the midrash He told him, go out of your astrology, since you saw in the constellations that you will not have a son: 'Abram has no son, but Abraham will; Sarai will not bear, but Sarah will'. Another midrash lifted him above the stars, hence the sense of looking down.
- Ramban (records): Ramban quotes Rashi's plain sense (He brought him out of his tent to see the stars) and the midrash (go out of your astrology), and objects that Abram, while still Abram, fathered Ishmael; he explains the midrash as meaning that Abram was seeking a son who would be his heir.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the word came to him in his tent, and in the vision He brought him outside, as in Ezekiel 8:3 'he brought me to Jerusalem in visions of God'. The stars after the dust of the earth in the earlier promise are both hyperbole.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'and he brought him out and said, Look now at the heavens and count the stars, if you are able to count them; and he said to him, So will your children be.'

#### Genesis 15:6

> וְהֶאֱמִ֖ן בַּֽיהֹוָ֑ה וַיַּחְשְׁבֶ֥הָ לּ֖וֹ צְדָקָֽה׃

**He trusted in the LORD, and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.**

Literal: and-he-trusted in-the-LORD and-he-reckoned-it to-him righteousness

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וְהֶאֱמִ֖ן | and he trusted — a perfect with וְ in a narrative sequence; an unusual form of continuing narrative that marks a state, 'and he was trusting'; the hifil of אמן takes בְּ for the object of trust | ו: and + אָמַן | אמן | conjunction + verb (hifil, perfect (qatal), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph 2 |
| בַּֽיהֹוָ֑ה | in the LORD — the Variants list notes that WLC points the divine name differently; the base text is kept | ב: in, with, by + יהוה | הוה | preposition + noun (proper name) |  |
| וַיַּחְשְׁבֶ֥הָ | and he reckoned it — wayyiqtol with a feminine suffix: the 'it' is his trust (a feminine noun implied); the subject is God, by Rashi | ו: and + חָשַׁב | חשׁב | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, feminine, singular) | Qal I.3 |
| לּ֖וֹ | to him | ל: to, for |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| צְדָקָֽה׃ | as righteousness | צְדָקָה | צדק | noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) | 1 |

Grammar:

- וְהֶאֱמִן: the waw with a perfect (weqatal) after a string of wayyiqtols; it gives the narrator's comment on Abram's state of trust, not a new event in the sequence. The hifil of אמן means 'consider firm', 'put trust in'.
- וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לּוֹ צְדָקָה: the verb takes an object suffix (feminine, 'it') and a double complement, 'to him' and 'as righteousness'. The feminine suffix refers to his faith or to the promise.
- The subject of וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ is not named. Rashi and Sforno take it to be God. Ramban's preferred reading takes Abram as the subject: he reckoned that God would give him seed out of God's righteousness; his second reading has God count the promise to him as righteousness (cf. Psalm 106:31 of Pinhas).

Note: The English names the LORD as the subject of 'reckoned', following Rashi and Sforno; the ambiguity of the Hebrew (Abram, or God) is kept in the phrase note and the commentary. צְדָקָה is 'righteousness'; Ibn Ezra explains it by Deuteronomy 6:25 and sets it apart from the Sages' sense 'charity'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Abram did not ask for a sign about this (the son); but about inheriting the land he asked for a sign, 'by what shall I know'. So 'he trusted' refers to the son.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the Holy One, blessed be He, counted it to Abram as merit and as righteousness for the trust he showed. A second reading takes בַּמָּה אֵדַע as asking in what merit Israel will endure, and God answers, by the merit of sacrifices.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: צדקה is as in וצדקה תהיה לנו (Deuteronomy 6:25) and like צדק ומשפט; he adds that the Sages' sense of צדקה as charity is different.
- Ramban (records): Ramban does not understand Rashi's 'merit' (why would Abram not trust a God of truth?), and suggests Abram trusted that God would give him a child out of His own righteousness, not Abram's; or that God counted the promise itself as righteousness.
- Radak (follows): Radak: God counted the complete trust as righteousness and uprightness of heart, since he and his wife were growing old and the promise was delayed, and yet he trusted.

Apparatus:

- The pack's Variants note: WLC reads בַּֽיהוָ֑ה where the base (MAM) writes בַּֽיהֹוָ֑ה; the same name, no difference in sense.
- Onkelos: 'and he trusted in the Memra of the LORD, and He counted it to him as merit (לְזָכוּ)'.
- בַּֽיהֹוָ֑ה: WLC reads בַּֽיהוָ֑ה (vowels)

#### Genesis 15:7

> וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אֵלָ֑יו אֲנִ֣י יְהֹוָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר הוֹצֵאתִ֙יךָ֙ מֵא֣וּר כַּשְׂדִּ֔ים לָ֧תֶת לְךָ֛ אֶת־הָאָ֥רֶץ הַזֹּ֖את לְרִשְׁתָּֽהּ׃

**He said to him, I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to take possession of it.**

Literal: and-said to-him I LORD who I-brought-you-out from-Ur Chaldeans to-give to-you [object-mark] the-land the-this to-possess-it

| אֵלָ֑יו | to him | אֶל |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 1 |
| אֲנִ֣י | I | אֲנִי |  | pronoun (personal, 1st person, common, singular) |  |
| יְהֹוָ֗ה | the LORD | יהוה | הוה | noun (proper name) |  |
| אֲשֶׁ֤ר | who | אֲשֶׁר | אשׁר | particle (relative) |  |
| הוֹצֵאתִ֙יךָ֙ | brought you out — hifil perfect, 1st person, with 2nd person masculine suffix | יָצָא | יצא | verb (hifil, perfect (qatal), 1st person, common, singular) + suffix (pronominal, 2nd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph 1 |
| מֵא֣וּר | from Ur | מ: from, than + אוּר |  | preposition + noun (proper name) |  |

Grammar:

- אֲנִי יְהֹוָה אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ: the formula of self-introduction, 'I am the LORD who ...', that recalls the earlier act as grounds for the promise.
- The relative אֲשֶׁר takes a 1st person verb, 'who I brought you out', and the English turns it into a normal relative clause with 'who brought'.
- לָתֶת לְךָ ... לְרִשְׁתָּהּ: two infinitives with ל expressing purpose. The first is of נתן, the second of ירשׁ with the feminine suffix referring to הָאָרֶץ.
- The zaqef qaton on כַּשְׂדִּים closes 'I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans'. In what follows the tevir on לְךָ divides 'to give you' from 'this land', and the tipḥa on הַזֹּאת sets the last word, לְרִשְׁתָּהּ, apart. The darga on לָתֶת is conjunctive and joins it to לְךָ.

Note: אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים is rendered 'Ur of the Chaldeans', the familiar English name; Ibn Ezra points out that the promise names Ur and not Haran because it was in Ur that the call came, as the Lekh Lekha section shows.

Commentary:

- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it says Ur and not Haran as proof that the call is told in the Lekh Lekha section and was given there, as he explained at that place; so the English keeps 'Ur of the Chaldeans'.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: Abram trusted God that his son would inherit; for the inheritance of the land he asked for a sign, as Gideon did, since every prophecy is conditional unless sworn. It bears on verse 8 and the sense of 'by what will I know', not on this verse.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: 'from the time I brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans and did a miracle for you, it was My will to give you this land'; not yet a decree, so Abram feared that the land depended on works.
- Radak (follows): Radak: I did not bring you out for nothing but to give you this land to inherit, meaning that his sons will inherit it, like an inheritance a man leaves to his sons.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno on לְרִשְׁתָּהּ: so that the sons will inherit it from you by an inheritance that has no end.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'I am the LORD who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to inherit it.'

#### Genesis 15:8

> וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אֲדֹנָ֣י יֱהֹוִ֔ה בַּמָּ֥ה אֵדַ֖ע כִּ֥י אִֽירָשֶֽׁנָּה׃

**He said, My Lord, the LORD, by what will I know that I shall take possession of it?**

Literal: and-said my-lord LORD by-what I-will-know that I-will-possess-it

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיֹּאמַ֑ר | and he said — wayyiqtol; the subject is Abram, as the vocative that follows shows | ו: and + אָמַר | אמר | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| אֲדֹנָ֣י | my Lord — plural of majesty with 1st person suffix | אֲדֹנָי | אדן | noun (common, masculine, plural, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 1st person, common, singular) |  |
| יֱהֹוִ֔ה | the LORD — pointed יֱהֹוִה so that the reader says Elohim after אֲדֹנָי | יְהֹוִה |  | noun (proper name) |  |
| בַּמָּ֥ה | by what — בַּמָּה: ב with the interrogative מָה, 'by what means?' | ב: in, with, by + מָה |  | preposition + particle (interrogative) | 1 |
| אֵדַ֖ע | will I know — imperfect, 1st person, with a modal sense: 'am I to know' | יָדַע | ידע | verb (qal, imperfect (yiqtol), 1st person, common, singular) | Qal 1.a |
| כִּ֥י | that | כִּי |  | conjunction |  |
| אִֽירָשֶֽׁנָּה׃ | I shall take possession of it — imperfect with a feminine suffix referring to the land; Radak: 'my sons will inherit it', cf. Genesis 48:22 | יָרַשׁ | ירשׁ | verb (qal, imperfect (yiqtol), 1st person, common, singular) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, feminine, singular) | Qal 1 |

Grammar:

- בַּמָּה אֵדַע: the interrogative with ב asks for the means or sign by which knowledge will come; it is not a statement of doubt, and Radak says Abram did not doubt that his sons would inherit.
- כִּי אִירָשֶׁנָּה: the כִּי introduces the content of the knowledge, 'that I shall inherit it'. The suffix -נָּה, with the nun, is an energic form on a feminine object.
- The etnaḥta falls on the first word, וַיֹּאמַר, which takes its pausal form (patah for the segol of וַיֹּאמֶר); it sets the speech apart from the narrative.

Note: There are no normative comments on this verse. Radak and Sforno agree that Abram asks for knowledge that the inheritance will be lasting, since his descendants might sin and lose the land; the English 'by what will I know' keeps the question open, as the Hebrew does.

Commentary:

- Radak (follows): Radak: Abram did not doubt that his sons would inherit, for he had trusted the LORD (15:6); he asked whether they would inherit it for ever, since they might sin and be exiled, and 'by what' asks in what way it will be made known to him, as the stars were shown for the offspring.
- Sforno (records): Sforno says Abram did not retract his faith in this question; otherwise it would not have been counted to him as righteousness (Ezekiel 18:24).
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: perhaps the sons will sin and not be worthy to inherit.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: 'and he said, LORD God, by what shall I know that I will inherit it?' (בְּמָה אִדַּע אֲרֵי אֵרְתִינַהּ).

#### Genesis 15:9

> וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלָ֗יו קְחָ֥ה לִי֙ עֶגְלָ֣ה מְשֻׁלֶּ֔שֶׁת וְעֵ֥ז מְשֻׁלֶּ֖שֶׁת וְאַ֣יִל מְשֻׁלָּ֑שׁ וְתֹ֖ר וְגוֹזָֽל׃

**He said to him, "Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon."**

Literal: and-said to-him take for-me heifer tripled and-she-goat tripled and-ram tripled and-turtledove and-young-bird

| word | gloss | lemma | root | parse | sense |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| וַיֹּ֣אמֶר | and he said — wayyiqtol | ו: and + אָמַר | אמר | conjunction + verb (qal, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Qal 1 |
| אֵלָ֗יו | to him | אֶל |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |
| קְחָ֥ה | take — imperative with paragogic he, which adds urgency | לָקַח | לקח | verb (qal, imperative, 2nd person, masculine, singular) + suffix (paragogic he) | Qal 1 |
| לִי֙ | for me | ל: to, for |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 1st person, common, singular) |  |
| עֶגְלָ֣ה | heifer | עֶגְלָה | עגל | noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) |  |
| מְשֻׁלֶּ֔שֶׁת | three-year-old — Pual participle of the denominative verb 'to do in threes'; see note | שָׁלַשׁ | שׁלשׁ | verb (pual, participle passive, feminine, singular, absolute) | Pu |
| וְעֵ֥ז | and she-goat | ו: and + עֵז | ענז | conjunction + noun (common, feminine, singular, absolute) |  |
| מְשֻׁלֶּ֖שֶׁת | three-year-old | שָׁלַשׁ | שׁלשׁ | verb (pual, participle passive, feminine, singular, absolute) | Pu |
| וְאַ֣יִל | and ram | ו: and + אַ֫יִל | אול | conjunction + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| מְשֻׁלָּ֑שׁ | three-year-old — masculine form, agreeing with the ram | שָׁלַשׁ | שׁלשׁ | verb (pual, participle passive, masculine, singular, absolute) | Pu |
| וְתֹ֖ר | and turtledove | ו: and + תֹּר |  | conjunction + noun (common, both genders, singular, absolute) |  |
| וְגוֹזָֽל׃ | and young pigeon | ו: and + גּוֹזָל |  | conjunction + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |

Grammar:

- קְחָה is the imperative with the paragogic ה, a mark of urgency or courtesy.
- מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת / מְשֻׁלָּשׁ is a Pual participle (feminine, then masculine) of שָׁלַשׁ; it agrees in gender with each animal.
- The accents group the three large animals, each with its participle, and the etnaḥta falls on מְשֻׁלָּשׁ; the two birds follow as a separate pair.
- The list is in a fixed order of three animals and two birds; the birds take no participle.

Note: מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת can mean 'three-year-old' (BDB: Pu three years old; Ibn Ezra's choice) or 'threefold', i.e. three of each (Rashi, Onkelos). I read 'three-year-old' and record the other in the commentary. הַגּוֹזָל is any young bird; Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as the young of the dove, which fits the pairing with the turtledove.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'three calves', an allusion to three bullocks (the Day of Atonement bullock, the community's bullock for an inadvertent error, and the heifer whose neck is broken). The English reads the Pual participle as an age instead.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: the three goats allude to the goat offered inside, the goats of the festival additional offerings, and an individual's sin-offering goat. This follows his 'threefold' reading and is not adopted.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: the three rams allude to the certain guilt offering, the suspended guilt offering, and an individual's sin-offering lamb; this too follows 'threefold'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi, citing Bereshit Rabbah: the turtledove and the young of a dove. The English 'young pigeon' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: some say three goats, but 'it is right in my eyes' that the goat was three years old. The English reads three-year-old.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אַיִל is the large lamb (כבש). The English 'ram' keeps the animal as the grown male sheep.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: גוֹזָל is the young dove, since only these are named among beasts and birds for burnt offerings and every sacrifice. The English follows.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos reads three of each ('three heifers, three goats, three rams'), against Ibn Ezra's three-year-old.
- Radak notes that גּוֹזָל can name the young of any bird, citing Deut 32:11, but takes it here as the young dove.

**He took all these for him, cut them in the middle, and set each half opposite the other; but the birds he did not cut in two.**

- The object is fronted in וְאֶת־הַצִּפֹּר לֹא בָתָר, which sets the birds against the animals: the animals were cut, the birds were not.
- אִישׁ בִּתְרוֹ לִקְרַאת רֵעֵהוּ is a distributive phrase, 'each one its piece opposite its fellow', as in Exod 26:3 (Ibn Ezra).
- The root בתר occurs three times: the Piel verb וַיְבַתֵּר 'he cut in two', the noun בִּתְרוֹ 'his piece', and the Qal verb בָתָר. From it the scene is called בְּרִית בֵּין הַבְּתָרִים, 'the covenant between the pieces'.
- The etnaḥta at רֵעֵהוּ closes the first half: the cutting and setting out of the animals.

Note: The text does not say who commanded the cutting; the commentators take it as part of the covenant rite. צִפֹּר is a collective singular; Ibn Ezra reads it as the turtledove and the young pigeon of v. 9, which I follow. The pointing הַצִּפֹּר is that of the base text; WLC reads הַצִפֹּר without the dagesh. בֶּתֶר at 15:10.11 is listed in the lexicon only with the sense 'cleft mountains', which does not fit here; I give no sense number and read 'piece, half', as the lexicon's gloss says.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: he divided each into two parts, for he was making a covenant, and covenant-makers divide animals and pass between the pieces (Jer 34:18). The smoking oven and flaming torch that pass between the pieces are the messenger of the Presence.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the nations are likened to bulls, rams and goats and Israel to doves, so the animals were cut as a sign that the nations will be consumed; a homiletic reading, not about the wording.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the birds were not cut as a sign that Israel will endure for ever; the second half of the same homily.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וַיְבַתֵּר means 'he cut them and separated them', as in 'the mountains of Bether' (Song 2:17) and 'between its parts' (Jer 34:18).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the word אִישׁ is like בַּעַל, 'owner', as in 'a man of war' (Exod 15:3) and 'the man Gabriel' (Dan 9:21), and it means the thing itself, as in 'a worthless man'. So it is used of animals as well, and of curtains, 'one to her sister' (Exod 26:3). He set the piece of each one opposite its fellow, 'for beast and man are two', meaning the word serves for both.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הַצִּפֹּר is the turtledove and the young pigeon, because צִפּוֹר is a general term.

Apparatus:

- 15:10.15 vowels: WLC reads הַצִפֹּ֖ר (no dagesh in the צ); base text הַצִּפֹּ֖ר. Meaning unchanged.
- Ramban records that the birds were not cut because of the rule of Lev 1:17 (the bird burnt offering is not divided) and notes Bereshit Rabbah on the difference between burnt-offering and sin-offering birds; not adopted as the plain sense.
- הַצִּפֹּ֖ר: WLC reads הַצִפֹּ֖ר (vowels)

#### Genesis 15:11

> וַיֵּ֥רֶד הָעַ֖יִט עַל־הַפְּגָרִ֑ים וַיַּשֵּׁ֥ב אֹתָ֖ם אַבְרָֽם׃

**The birds of prey came down on the carcasses, and Abram drove them off.**

Literal: and-came-down the-bird-of-prey upon the-carcasses and-caused-to-blow them Abram

| הָעַ֖יִט | the bird of prey — collective singular, 'birds of prey' | ה: the + עַ֫יִט | עיט | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, singular, absolute) |  |
| עַל | on | עַל | עלה | preposition | II.1 |
| הַפְּגָרִ֑ים | the carcasses — the definite article marks 'the' carcasses just prepared | ה: the + פֶּ֫גֶר | פגר | particle (definite article) + noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) |  |
| וַיַּשֵּׁ֥ב | and he drove away — Hifil wayyiqtol of נשב, 'to cause to blow'; the nun is assimilated, so the shin is doubled | ו: and + נָשַׁב | נשׁב | conjunction + verb (hifil, sequential imperfect (wayyiqtol), 3rd person, masculine, singular) | Hiph |
