Grammar:

- וַיַּשֵּׁב is a Hifil wayyiqtol of נשב ('to blow'), with the doubled shin standing for the assimilated nun; it means 'he blew them off'.
- הָעַיִט is a collective singular with a singular verb: 'the birds of prey'.
- The etnaḥta on הַפְּגָרִים divides the verse; the second half gives Abram's response.
- The pronoun object אֹתָם comes before the named subject אַבְרָם. This is the usual order when the object is a pronoun and the subject a noun, so no emphasis is implied.

Note: הַפְּגָרִים are the bodies of the animals that Abram had just cut up (Rashi: 'the pieces'; Ibn Ezra: 'the bodies'), so I write 'carcasses'. Radak argues that פְּגָרִים are whole bodies, i.e. the two birds; not adopted. For וַיַּשֵּׁב, Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take 'to blow away, make fly off'; Ibn Ezra also offers 'he made the carcasses return to drive off the bird', recorded in the apparatus.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the עַיִט is a bird that swoops and gasps after carrion, from עָט as in 'and you swooped upon the spoil' (1 Sam 15). The English 'birds of prey' follows.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'on the carcasses' means on the pieces. He argues against the Targums that render it as pieces (פלגיא), since פגרים is related to פגול.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַיַּשֵּׁב is 'blowing and making fly', as in 'he makes his wind blow' (Ps 147). The English 'drove off' follows; the allusion to David and the Messiah is not applicable to the plain sense.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: עַיִט is a bird, as in 'the speckled bird of prey is my inheritance' (Jer 12:9).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: פְּגָרִים are the bodies.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the shin has a dagesh in place of the absorbed nun, like יְגָרֵשׁ, 'he drove them away from the carcasses', as in 'he makes his wind blow' (Ps 147:18); or alternatively 'he returned the carcasses to drive off the bird'.

Apparatus:

- Ibn Ezra's alternative: וַיַּשֵּׁב from שׁוּב, 'he put the carcasses back' to scare off the bird; the English keeps the נשב reading, the one the lexicon lists.
- Onkelos renders 'and Abram scared them away' (וְאַפְרַח), in line with 'to blow away'.

Grammar:

- וַיְהִי with a time clause (הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ לָבוֹא) is a standard way to open a new scene: 'the sun was about to set'.
- The verb forms move from the qatal נָפְלָה, after its fronted subject וְתַרְדֵּמָה, to the participle נֹפֶלֶת: the deep sleep has fallen, and the dread is falling, still in progress.
- אֵימָה חֲשֵׁכָה גְדֹלָה: three words in a row, 'terror, darkness, great'; the adjective is feminine and may modify חֲשֵׁכָה alone or both nouns.
- הִנֵּה brings the reader into Abram's experience.

Note: The three nouns אֵימָה חֲשֵׁכָה גְדֹלָה can be read as a list ('a dread, a darkness, great') or as 'a dread of great darkness' or 'a great, dark dread'. The English keeps the apposition: 'dread, a great darkness'. The lexicon lists no sense for גָּדוֹל that matches 'great' (it lists 'loud', 'do great things', 'greatness'), so I give none at 15:12.11.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the dread and darkness are an allusion to the troubles and darkness of the exiles; a reading of the vision, not of the wording.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'the sun was about to set' is a sign that Abram took all these on one day, since he woke from the prophetic vision. The English reads the sunset as the same day's setting.

- יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע is the infinitive absolute before the finite verb of the same root: 'you shall surely know'.
- The accents join the clause 'your offspring will be a sojourner in a land not theirs' and then close it at the zaqef; the next verbs are a new clause, whose subject shifts without being named.
- The perfects with wāw (וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ) continue the future: 'and they will serve, and will afflict'.
- אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה is the number of years in apposition: the period comes at the end.

Note: In וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ אֹתָם the subject and object are not named; 'they will serve them … and they will oppress them' keeps that ambiguity, where 'they' is the people of the land. Whether 'four hundred years' counts the whole period or only the oppression is also open: Rashi counts four hundred years from the birth of Isaac, and Ibn Ezra counts from the day of the vision; the English keeps the number without fixing its starting point. Rashi's point that 'a land not theirs' is not only Egypt is followed.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: the four hundred years run from the birth of Isaac until Israel left Egypt (Isaac sixty at Jacob's birth, Jacob 130 at the descent, 210 years in Egypt), and he shows that the time in Egypt alone was less. The English does not fix the starting point.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: it does not say 'in the land of Egypt' but 'a land not theirs': from Isaac's birth Abraham, Isaac and Jacob all sojourned in the land. The English 'a land not theirs' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the גֵּר is like the grain cut from the branch, as the אֶזְרָח is the man with a family, like the branch attached to the root. The English takes the ordinary sense 'sojourner'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the four hundred years run 'to the end of this term from today'. The English leaves the starting point open.

Grammar:

- The object וְגַם אֶת־הַגּוֹי is placed first, before the subject אָנֹכִי; this puts the weight on the nation that will be judged.
- דָּן is a participle ('judging'), which here gives a near-future sense: 'I am about to judge'.
- אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ is a relative clause without a resumptive pronoun: 'the nation that they will serve'.
- בִּרְכֻשׁ גָּדוֹל, 'with great property', looks ahead to the Exodus, and the verb יֵצְאוּ 'they will go out' is the verb later used of it.

Note: The word order of the Hebrew puts the object first, and the English follows it. Rashi takes גַּם to add the four kingdoms to Egypt; this is recorded rather than adopted. Ibn Ezra's gloss for אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ ('so that they have servants') fits the plain sense of the nation as master.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'also' adds the four kingdoms, since they too will be destroyed for enslaving Israel. The English keeps 'also' without naming the kingdoms.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: the judgment is 'by ten plagues'. A more specific reading than the Hebrew states; recorded.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בִּרְכֻשׁ גָּדוֹל is 'with great wealth', as it says 'and they stripped Egypt' (Exod 12). The English follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹדוּ means that the nation will have servants, i.e. the nation that they will serve. The English follows.

- וְאַתָּה with the separate pronoun contrasts Abram with his descendants, who suffer in the previous verses.
- תָּבוֹא אֶל־אֲבֹתֶיךָ is a euphemism for death, 'come to your fathers' (Ibn Ezra).
- תִּקָּבֵר is a Nifal, 'you will be buried', passive of קבר.
- בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה means 'in a good old age'; the adjective follows the noun and agrees in gender.

Note: תָּבוֹא is rendered 'you will go': Hebrew בוא is 'come' or 'go in', and English 'go to your fathers' is the usual idiom for death. The lexicon sense used is Qal 4, 'go'. Rashi's comments on the repentance of Terah and Ishmael use the verse for homily and do not bear on the plain sense.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'and you will come [to your fathers]': and you will not see all this. The emphatic וְאַתָּה sets Abram apart from the exile foretold for his offspring. The English 'As for you' follows.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: Terah served idols, so 'to your fathers' teaches that Terah repented; a homily.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: 'a good old age' is a promise that Ishmael will repent and Esau will not go to bad ways in Abraham's days; a homily on the timing of Abraham's death.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'come to your fathers' is a figure for death, 'the way of all the earth'. The English 'go to your fathers' follows.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בְּשָׁלוֹם means 'in honour, and not as your offspring'. The English keeps 'in peace', which can bear that sense.

Grammar:

- וְדוֹר רְבִיעִי is a singular noun with a plural verb (יָשׁוּבוּ): the 'generation' stands for its members.
- הֵנָּה ('here') appears twice in the verse, once of place (in the land) and once of time (up to now: עַד־הֵנָּה).
- The reason clause כִּי לֹא־שָׁלֵם עֲוֺן הָאֱמֹרִי states why the promise is delayed: the Amorites' guilt is not yet full.
- The etnaḥta on הֵנָּה ends the first half, the return; the second half gives the reason.

Note: I follow Rashi in taking דּוֹר as 'generation' (BDB sense 2), so four generations: Jacob and his sons into Egypt, then the fourth generation returns. Ibn Ezra reads דּוֹר as 'a dwelling' of the lifetime of a person and also counts to the fourth after the sojourn; I record this. The Amorites are a collective singular; the word 'iniquity' is kept, and not softened to 'guilt'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: after they go down to Egypt there will be three generations there and in the fourth they return to this land (Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, and Caleb son of Hezron came into the land). The English 'fourth generation' follows.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: Israel's return is delayed because God does not exact payment from a nation until its measure is full, as in 'in measure, when you send her away, you contend with her' (Isa 27). The English follows.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: most commentators err about 'generation'; דּוֹר means a dwelling (as in 'to dwell in the tents of wickedness', Ps 84:11), measured by the span of a person's life, long or short. The fourth after they are strangers in Egypt: Kohath, Amram, Moses and Aaron, and their sons returned to Canaan.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'iniquity' is as in 'my iniquity is greater than I can bear' (Gen 4:13). The Amorite is named because of his strength; Moses killed the great kings, who were Amorite kings, and the five kings of the Amorites gathered against Joshua.

Apparatus:

- Ibn Ezra rejects deriving הָאֱמֹרִי from אמר ('to say'); the Amorites are named for their strength, as in Amos 2:9.

Grammar:

- וַיְהִי opens a time clause; both clauses that follow put the subject before the verb: הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בָּאָה, וַעֲלָטָה הָיָה (Rashi: וַיְהִי דָּבָר זֶה, 'and this thing happened').
- בָּאָה is accented on the first syllable (zaqef qaton on a mil'el form), so it is a perfect, 'had come', not a participle 'is coming' (Rashi, Radak).
- הָיָה is masculine although עֲלָטָה is feminine; the clause is impersonal: 'it was thick darkness'.
- תַּנּוּר and לַפִּיד are in the construct before עָשָׁן and אֵשׁ; Radak reads עָשָׁן as an adjective ('a smoky furnace').
- אֲשֶׁר עָבַר is singular after two nouns. That fits one apparition, a smoking furnace with the torch inside it (Ibn Ezra, Ramban); Radak has the torch pass between the pieces.
- The etnaḥta on הָיָה divides the scene (sunset, darkness) from the vision.

Note: Followed Rashi (and Radak) on בָּאָה: a perfect, the sun had set. Ibn Ezra agrees: in v. 12 (לָבוֹא) the sun had not yet set, and here it has. עֲלָטָה is a thick darkness. The verb עָבַר is singular: for Ibn Ezra and Ramban one figure passes, a furnace with a torch of fire inside it; Radak has the torch pass, to confirm the covenant of the next verse.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: ויהי השמש באה is like 'and it came to pass, they were emptying their sacks' (Gen 42:35), i.e. 'and this thing happened': a circumstantial clause.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: השמש באה means שָׁקְעָה, the sun set.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: ועלטה היה means the day grew dark.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the furnace of smoke hints that the kingdoms will fall into Gehenna; homiletic, not the plain sense of the words.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the accent being on the upper (first) syllable, בָּאָה is perfect, 'had already come'; with the accent below it would be a participle 'was setting', but the passage of the furnace came afterwards, so the sun had already set. The same holds for words like בָּא, קָם, שָׁב.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: 'at first' (v. 12) the sun had not yet set, as לָבוֹא is written there; here בָּאָה means that it has set. He agrees with Rashi.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: עלטה is darkness, as in Ezekiel; either the night was clouded or it means the time after the visible light in the clouds.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: it was in the likeness of a furnace from which smoke rises, with a torch of fire in it.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: בין הגזרים is בין הבתרים, 'between the pieces', and this is the oath, like 'the calf they cut in two' (Jer 34:18); hence 'On that day the LORD made a covenant' follows.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the smoking furnace is the cloud and fog of Sinai and the torch the fire from which Israel heard the words; the Presence itself passed between the pieces, which is the covenant.
- Radak (records): Radak: the passing between the pieces signals the covenant-making, as parties passed between halved animals; the torch stands for God, and also hints at the fire that will consume the nations of the exile.

Apparatus:

- גֶּזֶר: the plural גְּזָרִים occurs elsewhere only in Ps 136:13; Ibn Ezra and Radak equate it with the בְּתָרִים of v. 10.

- לֵאמֹר (ל + infinitive construct of אמר) introduces the speech; לְזַרְעֲךָ stands before its verb, which puts the weight on 'to your offspring'.
- נָתַתִּי is a perfect of certainty: the promise is spoken as already given (Rashi: the saying of the Holy One is as if done).
- מִנְּהַר מִצְרַיִם עַד־הַנָּהָר הַגָּדֹל: the boundaries are given as two rivers; נְהַר־פְּרָת stands in apposition to 'the great river'.
- יְהֹוָה is read 'the LORD' (decisions).

Note: 'I have given' keeps the perfect. נְהַר מִצְרַיִם is rendered 'the river of Egypt' because Ibn Ezra identifies it as the Shiḥor and not the Nile (היאור); the Hebrew word is unchanged. The token אֶת־ at 15:18.5 is parsed as a preposition (BDB a.gn.aa, 'with'): kept as given, the sense list of that entry has 'together with' but Abram here is the party with whom the covenant is cut, so 'with' is the reading.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: לזרעך נתתי, the saying of the Holy One is as if it were already done.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: it is called 'great' because it adjoins the Land of Israel, although it is last of the four rivers from Eden ('and the fourth river is the Perat'); proverb: 'a king's servant is a king'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: נהר מצרים is the Shiḥor and not the Nile (היאור).
- Ramban (records): Ramban: God promised Abraham the land several times, each time adding to it; here the borders and the ten nations are named and a covenant is made so that sin will not annul the gift. The earlier promises say אֶתֵּן (future), but at the covenant he says נָתַתִּי, for the covenant is made on a gift already given; Rashi's 'as if done' is not needed here.
- Radak (follows): Radak: נתתי means 'I have already given them by my word, which stands.'

Apparatus:

- Ibn Ezra: 'river of Egypt' = the Shiḥor, not the Nile.
- Onkelos: לִבְנָךְ יְהָבִית, 'to your son(s) I have given'; 'the great river' as נַהֲרָא רַבָּא.

**the Kenites, the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites;**

- The verse continues the list of objects of נָתַתִּי (v. 18); each name is a singular gentilic with the article, read collectively.
- Each name after the first takes וְאֵת, 'and (object marker)'.
- The pashta and zaqef qaton divide the three names; the silluq closes the verse.

- Rashi (records): Rashi: there are ten nations here but only seven were given; the three, Kenite, Kenizzite and Kadmonite, correspond to Edom, Moab and Ammon and will be an inheritance in the future (Gen. Rabbah).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: these are from the sons of Canaan, and they have two names (each of the three was also known by another name).
- Radak (records): Radak: the Kenites are named after the city they first lived in, Kayin (Judg 4:11), perhaps named after its builder; the family intermarried with the tribe of Judah, with the families of Rechab (1 Chr 2:55).
- Radak (records): Radak, continuing 15:19:1: perhaps the Kenite named here is a different people from the Kenite clan he has just described; but Onkelos renders it שַׁלְמָאֵי, as he renders the Kenite of Num 24:21.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos: שַׁלְמָאֵי, קְנִזָּאֵי, קַדְמוֹנָאֵי.

- הַחִתִּי, הַפְּרִזִּי are singular collective gentilics; הָרְפָאִים is plural.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the Rephaim are the land of Og, of which it is said 'that too is called the land of Rephaim' (Deut 3:13).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: this is the 'land of Rephaim' of Deut 3:13. Do not wonder that the Canaanite and the Jebusite follow: the seven nations are all Canaanites, Canaan had eleven sons, and after six are named 'the Canaanite' covers the rest; here the nations are listed one by one, elsewhere as a whole, as 'Judah and Israel' (1 Kgs 4:20) although Judah is part of Israel.
- Radak (records): Radak: the Hivite is not named in this list; perhaps it is the Rephaim that is named (the comment continues at radak:15:20:2).
- Radak (records): Radak, ending 15:20:1: the Hivite, missing from the list, is perhaps 'the Rephaim that he named' (הָרְפָאִים שֶׁזָּכַר).

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders הרפאים as גִּבָּרָאֵי, 'the mighty'.

Grammar:

- אִבָּנֶה is a Niphal imperfect 1cs of בנה (a III-ה verb): the dagesh in ב is the assimilated נ of the Niphal (from *ʾinbāneh). The sound-play with בֵּן 'son' is the point.
- בֹּא־נָא is a polite imperative: 'come now, please'.
- שָׁמַע לְקוֹל, 'to listen to the voice of', means to obey.
- The zaqef on מִלֶּדֶת and the etnahta on מִמֶּנָּה mark the two halves of her speech.

Note: The English keeps 'built up' so that the connection with 'son' is preserved in the notes. 'Listened to' keeps the idiom; 'obeyed' is the sense.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the verse teaches that one who has no children is not built up but ruined. This supports 'built up' as the metaphor.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'I shall be built up' through the merit of bringing my rival into my house. This reading of the cause is recorded, not adopted.
- Rashi (records): Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: 'to the voice of Sarai' means to the holy spirit in her. Recorded as homiletic.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אִבָּנֶה is from the word בֵּן 'son'; or else the son is called בֵּן because he is like a building (בניין) of which the father is the foundation, בֵּן having lost the ה of בנה. The English 'built up' keeps the building image and the notes give the link with 'son'.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra glosses וַיִּשְׁמַע אַבְרָם as 'he said so to her', that is, he assented to her. The English keeps 'listened to', the ordinary meaning of the idiom.

Apparatus:

- Ramban: Abram did not seek to be built up from Hagar himself; he consented only to do Sarai's will, and took no step without her (not normative).
- Radak: the plan seemed right to Abram, since he thought that, Sarai having ceased to bear, the promised seed would come through Hagar; he did not wait for God's word (not normative).

| אִישָׁ֖הּ | her husband | אִישׁ | אישׁ | noun (common, masculine, singular, construct) + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, feminine, singular) |  |
| ל֥וֹ | to him | ל: to, for |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) |  |

Grammar:

- Two wayyiqtols, וַתִּקַּח and וַתִּתֵּן, carry the narrative; the intervening phrases are all attached to the first.
- מִקֵּץ is a construct 'from the end of'; לְשֶׁבֶת is an infinitive construct of ישב with ל.
- The accents separate 'ten years' (zaqef) from 'of Abram's dwelling' (tipha).

Note: The English ties the ten years to Abram's dwelling in the land of Canaan, as Rashi reads it (years outside the land do not count). Ibn Ezra takes the verse as a support (asmakhta) for the rule of ten years; he says nothing about where they were counted. 'Took' is kept as plain narrative; Rashi's 'took her with words' is recorded.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: she took her by words, saying 'happy are you to cleave to such a holy body'. The English says only 'took'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: ten years is the fixed term for a woman who has lived ten years without bearing to her husband, after which he must marry another. This explains the mention of ten years.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the verse teaches that residence outside the land does not count toward the ten years. The English ties the ten years to dwelling 'in the land of Canaan'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: the ancients taught that a man should not stay with his wife more than ten years if she does not bear; the verse is a support (asmakhta) for this and it is good. The ten years are taken as significant.

Apparatus:

- Ramban accepts that years outside the land do not count, but rejects Rashi's reason (the promise 'I will make you a great nation'): the rule holds for everyone, and a couple who come to the land are given ten years from their arrival, as Abram and Sarai counted (not normative).

- וַתֵּרֶא כִּי הָרָתָה: ראה + כִּי 'saw that', with the perfect הָרָתָה giving the state seen.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: she conceived from the first union. The English 'went in ... and she conceived' fits this.
- Rashi (records): Rashi, from Bereshit Rabbah: Hagar said that Sarai's inner life did not match her outward show of righteousness, since she had not conceived in all those years. A homiletic reading of the cause, recorded.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the 'hidden letter' under the dagesh in וַתֵּקַל shows that it is of the Niphal stem. The pack parses it as Qal and the English reads the sense the same way.

Apparatus:

- Radak: Hagar thought that since Abraham's seed would come from her she would be the mistress, so she ignored Sarai's commands.

- The yod of וּבֵינֶיךָ carries puncta extraordinaria (WLC note 4); Radak takes it as a full spelling, and Rashi as a hint at a miscarriage.

- Hagar is addressed by name and by her status.

Note: The question is rhetorical: the angel knows the answer and uses it to open a conversation. The apparatus keeps the Ibn Ezra and Radak points on form.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the angel knew; he asks in order to open a conversation with her. 'Where did you come from' means, what place can you say you come from.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: אֵי is like אַיֵּה, as in אֵי הֶבֶל; the sense is 'from what place did you come'.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the resh has patah because of the following guttural, as in other forms. This concerns the vocalization only.

Apparatus:

- Radak: the opening וַיֹּאמַר has patah with revia as if at a pause (not normative).

**The messenger of the LORD said to her, "Go back to your mistress, and submit to her authority."**

- שׁוּבִי is a feminine singular imperative; the final -י marks the feminine.
- הִתְעַנִּי is hitpael, 'humble yourself, submit'; it recalls וַתְּעַנֶּהָ (16:6), where Sarai afflicted her.
- תַּחַת יָדֶיהָ, literally 'under her hands', means in her power.
- The etnaḥta falls on גְּבִרְתֵּךְ and divides the command into 'return' and 'submit'.

Note: מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה is 'messenger of the LORD'; the pack's sense 3 (theophanic angel) is followed. Rashi's note that a different angel spoke each time is a homily and is kept in commentary.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: a different angel was sent for each speech, which is why 'angel' is written each time; a homiletic reading that does not alter the plain sense.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the order to return and submit hints that Hagar's line would never go free of Sarah's; not adopted in the English.
- Radak (records): Radak: the threefold 'and he said' either intensifies, or marks three subjects, or (midrash) three angels.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'bear the affliction she inflicts, for it is good for you to live with Abraham, whose merit will multiply your seed.' Supports 'submit'.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos renders 'return to your mistress and be subject under her hands' (ואשתעבדי), agreeing with 'submit'.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno compares the idiom to 'shoot, and he shot' (2 Kings 13:17): the command shapes the future. Not for the plain sense.

- וְיֹלַדְתְּ is an unusual form, perhaps a blend of perfect and participle; here it is future, 'you will bear'.
- וְקָרָאת keeps the older ending -ת of the 2fs; it is read as a command, 'you are to call'.
- הִנָּךְ has the 2fs suffix; the final ךְ is feminine.
- יִשְׁמָעֵאל, 'God hears', has a silent א in its spelling; Ibn Ezra says the aleph is dropped in pronunciation to ease the tongue.

- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'when you return you will conceive'; the same words הִנָּךְ הָרָה are said to Manoah's wife (Judg 13:5), who had not yet conceived. Not adopted: 16:4 says Hagar had already conceived (Rashi's reading presupposes the midrash that she lost that pregnancy).
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וְיֹלַדְתְּ means 'and you are bearing' (like יוֹלֶדֶת), as in 'inhabitant of Lebanon' with a final -ת (Jer 22:23). The English takes it as future-near, 'you will bear'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וְקָרָאת שְׁמוֹ is a command, as in 'and you shall call his name Isaac' (17:19). Hence 'you are to name him'.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הִנָּךְ is the feminine, for הֵן is a particle like 'with', its pattern like עִמָּךְ; so 'here you are'.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: the aleph of the name is quiescent, not pronounced, to ease the tongue; a note on pronunciation, not on the sense.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the messenger commands Hagar to name him Ishmael; she tells Abram, who confirms the name. Rashi: Abram named him by the holy spirit.
- Radak (follows): Radak: she already knew she was pregnant; the opening phrase introduces the good news.
- Radak (records): Radak: the form is a blend of perfect and participle.
- Radak (follows): Radak: here the ת of וְקָרָאת marks the second person feminine, addressed to Hagar; in וְקָרָאת אֶתְכֶם (Deut 31:29), by contrast, the ת marks the third person feminine, like the ה of וְקָרְאָה.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'to your affliction' means the cry that she uttered in her affliction.
- Radak (records): Radak: עָנְיֵךְ also means 'your cry', like וַיַּעַן אִיּוֹב.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'the LORD has received your prayer' (צְלוֹתִיךְ), taking affliction as the cry in it.

- פֶּרֶא אָדָם is a construct: 'wild ass of man'. Ibn Ezra reports other readings: free among men (Job 39:5), or two items, 'wild ass and man'.
- יָדוֹ בַכֹּל, 'his hand in everything', is read by Rashi as a robber; יַד כֹּל בּוֹ, 'everyone's hand against him', answers it.
- עַל־פְּנֵי is 'in the face of, over against'; 25:18 uses נָפַל in the same phrase.
- The etnaḥta on בּוֹ divides the verse after the double saying about the hand.

Note: 'Wild ass of a man' keeps the construct. Rashi and Ibn Ezra differ on 'upon the face of all his brothers': Rashi sees a great offspring; Ibn Ezra identifies the brothers as the sons of Keturah. The English 'over against' is neutral to both.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: he loves the wilds, hunting animals, like 'he dwelt in the wilderness and became an archer' (21:20).
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: יָדוֹ בַכֹּל, 'a robber'.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: everyone hates him and provokes him; hence 'everyone's hand against him'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi (Gen. Rabbah): 'will dwell upon the face of all his brothers' means that his seed will be great.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: free among men, as in Job 39:5; no stranger of his family will rule him. Others: 'wild ass and man'. His own view: among men he is like a wild ass who overcomes all by strength, and later everyone's hand is against him; so too Daniel (the fourth beast).
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the brothers are the sons of Keturah; 25:18 says the same, and Midianites are called Ishmaelites.
- Ramban (records): Ramban cites Rashi and Ibn Ezra; his own view: 'wild ass of a man' is a construct, a wilderness-man who preys and is preyed on, which refers to his descendants' wars with all peoples.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'he' means he and his seed.
- Radak (follows): Radak: a man of the wilderness like a wild ass, for most Ishmaelites dwell in tents in the wilderness (Jer 3:2).
- Radak (follows): Radak: a wilderness man will lay hands on neighbours and they on him; still he does not flee but dwells before them (25:18).
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos: 'rebellious among men; he will need all, and men's hands will need him; he will dwell over all his brothers'.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: a wild ass by temperament from his Egyptian mother, a wild ass in the wilderness, and a man through his father.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: the ḥaṭef qamets shows it is a noun: 'a God of seeing, who sees the humiliation of the humble'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'have I even here in the wilderness seen the Lord's messenger, after seeing them at Abraham's house?' - an expression of amazement. The English keeps the participle sense.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: רֳאִי has the pattern of the noun עֳנִי in רָאָה עֳנִי (Lam 3:1); the sense is 'God of vision' (אֵל מַרְאֶה).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: הֲלֹם is like 'here' (1 Sam 10:22): have I seen the LORD's angel here, after He saw my affliction, for He is always my seer.
- Radak (records): Radak: she first took him for a man; when he vanished she knew he was a messenger, and named him 'God of sight'.
- Radak (follows): Radak: רֳאִי is of the same pattern as עֳנִי (Lam 3:1).
- Radak (records): Radak: she said in her heart: a man is seen after he leaves, but I did not see even here, so this was an angel.
- Radak (follows): Radak: רֹאִי means 'the one who sees me'.
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos: 'you are the God who sees all, for she said: have I indeed here (seen) after He revealed Himself to me?'
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: 'calling the name of the LORD' is prayer, which begins with praise.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: a God of seeing everywhere, not only in Abraham's house.

Apparatus:

- Hebrew difficulty: 'after my seer' (אַחֲרֵי רֹאִי) is retained; see note.

- וַיְהִי with a time clause (בֶּן־תִּשְׁעִים שָׁנָה וְתֵשַׁע שָׁנִים) sets the scene: Abram is ninety-nine, thirteen years after 16:16.
- The etnaḥta on שָׁנִים closes the age clause; the verse then divides at זָקֵף קָטָן on שַׁדַּי between the self-introduction and the two commands.
- הִתְהַלֵּךְ is Hithpael imperative: continuous walking to and fro; וֶהְיֵה is a second imperative joined by ו, not a result clause.
- Rashi and Targum Onkelos take הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי as "serve before me" (פְּלַח קֳדָמַי).

Rashi derives שַׁדַּי from דַּי "enough" (there is sufficiency in my divinity for every creature); Ibn Ezra takes it as an adjectival title meaning "mighty"; Ramban and Radak derive it from שׁדד "overpower". The English does not choose among these. תמים is rendered "whole" (complete, without lack), which covers Rashi's "whole in all my trials" and Ibn Ezra's "do not ask why circumcision".

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: שַׁדַּי means "I am the one in whose divinity there is enough (דַּי) for every creature", so walk before me and I will be a god and patron to you; wherever it occurs it means "his enough" as the context requires. The English keeps the name untranslated and records this derivation.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: as Targum פְּלַח קֳדָמַי, cleave to my service. The English "walk before me" keeps the idiom, with this sense in the notes.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: this is another command after a command, be whole in all my trials; by midrash, walk before me in the commandment of circumcision, since while the foreskin is on you you are blemished before me. The English follows the plain sense "whole".
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: שַׁדַּי is an adjectival title (שם התואר) meaning 'mighty' (תקיף), as in כְּקוֹל שַׁדַּי (Ezekiel 1:24) and Job 22:25; many derive it from שׁוֹדֵד, one who overpowers. The name is mentioned here so that Abram would fear and circumcise himself. The English keeps the name El Shaddai untranslated, as the decisions require, and records this reading.
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra on וֶהְיֵה תָמִים: "that you not ask why circumcision". A real alternative that the English "be whole" leaves open.

Apparatus:

- No variant readings in the pack. MAM writes the divine name with holem (יְהֹוָה); the morphology gives יְהוָה.

- Both verbs are cohortatives (אֶתְּנָה, אַרְבֶּה) and express the speaker's resolve.
- וְאֶתְּנָה follows the two imperatives of verse 1. A ו-cohortative after an imperative often gives the purpose or the consequence ('walk … be whole, and I will set'). Rashi's 'by means of this commandment' reads the covenant as following on the command.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: a covenant of love and the covenant of the land, to give it to you by means of this commandment. This bears on what the covenant contains, not on the translation of the words.
- Radak (follows): Radak: do not think that circumcision will weaken your seed; I will multiply you very much, and the doubling of מְאֹד multiplies the multiplying.

| אִתּ֛וֹ | with him — אִתּוֹ: with, not "to" | אֵת |  | preposition + suffix (pronominal, 3rd person, masculine, singular) | 1 |
| אֱלֹהִ֖ים | God | אֱלֹהִים | אלה | noun (common, masculine, plural, absolute) | 4 |
| לֵאמֹֽר׃ | saying — לֵאמֹר: infinitive construct introducing speech | ל: to, for + אָמַר | אמר | preposition + verb (qal, infinitive construct) | Qal 1 |

Grammar:

- פָּנִים is a plural noun used of one face; עַל־פָּנָיו 'on his face' is the idiom for prostration.
- וַיְדַבֵּר is a Piel wayyiqtol. The Piel is the ordinary stem of דבר 'speak'; it does not mark a conversation as opposed to a command.
- אִתּוֹ is the preposition אֵת 'with' with a suffix, not the object marker.
- The subject is אֱלֹהִים, though verse 1 names יְהוָה as the one who appeared: the speaker is the same.
- לֵאמֹר 'saying' is an infinitive construct with ל and introduces direct speech.

Note: Rashi reads the fall as fear of the divine presence; Radak and Sforno as prostration of thanks for the covenant; Ramban as preparing himself for prophecy. The English keeps "fell on his face" without choosing.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: from fear of the divine presence; before he was circumcised he had no strength to stand while the holy spirit stood over him. The English keeps the physical action only.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: to focus his mind for prophecy, as in Numbers 16:22.
- Radak (records): Radak: he bowed and gave thanks for the covenant God said he would set.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: to accept and give thanks for the covenant mentioned.

**As for me, here is my covenant with you: you shall become the father of a multitude of nations.**

Grammar:

- אֲנִי stands first for emphasis, "as for me", with הִנֵּה calling attention to the covenant.
- אִתָּךְ ends in pausal -ךְ (qamets under the tav under etnaḥta); this is the masculine pausal form of אִתְּךָ.
- וְהָיִיתָ is weqatal, continuing the promise: "you shall become".
- The pairing אַב הֲמוֹן is the explanation of the new name in verse 5.

Note: The morphology table labels the suffix of אִתָּךְ as 2nd person feminine. I keep the data but note it as the pausal masculine form (cf. Genesis 17:4 context, addressee Abram). הֲמוֹן is chosen as "multitude" (sense 3). Ramban: this is the covenant of circumcision, as the text goes on to say.

Commentary:

- Ramban (records): Ramban: this is the covenant of circumcision, as explained later ("this is the sign of the covenant"), and after the covenant you will be father of many nations.
- Radak (follows): Radak: as I said to you El Shaddai, trust what I said; my covenant is with you from now, and you will be father of a multitude of nations, not of one only.

Apparatus:

- The pack parses אִתָּךְ as 2nd person feminine; kept as data, flagged in the note.

Grammar:

- Niphal יִקָּרֵא governs אֶת־שִׁמְךָ: an object marker after a passive, which Radak compares with יֵחָלֵק אֶת־הָאָרֶץ.
- The explanation of the name is in כִּי אַב־הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם נְתַתִּיךָ; the wordplay is אַבְרָהָם with אַב הֲמוֹן.
- נְתַתִּיךָ is qatal: God has already established Abraham as father of many nations (Sforno: the name starts today because he is already so).
- The disjunctive tevir on עוֹד and the etnaḥta on אַבְרָם mark the first clause.

Note: Per the decisions, the meaning of the name goes in the notes and not in the English line. Rashi reads כִּי אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם as a notarikon (abbreviation) of the name אַבְרָהָם: the resh, which belonged to the name when he was father only of Aram, was not removed now that he is father of the whole world. Ibn Ezra explains the resh, which אַב הֲמוֹן does not account for, as coming from אַבִּיר: 'mighty one of a multitude of nations'. He also says the change of name does not take a letter away but only adds one, the he.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi: כִּי אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם is a notarikon of the name אַבְרָהָם. The resh, which belonged to the name when he was father only of Aram, his homeland, was not removed now that he is father of the whole world. Even the yod taken from Sarai's name complained before the Shekhinah until it was added to Joshua's name (Numbers 13:16).
- Ibn Ezra (records): Ibn Ezra: the resh in אַבְרָהָם, which is extra beyond אַב הֲמוֹן, stands for אַבִּיר, so the name means 'mighty one of a multitude of nations'. The change does not take a letter away from his name but only adds one. The English line does not render the name; the gloss gives the text's own explanation, and this reading is recorded in the note.
- Ibn Ezra (not-applicable): Ibn Ezra: שָׂרָה is a general title, not like שָׂרַי, and praise to God that he commanded circumcision before Sarah conceived, so that the seed be holy. This bears on 17:15, not on the English of this verse.
- Radak (follows): Radak: אֶת after a Niphal is for added clarity, as in Numbers 26:55; also the Rabbis say a change of name tears up a person's sentence.
- Sforno (follows): Sforno: "from now" on.

- Sforno (records): Sforno: to unite my name upon you directly, as on all eternal things; through keeping the covenant he and his seed will be eternal.

- מְגֻרֶיךָ is plural, 'your sojournings': the places where Abraham has lived as a גֵּר, a resident alien.
- לְךָ carries telisha gedola, a disjunctive accent written on the first letter of the word and repeated here on the stressed syllable. It marks a minor pause, not emphasis. The geresh on אַחֲרֶיךָ, the revia on מְגֻרֶיךָ and the etnaḥta on עוֹלָם divide the recipients, the land and the term.
- וְהָיִיתִי לָהֶם לֵאלֹהִים repeats the formula of verse 7 (לִהְיוֹת לְךָ לֵאלֹהִים), now with the plural 'to them'.

Note: Rashi: there I will be your God; one who lives outside the land is like one who has no God (a homily). Radak: even if they go into exile, the possession is everlasting and they will return. Sforno: so that you can do my will in it.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: and there I will be God to you; one who lives outside the land is as one who has no God. This is a homily on the second clause and does not change the plain sense.
- Radak (records): Radak: even though they will be exiled for a time, the land is an everlasting possession and they will return to it.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: "to you" completes the clause; I will be God to you.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: so that you can do my will in the land, as in Psalm 105:44-45.

- Radak (records): Radak: a Niphal infinitive, 'every male shall be circumcised'; or a noun with added he.

- The zaqef gadol on וּנְמַלְתֶּם and the etnaḥta on עָרְלַתְכֶם close the command; the sign clause follows.

Both read it as active, 'you shall circumcise', though the pack parses it Niphal; the English follows them. - Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וּנְמַלְתֶּם is like וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם, and the nun is a root letter, as in לֹא יָדוֹן רוּחִי (Gen 6:3) beside נִדְנֶה (Dan 7:15).
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the sign serves as a memorial, as tzitzit and tefillin do, but it is the strongest of them.
- Sforno (not-applicable): Sforno: a constant reminder to walk in His ways, like a master's seal on his slave.

- The verb stands first and the subject follows: 'must be circumcised, the one born ...'.
- וְהָיְתָה is feminine because its subject בְּרִיתִי is feminine; the weqatal carries on from the command.
- In לִבְרִית עוֹלָם the preposition לְ marks what the covenant becomes, 'as an everlasting covenant'; בְּרִית עוֹלָם is a construct pair, 'a covenant of perpetuity'.

Note: The English follows Rashi's view that the doubling is deliberate: it includes a house-born slave circumcised later than the eighth day. This bears on the sense of the doubled form, which the English renders by 'must'.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: here the verse doubles the verb and does not say 'at eight days', to teach that there is a house-born slave who is circumcised after eight days (see Shabbat 135b).
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: this is said to Abraham, that his household be circumcised with him, since two faiths cannot coexist in one house.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the slaves, house-born and bought, are included in 'your flesh', since they are theirs.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: בָּשָׂר is a euphemism for the organ of generation in the holy language, so the sign points to the perpetuity of the covenant and its continuance through sons.

- נִכְרְתָה is a weqatal Niphal (passive of 'cut off'), feminine because נֶפֶשׁ is feminine.
- The fronted object אֶת־בְּרִיתִי before הֵפַר emphasizes what is broken.
- The suffix of מֵעַמֶּיהָ is feminine singular agreeing with נֶפֶשׁ, and עַמִּים is plural: 'from her peoples'.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: here the verse teaches that circumcision is at the place that distinguishes male from female.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'who does not circumcise' applies once he has reached the age of liability; his father is not liable to kareth, but transgresses a positive commandment.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: 'cut off' means he goes childless and dies before his time (Shabbat, cited as 24).
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: יִמּוֹל is of the pattern יִפְעֹל, like יִדֹּר נֶדֶר (Num 30:3), from וּנְמַלְתֶּם: if he is of age and does not circumcise himself, he is liable to kareth at the hands of heaven, since a small boy's duty rests on the father. Those who think an uncircumcised child has no share in the world to come are wrong: נֶפֶשׁ means 'person', a body with a soul. Kareth is either death before fifty-two or the cutting off of his name at the death of his seed, hence 'from his kin'.

Apparatus:

- Variants: none noted in the pack.

- Rashi (records): Rashi: שָׂרָה is 'a plain name', that she be 'sarah' over all (b. Berakhot 13). The reading is kept as the reason for the change; the English line only states it.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: only the husband calls the wife by name; the wife does not call the husband by name out of respect. This explains why Abraham alone is addressed; it does not change the English.
- Radak (records): Radak: כִּי שָׂרָה שְׁמָהּ means 'shall be her name', as in 17:5, and others will call her so once Abraham does.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos renders the verse closely, 'do not call her name Sarai, for Sarah is her name'.

- The etnaḥta on בֵּן separates the gift of the son from the second blessing.
- The pashta on וּבֵרַכְתִּיהָ is written twice because pashta is postpositive: the second sign stands on the last letter, and the first marks the stressed syllable (-תִּי-), which is not final.

These readings are kept in the commentary entries and not added to the English. מִמֶּנָּה, 'from her', is kept as in the Hebrew.

- Rashi (records): Rashi: the first blessing is that she was restored to her youth (Gen 18:12 'I have had pleasure'). Kept as an interpretation; the English says only 'bless'.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: the second blessing is that she could nurse at Isaac's weaning feast, when she nursed the children brought by the other women. Kept as an interpretation.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: וְגַם נָתַתִּי is like נתתי כסף השדה (23:13); both perfects stand for the future. The English uses the future.
- Radak (records): Radak: the blessing is that she regains menstruation and the way of women, and then bears.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos has the same sequence of blessing, a son, nations and kings.

Grammar:

- וַיִּצְחָק, 'and he laughed', uses the root of the name יִצְחָק (17:19) before the name is given.
- הַלְּבֶן and הֲבַת open the questions with the interrogative ה; the second question continues with וְאִם ('and if / or').
- The etnaḥta on וַיִּצְחָק separates the act from what he said in his heart.
- יִוָּלֵד is Niphal ('be born') and תֵּלֵד is Qal ('bear'): the verbs are chosen to fit the subject.

Note: Whether וַיִּצְחָק is laughter of joy or of mockery is the ambiguity of the verse. Rashi (and Onkelos וַחֲדִי, Radak, Ramban) take Abraham's laughter as joy, in contrast to Sarah's laughter in 18:12 as scorn; the English keeps the plain word 'laughed' and the reading goes in the commentary. The questions express wonder, not doubt: Rashi reads the first as a question that affirms (has such kindness been done for anyone else?), and Ibn Ezra as amazement. בֶּן מֵאָה שָׁנָה, 'a son of a hundred years', is the idiom for a man a hundred years old and is rendered 'a man a hundred years old'; the subject of יִוָּלֵד, 'a child', and the object of תֵּלֵד are not in the Hebrew and are supplied by the English.

Commentary:

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַיִּצְחָק is the laughter of joy (Aramaic חֲדִי), unlike Sarah's laughter of mockery; Abraham believed and rejoiced, Sarah did not believe.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: some questions are affirmations (תְּמִיהוֹת שֶׁהֵן קַיָּמוֹת), as הֲנִגְלֹה נִגְלֵיתִי (1 Sam 2:27) and הֲרֹאֶה אַתָּה (Ezek 8:6), and this is one: Abraham said in his heart, 'Has such kindness been done for anyone else, as the Holy One does for me?'
- Rashi (follows): Rashi paraphrases the question: 'is Sarah, at ninety, fit to bear?' Although the early generations begot at five hundred, by Abraham's time lifespans had shrunk and weakness had come into the world, as the ten generations from Noah to Abraham, who had children at sixty and seventy, show.
- Ibn Ezra (follows): Ibn Ezra: Abraham marvels; the seed of an old man is cold, and the greater wonder is that a woman whose blood had stopped should bear.
- Ramban (follows): Ramban: the laughter is joy (Onkelos); the question is a wonder, not disbelief.
- Radak (follows): Radak: he rejoiced in his heart, not in mockery.

Apparatus:

- Radak: the wonder is not unbelief (Gen 15:6 'he believed in the LORD').

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'with him and not with others': Ishmael's sons and Keturah's sons are not in the covenant.
- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the repetition teaches that Isaac was holy from the womb; or a kal vahomer from the son of the mistress over the son of the maid. A derivation.
- Rashi (records): Rashi: the covenant of circumcision is entrusted to the descendants of Isaac.
- Ramban (records): Ramban: אֲבָל is like אֲבָל בֵּן אֵין לָהּ (2 Kings 4:14), 'only': only the son I announce, by Sarah, bears the covenant; Ishmael will be blessed with many descendants but not with the covenant.
- Radak (records): Radak: not this alone, but also Sarah your wife will bear a son.
- Radak (follows): Radak: the name Isaac is from 'you laughed'.

Apparatus:

- אֲבָל: Ramban and Radak read 'but, only', not 'truly'.

- הִנֵּה is 'look', calling attention to what is already done: בֵּרַכְתִּי is a perfect.
- The following weqatal verbs (וְהִפְרֵיתִי, וְהִרְבֵּיתִי) are future.
- בִּמְאֹד מְאֹד is a doubled adverb for the superlative.
- שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂר נְשִׂיאִם: the number precedes the noun. Rashi plays on נְשִׂיאִים 'clouds' (Prov 25:14) to say these princes will pass away like clouds; the plain sense 'princes, chieftains' stands.
- The zinor on וּלְיִשְׁמָעֵאל and the segolta, written twice, on שְׁמַעְתִּיךָ set off 'As for Ishmael, I have heard you' as the first division of the verse's first half.

Note: וּלְיִשְׁמָעֵאל שְׁמַעְתִּיךָ plays on the name יִשְׁמָעֵאל ('God hears'); the English cannot, so the point goes here. The verb שָׁמַע is Qal here, and the entry lists no Qal sense, so I give no sense for it. In the Hebrew שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר is a single number; the tokens for 'two' and 'ten' are combined in 'twelve'. נְשִׂיאִם is 'chieftains'; Rashi, citing נְשִׂיאִים וְרוּחַ (Prov 25:14), adds that these princes will pass away like clouds, a play on the word that leaves its sense in place.

Commentary:

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi: the twelve princes 'will pass away like clouds' (כַּעֲנָנִים יִכְלוּ), playing on נְשִׂיאִים 'clouds' in נְשִׂיאִים וְרוּחַ (Prov 25:14). He does not deny that they are princes; the comment is on their impermanence, a homily that leaves the plain sense 'chieftains' in place.
- Radak (follows): Radak: 'I have blessed him to be fruitful and multiply and to give him greatness.'
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: twelve will come from his sons as from Isaac.
- Radak (records): Radak: the blessing was by the angel who appeared to Hagar, 'I will bless Ishmael'; the covenant is kept with Isaac.
- Targum Onkelos (records): Onkelos: 'I have received your prayer'; so 'I have heard you' is rendered as 'I have heard your prayer'.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: 'from upon Abraham' is a clean way to speak of the Divine Presence; the righteous are the chariot of God (Genesis Rabbah).
- Ramban (records): Ramban: the same as Rashi, and the Genesis Rabbah reading that the patriarchs are the chariot.
- Radak (follows): Radak: until here he finished speaking to him that day.
- Radak (follows): Radak: his visible glory withdrew from him at the end of this prophecy.
- Targum Onkelos (follows): Onkelos: 'the glory of the LORD went up from Abraham'; the English keeps 'God'.
- Sforno (records): Sforno: the opposite of 'Cain went out from before the LORD' (4:16).

- The zaqef gadol after זָכָר sets 'every male' apart as a summary of the groups just listed, closed by the etnaḥta on אַבְרָהָם.
- כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר links the act to the command of 17:10-14: the obedience is exact.

Note: The Piel perfect דִּבֶּר after a narrative verb is rendered as a past perfect in English ('had spoken'). עֶצֶם is rendered 'very' following Rashi's sense of the same day, not a later one. Parse note: lemma מוּל; the pack lists root מול and no Qal sense number is separate from 'Qal'.

- Rashi (follows): Rashi: בּוֹ בַּיּוֹם שֶׁנִּצְטַוָּה, on the very day he was commanded; by day and not by night. He feared neither the gentiles nor the scoffers, and he did it openly so that his enemies and his generation could not say 'had we seen him, we would not have let him circumcise and keep the command of the Omnipresent'. The English 'on that very day' follows.
- Rashi (follows): Rashi: וַיָּמׇל is לְשׁוֹן וַיִּפְעַל, an active form, 'and he circumcised' (Abraham did the act), not a passive 'was circumcised'. The English 'he circumcised' follows.
- Radak (follows): Radak: כׇּל־זָכָר means both adults and children, 'every male' without age limit.
- Radak (not-applicable): Radak: the verse includes both cutting and uncovering (מִילָה וּפְרִיעָה); a legal point beyond the plain wording.

Apparatus:

- Onkelos renders מִקְנַת כַּסְפּוֹ as זְבִינֵי כַסְפֵּיהּ, 'those bought of his silver', as the English does.

- Radak (follows): Radak: the Nifal does not govern an object, so בְּשַׂר עׇרְלָתוֹ is explained as the part affected, as in 'torn of garments'.

- אֵת after the Nifal בְּהִמֹּלוֹ: the particle can stand before the noun with a passive verb (21:5 בְּהִוָּלֶד לוֹ אֵת יִצְחָק); Radak reads it here as 'from' (like מִן): circumcised from the flesh of his foreskin.
- The zaqef qaton on בְּהִמֹּלוֹ and tipḥa on אֵת set the object apart.

Rashi (from Bereshit Rabbah) explains why the particle is written here and not in 17:24: Ishmael needed uncovering (פְּרִיעָה) as well as cutting. The English is consistent with both and keeps them in the commentary.

Commentary:

- Rashi (records): Rashi (from Bereshit Rabbah): of Abraham 'et' is not said because he lacked only cutting of flesh, already pressed by use; Ishmael, a child, needed cutting and uncovering (פְּרִיעָה), hence אֵת. A homiletic reading of the particle; not adopted for the English.
- Radak (records): Radak: this verse is clearer than 17:24 because it writes אֵת: he was circumcised from (מִן) the flesh of his foreskin; אֵת is like מִן, as in הֵם יָצְאוּ אֶת הָעִיר (44:4) and חָלָה אֶת רַגְלָיו (1 Kgs 15:23). He also gives the midrash (Bereshit Rabbah 47) that Rashi gives, and draws from it that Abraham was commanded uncovering as well. The English 'in the flesh' does not take his 'from'.

Apparatus:

- Radak 17:25:1 notes that Ishmael's age is derived from Abraham being eighty-six at his birth, and that thirteen is the age of obligation.

- The pashta is written on the last letter of its word; עֶצֶם is stressed on the first syllable, so the pashta is repeated there to mark the stress.

- Rashi (not-applicable): Rashi's comment on נִמּוֹל אַבְרָהָם וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ is empty in the text provided (only a colon).

Apparatus:

- Ramban 17:26:1 disputes Rashi's note on the ages and says the verse tells the zeal of Abraham and his household.
